Child Poverty—Prime Minister’s Statements
1. Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE (Lea der of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister:
Does he stand by his statement that “there are more children in poverty than at some
point in the past”, and if s o, does he remain concerned ab out child poverty levels in
New Zealand?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, and I think all New Zealanders would
like to see child poverty levels lower. That is why the Government is investing hundreds
of millions of dollars in helping people to get off welfare benefits and into work,
because full-time paid work is the best wa y of lifting children out of poverty. That is
why we have borrowed billions of dollars to maintain income support for lower-income
families through a very significant recession. And that is why we are doing concrete
things to help families—for example, through  home insulation, free after-hours visits to
the general practitioner, increased fundi ng for early childhood education, increased
immunisation, rheumatic fever prevention, and the Children’s Action Plan. This
contrasts with the idea that you  can simply legislate to st op child poverty, which is the
Greens’ policy, or give well-off families $60 a week, which is Labour’s policy.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Given all of the above, does he agree with the Salvation Army,
which today said: “little has been achieved in reducing the rates and incidence of child
poverty and our housing situation appears to have got worse.”; if so, why?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, and just to quote from the report, under the heading
“Child poverty”, the very first thing it says is “Child poverty rates may be easing”. The
second thing it says, in the housing area, is  that a number of the indicators are
improving. The third thing is that this is the Government that has actually insulated
320,000 homes in New Zealand. This is also th e Government, I might add, that has put
in $1.8 billion when it comes to income-re lated rents and accommodation supplements.
By the way, the very report that the memb er is talking about was actually in the New
Zealand Herald today. I myself looked at it and th ere it was, under th e headline “Good
news on state of our nation”.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: What grade is the Prime Minister  used to receiving if he takes
the D he got from the Salvation Army fo r child poverty to be good news, or was he
talking about the D he got for housing availability, the C+ he got for affordability, or the
C- he got for housing-related debt?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The first thing is, if we look at  the report, it has 22 indicators.
Eleven of those indicators have actually improved and four have been reasonably flat.
Seven, in the view of the Sa lvation Army, have got worse. The Government is actually
very confident in its record that it is doing a great deal. Of course, there is always more
that can be done.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Does he agree with the Salvation Army, which today said that
“the Skycity convention centre deal has blat antly traded off social harm for economic
development”; if not, why on earth not?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, and I am a little bit surprised the member has asked that,
because under its indicators in the report on social hazards, gambling per capita has
15830 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Feb 2014
gone down and it gets the nice, big, green  tick up, actually, under a National-led
Government.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: He is grasping at straws. Do es the Salvation Army’s finding
that housing availability is rated as “no pr ogress or going backwards” concern him, or
does he think that is good news too?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: If the author of that report rea lly meant what they said, then
the author actually needs to get out a bit mo re, because this is a Government that has
done in Auckland a housing accord, which the Labour Government sat on its hands and
did nothing for. This is a Government that has reformed both building practices in New
Zealand and planning. This is a Government th at has overseen interest  rates that are 50
percent of what they were. Th e Labour Government sat there,  for year after year after
year, and did absolutely nothing. By the way, the officials who used to advise Helen
Clark are some of the same officials who advise me, and they spent virtually their entire
time in the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet giving her advice on housing,
for which she did absolutely nothing. So if the author does not understand—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That answer is long enough.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: When the Prime Minister gets out more in the leafy suburbs of
Parnell and St Stephens Avenue, I am sure  he will notice that rents have gone up—
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Order! The level of interjection is unacceptable, but it would
be helpful if the Leader of the Opposition could phrase his question slightly differently.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I am here to help. With rents up 17 percent nationwide, 18
percent in Auckland, and 37 perc ent in Christchurch since he took office, how does the
Prime Minister expect struggling families to afford a roof over their heads?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Two things. The first is that  the Government has put $1.8
billion in the last 12 months alone into subsidising housing through income-related rents
and the accommodation supplement. The second th ing is, yes, I live in Parnell and I am
proud of it. That member lives in Herne Ba y. He just does not want his supporters to
know he does. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Would the member just proceed with his supplementary question.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: I think it’s the commute to Helensville that’s getting him
down, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And that is not helpful. W ould the member just ask his
supplementary question.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: Perhaps he just takes the helicopter view.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: In all seriousness, how does the Prime Minister, with all his
worldly experience, expect young families to buy their own home when his Government
is requiring a minimum 20 percent deposit, wh ich Quotable Value data shows reduced
the number of first-home buyers to its lowest  level in 3 years—its lowest level in 3
years?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Firstly, the biggest determining factor for people when buying
a house is paying the interest rates on their mo rtgage. They are at a 50-year low and are
half the rate they were under a Labour G overnment. Labour, I mi ght add, forced those
interest rates up. Let us be  honest: its programme of mi smanaging the economy drove
interest rates up and drove peopl e out of their homes. That is  the first thing. The second
thing is that to actually get into a home, pe ople have to be able to pay the mortgage by
having a job. Under this Government, 1,500 people a week are goi ng off welfare and
into work. The Greens and Labour are opposed to jobs and growth. That is the truth.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: What does the Prime Minister say to the struggling middle-
income families who, a major bank predicts , if they are on a $500 a week mortgage
12 Feb 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 15831
now, will be paying another $136 a week within 3 years because of the interest rate rises
under his Government?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I would say this. First, they will  be grateful that Labour is not
in power, because it would have been $1,000 a week—[ Interruption] Well, that is what
it was. The exact numbers would have been $1,000 a week. It is as simple as this. This
is an Opposition that will spend as much money—not its own money, by the way; other
people’s money—to try to get into office. There is only one impact of that: interest rates
will go up faster if Labour gets into office. I say to that family: “Do what you’ve always
done. Stick with National, and you’ll be doing the right thing.”
Economic Programme—Progress
2. JAMI-LEE ROSS (National—Botany)  to the Minister of Finance : How is the
Government’s economic programme supporti ng stronger economic growth, more jobs
and higher incomes?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The steps taken by the Government
over the last 5 years are star ting to deliver results as we are working alongside New
Zealanders to recover from the recession and build a platform for growth. Last week’s
household labour force survey and quarterly employment survey exceeded expectations,
with annual jobs growth to the year to December at 66,000. That is, 66,000 more people
were employed at the end of 2013 compar ed with the end of 2012. Labour force
participation increased to 68.9 percent. Th at is 68.9 percent of the adult population
available for work. This is the second-highest le vel ever recorded. So the decrease in
unemployment has occurred at the same time as the number of people available for
work is at its second-highest ever level. In resp ect of the crisis in manufacturing,
employment and manufacturing suffered yet another blow, because employment grew
by 3,000 to 169,000! Incomes are rising. Since 2008, after-tax average wages have
increased by 25 percent, at a period when the cost of living has increased by 10 percent.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: How has New Zealand’s stronger economic performance benefited
New Zealanders by delivering higher incomes?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It has delivered higher income s, although not as rapidly as
we would have liked, and not yet for every New Zealand household. Last week’s labour
market statistics showed that 2013 weekly earnings grew by 2.8 percent in 2013, above
the 1.6 percent increase in the cost of living. This is from the quarterly employment
survey, which is the best measure of wage  growth. This measure has been used by
successive Governments to adjust New Zealand superannuation and paid parental leave.
I would also note the average wages used by the Green Party for its policies on
minimum wages and welfare benefits, desp ite arguing here that the quarterly
employment survey is not the right measure of wage growth.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why does the Government use the Labour Cost Index in its
determination of the minimum wage? Is it b ecause the index is the official measure of
the change in wage rates?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government does not us e the Labour Cost Index to
determine the minimum wage. Second, the La bour Cost Index does not measure what
people get paid. It is an index of the value of labour for specific skill sets and specific
industries. What measures what people get paid is the quarterly employment survey,
and that shows rising real incomes.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I seek leave to table the document that shows that the
Government uses the Labour Cost Index as the basis—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I need the source of the document.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: It is a combination of Statistics New Zealand information and
information released by the Government at the time the minimum wage is set.
15832 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Feb 2014

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think it is a marginal call, but  on the basis that the House can
decide, leave is sought to table that documen tation. Is there any obj ection to that being
done? There is objection.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: What other reports has he seen on the improving performance of the
New Zealand economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There are a wide range of reports on improvements in the
New Zealand economy. The most recent quarter ly survey of business opinion shows a
near 20-year high in business confidence. Th e manufacturing crisis can be measured by
the BNZ-Business New Zealand Performa nce of Manufacturing Index, which has
shown growth in manufacturing for 15 consecutive months. The most recent
performance of manufacturing index recorded the highest rate of employment growth in
manufacturing since 2007—yet another sign of the manufacturing crisis! Recent data
from the job site SEEK shows that job ads are up by 13 percent compared with January
last year.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: How is the improving economy helping vulnerable families to get
ahead?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government believes that  the most important way to
help vulnerable families is through more j obs and a business environment where they
can be paid more. There is no better news for those who are vulnerable and dependent
on the State than to see a continued improve ment in the jobs ma rket and rising real
wages. Those people stuck in long-term we lfare dependency will never benefit from a
strong economy if they are left in that de pendency. The Government is continuing to
work with those families through ongoing investment in the welfare system, and over
the last two Budgets we have invested around half a billion dollars to help people off
welfare and into work. In the last 12 months 17,000 people have come off a benefit.
Child Poverty, Abuse, and Neglect—Government Measures to Address
3. JACINDA ARDERN (Labour) to the Minister for Social Development: Do her
measures of success for vulnerable children include lowering child poverty, child abuse
and child neglect rates; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Does she agree with the Salva tion Army’s assessment that a D
should be awarded for child pover ty, as “virtually no effort has been spent in actually
addressing the underlying causes of this poverty.”; if not, wh at evidence does she have
to prove otherwise?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: No, I do not, and I think the Minister of Finance has just
given one of the best analyses that I have heard of the difference that we can make for
those vulnerable children and their families. So it is about more jobs being on board and
17,000 fewer people on benefits in the last 12 months. It is certainly seeing that
acknowledgment of food in schools. It is an increase of thos e in early childhood
education. It is the increase that we are seeing for those who are achieving National
Certificate of Educational Achievement and e ducation results. It is a very long list, and
not one I am sure you would want me to take the time of the House on.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Can the Minister tell the Hous e what percentage of working
families are in poverty?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I do not have that figure with me.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Does she agree with the Salva tion Army’s assessment that a C
minus should be awarded for lack of progress for children at risk when the number of
substantiated child abuse or neglect cases ro se 4 percent in the la st year and by 41
percent in the last 5 years; if not, what evidence does she ha ve that things are getting
better for these children?
12 Feb 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 15833

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: No, I do not, and at the end of the day what we have is a
higher public awareness. As the member would know, in 2008 police changed how they
notified to Child, Youth and Family. We are now aware of those children who are not
being harmed themselves but are perhaps in families where they are witnessing family
violence. We take that far more seriously th an we ever have. We report on it. It means
there has been a dramatic increase in notifications, but as a consequence of that—

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Substantiated—the question was substantiated.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: We also have an increase of substantiated, because we
are getting into more of those families where we are seeing it. We share information
with police more than we ever have. That is why we have the Children’s Action Plan,
which has more than 30 initiatives addressing the very heart of what is a very complex
and intergenerational problem.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Is she satisfied with the current  delivery rate of her Children’s
Action Plan, when, based on her answers to wr itten questions, at cu rrent rates it will
take almost 190 years for her Children’s Teams to reach New Zealand’s vulnerable
children?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The member has made that  number up. There is no
number like it. What I would say is, no, I am  not satisfied. Five years ago when I came
into this job, I would have quite liked there to have been a plan for these vulnerable
children, but I had to start the work from  scratch. There was not hing there for them.
They were ignored. They were hidden. It was ac tually easier just to think that it was not
happening. I have had to start from scratch and get it go ing. As I say, it is complex and
intergenerational, and we will make a difference for them.
Health Personnel—Recruitment and Retention
4. Dr CAM CALDER (National)  to the Minister of Health : What is the
Government doing to assist areas that face difficulties recruiting and retaining health
professionals?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I am pleased to advise the House that
registrations of interest for the 2014 Voluntary Bonding Scheme are now open. The
scheme works by encouraging health profession als to start their car eers in hard-to-staff
communities and specialties by offering payments  to their student loans after a 3 to 5-
year bonded period. There are currently 2,700 part icipants, and Vote Health has so far
paid out $11 million. Registrations of interest  for this year’s intake are open for new
general practitioner trainees ; graduate doctors, nurses, and midwives; radiation
therapists; and medical physicists until the middle of March.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: What other initiatives are aimed at improving health care in higher
need communities?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Hon Tony Ryall—I ask the Minist er to talk a bi t closer to the
microphone; it was hard to hear.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Last September I announced that the Government will invest
an extra $16 million to support our high-need s general practices. This included a $1.5
million scholarship fund for 30 graduate nurses. As the Government wants even more
graduate nurses working in our high-needs communities, we have increased that
scholarship fund to $2.4 million, which mean s 48 graduate nurses will now receive
$50,000 scholarships to work in general practice.  This is a considerable investment in
helping general practices in some of our most needy communities in New Zealand.
15834 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Feb 2014
Child Poverty—Measurement
5. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Minister for Social

items.speaker: Development
items.text: What papers or reports, if any,  did her office produce in the last 12
months relating to the measurement of child poverty?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: In respect of the
measurement, none.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Can the Minister confirm for the House that she did not seek any
reports on the Children’s Commissioner’ s $500,000 project to measure and monitor
child poverty, or even seek advice on whether such a measure was necessary?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I have definitely received reports on child poverty. I am
part of the Ministerial Committee on P overty, but I have not sought from my
department an argument on the measurements. We are more interested in the actions
that need to be taken, and those are the reports that I expect from my department.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Upon whose expert advice did the Minister write off the Children’s
Commissioner’s child poverty monitor work?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: It was certainly discussed at the Ministerial Committee
on Poverty. That is where the discussion took place. That is the advice that I sought.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Minister see, then, any connection between the Salvation
Army’s D ranking of her failure over child pov erty with her expre ss refusal to engage
with the Children’s Commissioner’s child poverty monitor project?

items.speaker: Rt Hon John Key
items.text: You mean D as in Dotcom?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I have heard it said that it might be D for Dotcom, but
what I would say is that th e Ministry of Social Devel opment household income report
comes out. It does an accurate analysis of  a number of measures. We report it
transparently and publicly. It is certainly what  we, on this side of the House, take notice
of. As I say, it is ve ry transparent. The member can get a copy of it any time. It is that
advice that I take.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: If a parent was given a D for l ooking after their child, would she
consider that they were doing a good job, or not?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: For me this gets to the heart of the actual issue. So the
member thinks that it is only the Government’s throwing money around and getting into
every household and giving them 60 bucks a we ek for a newborn baby that is going to
make the difference. I actually think it is not  about just the Government; it is about the
Government, community, and parents themselv es actually putting their children first in
many instances. It is about what is happe ning in the streets. It is about what
organisations like the Salvation Army do. So I do not think it is a D for the Government.
In fact, what the Salvation Army did say was that “as a national community, we have
made credible and worthwhile social prog ress. It is important to acknowledge and
celebrate this because, for the most part, it is intentional and hard won. The Government
should be applauded for its contribution to this progress.”

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Well, then, how does the Minister explain that for all her rhetoric and
chest-thumping and political bluster, the reality remains—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Would the member like to start her question again.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. How, then, does the Minister explain that
for all her rhetoric, chest-thum ping, and political blus ter, the reality re mains that one in
every five children in this country remains living in poverty after 5 long years of her
Government?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: What we have seen by every measure is that it has flat-
lined. What we have done through the worst global financial crisis—and people might
like to write that off and pretend it did not happen, but actually what we did was we put
12 Feb 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 15835
more money, more support, into those familie s that really needed  it. We are seeing
improvements when we look at the number of jobs that are on board and the
opportunities for people to take them up. I am  very confident that you are going to see
the real results of that.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is the Minister refusing to acknowledge the seriousness of having
one in every five New Zealand children st ill living in poverty, and is she actively
snubbing the commissioner’s work on monitoring child poverty because she does not
want to be held accountable for her failure to make any improvement in the lives of
those one in five New Zealand children?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: And that, ladies and gen tlemen, was chest-thumping.
Right, so what we have here is, actually, I do not agree with the member. This is the
Government that has introduced the Childre n’s Action Plan. This is the Government
that has put more emphasis on early chil dhood education and that has increased the
amount that goes into accommodation help. It  has put an emphasis on rheumatic fever,
which, quite frankly, we have not seen at all. We have got after-hours for under-6-year-
olds now. We have got food in any school that wants to take it for breakfast. More than
$500,000 is going to KidsCan to actually help those children. I do take it seriously. I
want to see every child in this country  thriving and achieving and having the best
possible start that they can.
Pest Control—Use of 1080 Poison
6. RICHARD PROSSER (NZ First)  to the Minister of Conservation : Does he
stand by all his statements on the us e of 1080 poison by the Department of
Conservation?
Hon AMY ADAMS (Minister for the Environment)  on behalf of the Minister of

items.speaker: Conservation
items.text: Yes. The Minister gave a comprehensive speech on 29 January
announcing the Battle for our Birds, which clearly sets out why 1080 use is essential for
dealing with this year’s beech mast. It is a very good speech and I would encourage the
member to read it.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: Is he aware that bird repellen ts being trialled for use with 1080
poison have been shown to be ineffective a nd that researchers are unlikely to have an
effective bird repellent available in time for his department’s planned increase in the use
of aerial 1080 this year?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Well, what I can tell the memb er is that the Minister is
absolutely aware that this is all about the need to protect New Zealand’s native birds.
What we do know is that without the use of 1080, 99 percent of kea chicks die; with the
use of 1080, 100 percent of them  survive to 1 year. Without this, our native birds are
seriously at risk of eradicat ion, and there is no question in the mind of any sensible
person that this is absolutely necessary.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: Can he assure the House that there will be no increase in the
planned use of aerial 1080 until a suitable bi rd repellent is ava ilable to protect our
endangered native species such as kea, give n his department’s ow n findings that 20
percent of kea in the areas to be poisoned will be killed by 1080?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: No, I absolutely will not give that assurance, because what we
do know is that if we were to  delay the use of 1080 through this year’s beech mast, we
would face the eradication and lo ss of more species, as happened last time. What we do
know is that if we do not use 1080 to protect our native wildlife, th ere is a serious of
loss of species or serious degradation of  the populations. I do not think that is
acceptable to New Zealanders.
15836 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Feb 2014

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: Can the Minister describe to  the House the process by which
stoats are killed by 1080, given that stoats do not directly eat the cereal-based 1080 baits
that are used in aerial poisoning applications?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: No, I cannot give him a detail ed biological indication of the
impact of 1080 on stoats, but what I will repe at for the member’s benefit is that we
know that if we do not use 1080, particularly during this significant beech mast event,
we risk serious loss of our native bird popula tion. The facts are these, once more for the
member. It does not kill kiwis. Yes, there is  some damage to some species, but without
the use of 1080, 99 percent of kea chicks ri sk being lost. I do not think that is
acceptable.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: I seek leave to table seven documents. They are—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will allow the member to list all seven documents at once if he
could do so briefly.

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: They are pathology reports prepared for the Department of
Conservation about seven radio-tagged kea found dead in north Ōkārito.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: All right. Second document?

items.speaker: Richard Prosser
items.text: They are all the same—seven separate pathology reports.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member is seeking leave to table seven separate pathology
reports. Is there any objection to  that course of action? Th ere appears to be none. They
can be tabled.
Documents, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
Freshwater Management—Water Quality of Rivers
7. EUGENIE SAGE (Green)  to the Minister for the Environment : Why do the
Government’s proposals for improving fres hwater management allow New Zealand
rivers to have higher concentrations of nitrogen pollution than China’s Yangtze River?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: As usual, the member is
deliberately scaremongering on water quality. Although the Yangtze River indeed has
serious pollution issues, nitrogen is not the only pollutant there is and, even according to
the World Wide Fund for Nature, it is not th e pollutant of particular concern for the
Yangtze River, where the issue is, in fact, primarily around industrial and sewage waste
and the management of sediments. The Government’s proposals for freshwater
management will improve water quality and not allow the degradation of New Zealand
rivers, something that that member’s part y failed to do in 9 years of propping up a
Labour Government. Furthermore, the nitrate toxicity threshold fo r the bottom lines is
only one of the ways that nitrogen must be  managed to meet the national bottom lines,
and most rivers will need to be more aggres sively managed for nitrogen levels to meet
periphyton standards, a fact that the memb er either does not understand or deliberately
chooses to ignore.

items.speaker: Eugenie Sage
items.text: Will she review her proposed nitrate toxicity bands and the national
bottom lines for rivers, which Fish and Game has described as an “abject failure” and,
effectively, a licence to pollute in relation to farm nitrate pollution?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: The first point I would make in response to that question is that
they are not my nitrate toxicity  levels; they are the levels that have been devised by an
expert panel made up of more than 60 water-q uality scientists. They are specific levels
that none of my colleagues or I have had any input into. Furthermore, as I mentioned in
answer to the primary question,  the nitrate toxicity level is  only one of the ways that
nitrogen is measured in our rivers.
12 Feb 2014 Questions for Oral Answer 15837

items.speaker: Eugenie Sage
items.text: Will she change her proposals, given that nitrogen pollution can have
significant impacts on river health at much lower levels than her proposed bottom line
of nitrate being toxic to fish and aquatic life?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: The National Objectives Framework levels have been out for
consultation. We are now working through th e submissions that have come in, and no
final decisions have been made. But again I would reiterate for the member that the
nitrate toxicity level is set, which is only one of the ways that nitrogen is controlled, at a
level where there is full species protecti on for 80 percent. And for the remaining 20
percent, it is the level at which you would start to see so me impact on growth. I think it
is a very reasonable level and it is the level that was chos en by the expert science panel
and the work that it did to come up with these levels.

items.speaker: Hon Tariana Turia
items.text: Does the Minister agree with Te Wai M āori Trust that if the
Government waits to develop additional attr ibutes, there is a danger that nothing will
happen; if so, will she agree that the implementation deadline should be dropped from

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: I do not agree that nothing will happen. There are two aspects
to that question. One is around developing add itional attributes. I ce rtainly agree, and I
have been saying for some time, that the National Objectiv es Framework would
continue to be a developing t ool, and there certainly will n eed to be more work done,
but we need to start and start now with what we have. In respect of the time line for
implementation, that is something that we can certainly continue to talk about, but I
would point out to the member that in actual fact the information that I have suggests
that most councils are well on track to havi ng these guidelines in place between 2016
and 2020. There is a review set in 2016, where we can certainly lo ok at it, but the
indications that I am seeing s uggest that councils are actuall y taking to this with some
vigour.

items.speaker: Eugenie Sage
items.text: Will she strengthen her weak wate r-quality proposals, given that the
Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environmen t has described them as “not adequate
for protecting water quality to even current levels in New Zealand,”?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Well, I think the best way to address that question is to remind
the House of what the national bottom line on nitrogen pollution was under the Labour-
Greens Government, which was: do what you li ke. There were zero limits from central
government. It had no interest  in requiring counc ils to lift their standards. This
Government has. This Government is lif ting them. Can I remind members also that
quite apart from bottom lines, we still have an  obligation to maintain or enhance. No
river quality is allowed to deteriorate under this framework, despite the member’s
scaremongering.

items.speaker: Eugenie Sage
items.text: If the Minister is so confident that her proposals will maintain water
quality, how does she respond to the submission and anal ysis of the New Zealand
Freshwater Sciences Society, the professional body of freshw ater scientists, which says
that her proposals have “the potential for New Zealand rivers to become some of the
most nitrogen polluted among OECD countries.”?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Very easily. I respond by saying that they are simply wrong.
Tertiary Institutions—Governance of Universities and Wānanga
8. COLIN KING (National—Kaik ōura) to the Minister for Tertiary Education,

items.speaker: Skills and Employment
items.text: What steps is the Governme nt taking to strengthen the
governance of New Zealand universities and wānanga?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for T ertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): Yesterday I announced that the Government will reform the
composition of university and w ānanga governance councils, to create smaller skills-
15838 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Feb 2014
based councils that can res pond more quickly and strategi cally to the challenges of
modern-day tertiary education. New Zeala nd universities face a nu mber of critical
challenges, such as rapidly changing skill s needs in the employment market, an
increasingly competitive international university environment, and rapidly changing
technologies in teaching and learni ng. Although our universities and w ānanga have
been performing well, these reforms will al low them to respond to these and other
challenges more quickly and strategically. Si milar reforms to our polytechnic sector in
2009 have been very successful, and I expect these will be too.

items.speaker: Colin King
items.text: What are the main components of the reforms?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The main changes are to decrease the size of councils from
the current 12 to 20 members down to 8 to 12 members, to allow council membership to
be more flexible, and also requiring counc il members to have governance capability.
One university has already indicated its desire to reduce the size of its council to 12, but
has been unable to do so due to the legislative requirements, which we are now
changing. The changes for w ānanga are particularly important. The governance settings
for w ānanga were not written with them  in mind. The changes will allow w ānanga
much more flexibility, to reflect their unique stakeholders on their councils.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: It’s a top-down, boss-driven politicisation.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: These reforms will not—as some members opposite have
asserted and seem to be repeating their assertions now—compromise academic freedom
or eliminate the input of students and staff into decision making.

items.speaker: Colin King
items.text: What other steps is the Government  taking to strengthen our tertiary
sector?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: This Government has a very good record in terms of the
progress it has made with the tertiary se ctor. Since 2009 it has made a series of
incremental reforms to improve perf ormance, including the introduction of
performance-linked funding, educational pe rformance indicators, and reducing low-
value spending. These reforms have been bear ing very good fruit. In 2012 a total of
162,000 qualifications were completed in the New Zealand tertiary education system.
That is up 23 percent from just 4 years previously. More young people are now moving
from school to degree-level study, from  13,500 students in 2007 to 16,500 in 2012,
including many more young Māori and Pasifika.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of his view that g overning bodies of 20 cannot act
quickly or strategically, has he approached the Prime Minister to reduce the size of
Cabinet to perhaps eight or 12 people?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: In so far as there is ministerial responsibility, the Hon Steven Joyce.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am sorry but that is a little  shallow—in fact, shallow as a
bird bath, as is usual from Mr Robertson. In fact, it may have escaped the member in his
many years of moving back and forth be tween university and Parliament, but
fundamentally a university council gove rns a university, which is a single
organisation—it can be quite large—while a Ca binet governs an enti re country. It is a
subtle difference, and maybe one day Mr Robertson—in the dim, distant future—may
get to see it for himself.

Broadband, Ultra-fast and Rural—Connection Statistics
10. JONATHAN YOUNG (Nat ional—New Plymouth)  to the Minister for

items.speaker: Communications and Information Technology
items.text: What recent reports has she received
on the number of end users able to connect to the Government’s Ultra-Fast Broadband

Hon AMY ADAMS (Minister for Communications and Information
Technology): I am pleased to announce that at th e end of 2013 more than a quarter of

stage of the Rural Broadband Initiative the build is more than 60 percent finished—
360,000-plus end-users can now connect to u ltra-fast broadband, an additional 179,000

60,000 can connect through upgrades to fixed line services. In terms of priority users, an

items.speaker: Jonathan Young
items.text: How is uptake of fibre and improved rural broadband coverage
tracking?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Over the last quarter of 2013 we saw a 40 percent increase in

broadband, internet, and fibre connectivity are absolutely critical to New Zealand’s

to New Zealand end-users.

12. Dr PAUL HUTCHISON (National—Hunua)  to the Minister of Veterans’

items.speaker: Affairs

commemoration has now closed, and 10,112 applications for the 1,000 double passes

Salvation Army—State of the Nation Report

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Honourable members, I have receive d a letter from Jacinda Ardern
seeking to debate under Standi ng Order 386 the release of Striking a Better Balance: A
State of the Nation Report  from the Salvation Army . For there to be an urgent debate
there must be a particular case of recent occurrence that involves the administrative or
ministerial responsibility of the Government and that requires the urgent attention of the
House. An urgent debate is a way of holdi ng the Government to account for an action
for which it is responsible. It must be distinct responsibility for the particular case that is
sought to be debated. There is no ministeria l responsibility for a re port that is released
by the Salvation Army. The report undoubtedly addresses issues of importance to which
the Government may respond, but the urgent debate procedure is a means of debating
matters that have occurred. It is not a means of debating ma tters that might or might not
occur in the future. The application is therefore declined.
DEBATE ON PRIME MINISTER’S STATEMENT
Debate resumed from 11 February.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: What a great time it is to be a member of
the National caucus. It is a great time to be a member of this caucus because as we head
into the election later this year, we have got  a leader who is charismatic, we have got a
leader who is effective, and we have got a l eader who is on top of his job. We have also
got a leader who is one of the most popular Prime Ministers at this stage in the electoral
cycle we have seen in the last 50 years. The party of the member s opposite is jealous
because its leader is tricky. Its leader makes things up on the hoof. Its leader does not
have caucus support either. Every single pers on sitting behind him is questioning right
now whether their party made the right deci sion. We like to say on this side of the
House that Labour’s Best Start policy was actually a bad start to the year. I want to take
a different spin on it, and say that it was not just the worst start to the year for them;
actually, it was a bit of a best start. It was a best start fo r the “ABC” club. It was a best
start for the “Anyone But Cunliffe” club. It wa s a best start for t hose people who know
15844 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
that their leader is no t up to it, and who know that their leader is not fit to be the Prime
Minister of New Zealand. New Zealanders around the country know that as well.
New Zealand as a country is doing ex ceptionally well right now. We are doing
exceptionally well because New Zealanders are seeing significant growth rates. We are
one of the best countries in the OECD at the moment when it comes to growth. Sixty-
six thousand jobs in the New Zealand ec onomy were created last year for New
Zealanders. When you think about what is  happening overseas, and when you think
about our neighbours in Australia, and wh en you think about the difficult global
financial crisis that many countries ha ve gone through, seeing 66,000 new jobs in the
economy created for New Zealanders is a huge achievement.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Not at Goodman Fielder in Hamilton.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Andrew Little over there likes to yell and scream, but he is a
former union leader, and he knows that many of the policies that his group, his party,
and his former clan in the unions want to pursue will actually lead to fewer jobs for
New Zealanders. We have the policies that are seeing more jobs for New Zealanders.
They do not like to hear it, but it is abso lutely the truth. In this country, business
confidence is at a 20-year high. New Zeala nd businesses are feeling the positive effects
in the economy. They are wanting to invest more money, and that investment is leading
to more jobs.
I think one the proudest achievements so fa r of this Government has been in the
welfare area, where 17,000 Kiwis came off the be nefit in the last year and moved into
work, training, or other forms of education. Seventeen thousand people now have a new
start to life. Seventeen thousand people are no longer trapped in the welfare trap. We
know that the Opposition likes to see them stay there, because it actually seems to
benefit the Opposition, but in the long term the best thing for people on welfare to do is
to get into jobs, get into training, or get into education, because that is the key to
success. Despite the squawking on the other side of the House a bout manufacturing in
the last year, manufacturing is growing in  this country too, and New Zealanders are
really seeing the impacts of that.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: What about exports outside primary?

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: “Exports”, says Mr—what is your  name? Mr Parker. “Exports”,
says Mr Parker. Exports are growing hugely. My colleagues on this side of the House
can see exports growing in this country too; New Zealanders can see it as well. When it
comes to real, after-tax wages, despite wh at the Opposition members want to say, after-
tax wages are up 25 percent since we have been in office, despite the inflation rate being
at about 10 percent.
I just want to turn a little bit to Austra lia because we know that our Prime Minister
was in Australia recently. We know that the Opposition thinks that nothing came of it.
Actually, the relationship between New Zealand and Australia has considerably
strengthened in the last 2 years, so much so  that Australia is looki ng to this country for
ideas as to how to improve its economy. T ony Abbott, the Prime Minister of Australia,
gave a speech recently to the Trans-Tasman  Business Circle. He said: “When I look at
New Zealand I see a country which at this point  in its history has much to teach us.” He
talked about the fact that the Key Governme nt has seen growth in Government slow.
The other side of the House likes to see G overnment continue to grow and grow. This
side of the House actually believes that pe ople should be empowered, not so much see
Government growth. In this country, the G overnment percentage of GDP has reduced
from 35 percent to 30 percen t. I think the best quote th at I could take from Tony
Abbott’s speech was this: “As government gets smaller, citizens get bigger and that is
what this government wants to achieve in this country—empowered citizens.” That is
exactly what the National Party is purs uing—empowered citizens, a stronger economy,
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15845
lower crime rates, more people getting into  health and education, and New Zealanders
succeeding around the country.
But Tony Abbott also knows a bit about watching a Green Party in Government,
because in Australia they had the Green Part y participating considerably in the last
Labor-Greens Government. When we go to the polls later this year we know that New
Zealanders have two options on their hands. They have got the strong, stable, National
Government, which is succeeding for New Zealanders, or they have got the alternative
Labour-Green-Mana-Winston Government, whic h would be an absolute disaster for
New Zealand. We know that th e Greens are bad for economi es, because Australia is
facing exactly the same types of problems th at this country was left with in 2008.
Australia is seeing massive growth in debt  on its books. It is seeing huge amounts of
unemployment facing it. It is seeing growth rates in its economy considerably down as
well. Those are the issues that we had to face in this country and we know that if Labour
and the Greens got back into office, that is exactly what we would face as well.
There is another strand to this story about  the Green Party that I think we have to
explore in this House. As much as the Gr een Party likes to talk about dodgy deals when
it looks at us, I think the last 24 hours have shown us that there is one dodgy deal that is
brewing in this country that absolutely n eeds public scrutiny and public examination.
We know that Russel Norman has recently been visiting one Kim Dotcom. We also
know that one Russel Norman has said publicly to TV3 and other media outlets that he
is willing to intervene in any extradition process for Mr Dotcom. We also know that Mr
Norman has said on record that he has aske d Mr Dotcom to pull back from his political
interventions through his Internet Party, know ing that the Internet  Party would likely
take some votes from the Green Party. If  there is any dodgy deal in this country
whereby politicians are considering intervening in judicial processes, where politicians
are considering intervening in whether this Government extradites an individual to the
United States, and asking at the same time th at that individual doe s not do anything to
hurt them politically—if there is any party in  this country that is entertaining dodgy
deals, then it is the Green Party and it is Russel Norman.
As much as they like to squawk and point fingers at this side of the House, and
complain about the quite legitimate electorate deals that this party sends to the people,
there is one party in this country that is corrupting the political process, and it is the
Green Party, and its members should be as hamed of that. Green Party members also
used to be against big money in politics. Th ey also used to be against business people
getting involved in the political process. But, actually, the Green Party is completely the
one that is doing an about-face and changing its style completely. I am appalled by what
I have seen when it comes to the extradition process and the Green Party, and New
Zealanders should be appalled by it as well.
We have got a strong story to tell in this country. We know that the economy is
growing. We know that New Zealanders are starting to feel the positive impacts of
economic growth. We are seeing more jobs , fewer people in unemployment, fewer
people in the welfare queue, and more peopl e getting operations. We are seeing that we
are going to get back to surplus next year. We are also going to see this country start to
grow even more and continue to be a br ight, shining star in the world economy. The
contrast on the other side is not flash. We know that the policies that that side is coming
up with are made on the hoof. The policies do not stack up. We know that the numbers
do not stack up either. The Labour Party is tricky. The Green Party is dodgy. This
Government has the recipe to see New Zeala nd continue to grow, a nd that is what we
will be putting to the people later this year.

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: Greetings in the year 2014. This is the first time
that I have stood as a parliamentarian and t horoughly appreciated the value of absolute
15846 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
privilege, because today I am going to fulf il my duties as a member of the House of
Representatives and I am going to bring to the attention of the House and my fellow
New Zealanders a quality of conduct being visited upon New Zealand firms selling
products, produce, and stock to an Australia n-owned supermarket called Countdown in
New Zealand. The people who have requested that I publicise this issue live in fear.
They live in a climate of threat, intimidation, and menace. It is without a sliver of doubt,
I believe, that in this speech I am fulfilling my duties as a parliamentarian to alert us to a
level of extortion that is going unchallenged in our food and grocery sector.
It was galling enough for us as New Zealanders  to watch the violation of the CER. It
was disgraceful for us to see our New Zealand exporters blacklisted by Woolworths and
the other Australian supermarkets. We ha ve come to understand that the Aussie
corporate culture in that sector is akin to  a dingo culture, but we never thought that our
Prime Minister would go there, be confront ed by the dingo culture, and come back as
Abbott’s poodle. Well, I want this Prime Minist er and I want us as parliamentarians to
challenge a more repugnant story of superm arket behaviour, of monopolistic malice,
and of extortion. Once I have laid out the sequence of events, I have got no doubt that
members of this House will regard this episode as the “Countdown shakedown”.
Let me elaborate, without any ambiguity, on what is happening to Kiwi firms that are
employing thousands of New Zealanders up and down the country as they seek to
secure business opportunity w ith the Countdown supermarket chain, which is run by a
corporate culture that can be described onl y as something that Tony Soprano would be
very proud of—something of racketeering, something of extortion, and certainly
something imported from Austra lia that corrupts established commercial practice in
New Zealand. A number of firms have cont acted me. They have, however, sworn me
not to reveal their identities. They have been  ordered to meetings with managers of the
Countdown supermarket chain, they are taken into a meeting room, and the following is
happening to our fellow New Zealand empl oyers and businesses and, indirectly,
employees. They are being told by the Austra lian-owned supermarket that “Our profit
margin did not suit the shareholders’ expectat ions last year. We want more profit out of
you.” Naturally, our Kiwi suppliers say: “It’s not flash on our side either. What can we
do to assist?”. The Aussie managers are sa ying to our Kiwi employers and our Kiwi
firms that “We’re not here to talk nurse ry rhymes.” They are demanding of Kiwi
businesses payments, backdated cheques,  and recompense for the losses the
supermarkets assert they suffered last year. If they do not pay these cheques, they are
being told they will have no shelf space into the future.
In any other sort of country, that is black mail. That is extortion. Why should we, as
New Zealanders, allow the Australian shareh olders and the Australian supermarket
chains to treat our fellow citizens, our fellow taxpayers, and our fellow businessmen and
businesswomen in that fashion? It is an offence. OK, in Australia, it may be the
corporate culture that extortion is some sort of casual liaison between consenting adults.
That type of extortion that I have outlined is  an offence in our country. Now, let me be
very clear. A number of firms have been told their products will not be placed on the
shelves of our supermarkets unless they  make backdated payments and offer
remuneration for losses sustained by the superm arket. It is not the fault of New Zealand
producers that an Aussie-owned supermarket could not compete with our New Zealand
- owned cooperative supermarket chain. Not only is that anti-competitive, that is a type
of commercial culture repugnant  to most New Zealanders. This is how it works. The
Aussie-driven owners and managers of th e supermarket chain—and I know their names
because I have been contacted by the people who were in the room—are saying to our

items.speaker: Kiwi managers and our Kiwi firms
items.text: “You will hand over a cheque for my historic losses
or you will never gain shelf space in the supe rmarkets. If you breathe one word of this,
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15847
we will blacklist you permanently.” That is not  extortion; that must be approaching a
crime. What better place than to use the highest court in th e land to outline and air their
grievances?
Without a doubt, the first thing that I am goi ng to do after delivering this speech is
deliver an official letter of complain t to the Commerce Commission, because this
monopolistic abuse, these threat s, and this intimidation are driving our fellow Kiwis to
their wits’ end. They begin to  fear now whether their busin esses are viable and they
have told me that if they are forced to  make these retrospective backdated cheque
payments, they will start laying off workers. This is the feral culture in this Australian-
owned supermarket chain that saw them bring a Tasmanian devil out 6 years ago to
smash the union movement. They sought to smash the union movement in that
particular supermarket chain. Eventually, c onsumers turned and supported the workers.
I only hope my fellow citizens and consumers from all around the country say they will
not acquiesce with the importation of this corrupt culture from the Australian
shareholders into our business environment.
Let me be absolutely explicit. This covers a whole host of sectors in the New
Zealand economy. Let me be absolutely explicit. This type of behaviour is causing God-
fearing Kiwi businesses to live in abject fear . Indeed, they have sought legal advice as
to whether they should even have spoken to me . But I feel that we, as parliamentarians,
ought to stand up for our fellow Kiwis in the f ace of this type of supermarket fascism.
What possessed the Government, the Minister s, and, apparently, the richest man in
Parliament, our Prime Minister, to come b ack after a brief discussion with Ralph
Waters—a man who chairs Woolworths, made a handsome fortune out of New Zealand,
and has done nothing to lift his finger or to change this operational corporate culture,
and obviously convinced our Prim e Minister, because he is from the big end of town—
to let it slide?
Well, it might be slippery enough for him, but  on this side of th e House let us stand
up against this monopolistic, extortionate, and menacing behaviour, because once these
people start to lay off workers the employment  rate will only worsen in the regions. We
should not be intimidated by their corporate lawyers. We should not be intimidated by
their lobbyists. We should say, as I am today, to the Countdown management: stop
threatening. Stop your Mafioso tactics agai nst Kiwi businesses. Treat them with a
decent shot. Give them a fair go. Stop thre atening that they will be bankrupted or
blacklisted if they squeak about this extor tionary behaviour. This verges on corruption.
It has been imported into our  business culture by the Aust ralian-owned supermarkets. I
will go to Pak ’N Save because the Aussies should pack up and go home. Kia ora tātou.

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: It is my delight to rise to
support wholeheartedly the Prime Minister’s motion that this  House have confidence in
the National-led Government. Why would it  not? Why would it not when we are
heading into 2014, into another election year, and the record of this country under the
leadership of John Key and this Government is the envy of so many in the rest of the
world? They look at New Zealand—and we have seen this just this last week with the
visit to Australia—and they wonder how we have done it. How has this Government led
us through the toughest of times, protect ed its people, and put  us on a path to
prosperity? Take a moment to look back, as I am sure the country will as we head into
the election. Despite all of the bombastic  table-thumping obfuscation we are seeing
from the Opposition, and despite the shady deals and desperate horse-trading of some of
the minor parties, which are desperate to do whatever they can at whatever cost to get
back on to the Treasury benches—they do not care how much of your money they blow.
They do not care how much debt they lay on our future generati ons. Now we have a
15848 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
serious question as to whether they even  care about our justice system. They are
prepared to horse-trade to get back in.
But here is the reality. This is what Ne w Zealanders are going to know when they
head into this election. They know that in November 2008 we picked up a country
where Treasury had forecast that after 9 ye ars of Helen Clark and Michael Cullen’s
leadership, we were facing never-ending deficits. We had a manufacturing and a
productive sector that had been in declin e for the last 5 years, despite the best
international conditions we knew. Government spending had blown out by 50 percent in
just a few years with very little to show fo r it, actually, other than a very bloated union
sector. That Labour-Greens Government was thrown out, quite rightly, by the people of
New Zealand for economic sabot age; for its high-handed, na nny State ways; and for its
innate belief that it knew better what to do with the average Kiwi’s money than the
Kiwi family did. New Zealand re jected that. It rejected it comprehensively, and it did it
again in 2011.
Even after taking on the economic shambles that Labour and the Greens left us, we
faced the global financial crisis, which actua lly turned out far worse than was predicted
even at those early stages, and, of course, we had the tr emendous devastation of the
Canterbury earthquakes, the total cost of which is now approaching somewhere north of
20 percent of New Zealand’s GDP. These are si gnificant hits that this Government has
had to deal with, and yet wher e are we now? Well, unemployme nt is at 6 percent, even
though we have participation rates at some of  their highest levels, and they are falling.
We have crime at a 30-year low, with more  foot patrols thanks to the work of my
colleague Minister Tolley. We are getting more elective surgery and more access to
medicines. For the first time, we have decen t rheumatic fever treatment. We are getting
more children being immunised, more child ren in early childhood education, and more
children getting National Certificate of Educational Achievement results.
We have one of the best growth rates in the OECD, and it is  the envy of many
countries. Confidence is at an all-time high. For the first time, we are going to have
New Zealand - wide frameworks to address serious issues that were neglected under the
last Government, like our water quality and like the environmental protection of our
exclusive economic zone. Those members talk a big game in the environment, but look
at the record. This National Government ha s done more for environmental protection
than Labour and the Greens ever have.
Let us look at the issue of  Treaty settlements. Labour and the Greens talked a big
game there, but let us look at the reality. Since the Treaty settlement process started,
which was under a National Government, th ere have been 60-odd Treaty settlements
completed, with more than 40 of those in the last 5 years under the very successful
leadership of the Hon Christopher Finlayson. That is the biggest single thing that we can
do to advance the M āori economy and to help M āori communities take their place, as
they should, in our society and in our economy.
We have, in my portfolios, the very successf ul roll-out of the ultra-fast broadband
and rural broadband projects, which is going to improve connectivity for 97.8 percent of
New Zealand. Let us just remember that all of these things that  I am talking about—
ultra-fast broadband, the Rural Broadband Initiative, exclusive economic zone
protection, water quality frameworks, water quality clean-up—were all voted against by
Labour and the Greens. They voted against them. So now those members stand up and
bleat and moan, but the reality is that Labour and the Greens opposed our improving
internet connectivity for 97.8 percent of New Zealand. Not only are we doing that but,
as the figures I announced today show, we  are well on track—in fact, ahead of our
build. We are doing it in a way that, frankly, is the envy of many other countries that are
rolling it out.
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15849
We have also improved cellular connectiv ity. We have completed, obviously, the
digital switch-over, and we are working through the auction of the spectrum that will be
used for fourth-generation mobile services. I can tell you that the re quirements that we
have put into that auction mean that w ithin 5 years more than 90 percent of New
Zealanders will have access to fourth-gener ation mobile cellular connectivity, giving
them download speeds on their mobile devices  of up to 100 megabits a second. That is
world leading—well, certainly it is lead ing for this part of the world—and it is
something that New Zealanders can be very, ve ry proud of. In this year we are going to
complete, as the Prime Minister said in his statement, our work on trans-Tasman mobile
roaming, to make sure that New Zealanders do not pay more for their roaming than they
need to. Again, this issue was completely neglected under previous Governments.
In the environmental portfolio, I will be ve ry proud to be introducing into this House
shortly a bill that will, for the first tim e ever, mandate independent, arm’s-length,
statutorily required environmental reportin g—something that this House, this
Parliament, and this country have never ha d. This is the Government that has the
courage of its convictions and is prepared to say that we are not  going to screw the
scrum if we get numbers we do not like. We  saw that in 2007, when Labour deleted a
chapter of a report that did not work for it. We have the courage a nd the principles to
say that, no, New Zealand deserves environmen tal reporting that is honest, that is arm’s
length, that is completed to the highest standa rd, that is independent ly reviewed by the
Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environm ent, and that will give New Zealanders,
for the first time, an honest analysis of what is going on in their environment.
Can I say in that regard that I find it abso lutely outrageous that we have members of
this Parliament who would look to beat up our international reput ation and all of the
good work that our agricultural sector, that our councils, an d that our stakeholders are
doing around water management. They w ould absolutely go out and trash New
Zealand’s reputation in the media and in th e international fora simply to push an
agenda. I can only surmise that  either they do not know wh at is going on or they are
deliberately throwing New Zealand’s reputation to the wolves to score cheap points. For
a party that prides itself on protecting the en vironment, that is ou trageous. Were that
party to ever gain Government, I think we should all have reason to be very, very
nervous about what it would do to this coun try’s economy and what it would do to the
standard of living of New Zealanders. We already know that it would print money and
that it thinks that is a solution to ever ything. We know that Labour will come in and
throw money around—never mind the debt; never mind the fact that my grandchildren
and my children will have to be paying for those promises and that spending
extravagance.
What we have learnt, of cour se, is that we cannot trust what those members tell us
anyway. We have learnt that every word th at comes out of David Cunliffe’s mouth has
to be checked very, very carefully. Then it pays to also check with Phil Goff to see
whether he has got a different  position, and then, of course , we would need to just
double back and see whether Kim Dotcom has put a rider on a nything that those
members have to cross-check against.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: And is Trevor Mallard prepared to support it?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: That is right. Well, Trevor Mallard is a law unto himself. We
know this, of course. But what we have  on the Opposition benches is a party of
desperation, a party that is prepared and has shown itself willing to mislead, to throw
this country to the wolves, and to run down all of the good work that this Government
has done to get New Zealand into a strong state.
There is one way that we can provide for Ne w Zealanders, and that is to ensure that
we have the wealth that this country deserv es to have to ensure that we can provide
15850 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
them with schools, the edu cation, the lifesty le, the standard of living, and the
opportunities that they deserve. This is the G overnment that is delivering on it. This is
the Government that has a track record that the rest of the world looks at and marvels at.
This is a year when we will be saying to the New Zealand public that we cannot afford
to put that at risk. We are on a fantastic  path. We are on a pa th that is, frankly,
remarkable, considering the challenges that we have come through. New Zealand has
every reason to be very proud of  the position that it finds it self in, and I have no doubt
that New Zealanders will continue to s upport this John Key - led Government through
2014. That is why I absolutely support the Prime Minister’s motion.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: I rise to take a call in this debate on the Prime
Minister’s statement, which welcomed the New Year and invited the nation and this
House to have confidence in him and his Government. We politely decline this
invitation. We decline because confidence in this Government is not warranted, as is
evidenced by its quite woeful track record with regard to law and order and the parlous
state of our beleaguered police force. Flat budgets, undermanning, under-resourcing,
and diminishing morale—that is what this  John Key - led Government has brought to
the thin blue line.
Our boys and girls in blue are being asked to  do ever more and more with ever less
and less. Crime is falling, they proclaim fr om the benches opposite. The reality, as we
all know, is that crime is ri sing but reporting is falling. Pe ople are simply not bothering
to report crimes, because they know that the police do not have the resources to be able
to respond. Back-office staff are being cut, and real numbers of officers on the front line
are falling away. People are l eaving the police in droves, demoralised and lured by the
promise of actual decent money across the Tasman. Good police officers are heading for
Australia while crime rates on this side of the Ditch soar unreported, and New
Zealanders live in fear in their own homes and on their own streets.
It is not good enough. We need to be spendi ng more on the police, not less. We need
to be recruiting more officers, not fewer, and we need to be paying them decent money,
not the insulting pittance that this miserl y Government, with its warped sense of
priorities, appears to believe is someho w adequate. And we are invited to have
confidence in the Government at the same time—confidence! You can have confidence
in John Key’s Government—Tui billboard!
The current trial of a man charged with th e murder of Christchurch woman Mellory
Manning is deeply disturbing. It has exposed a dark underbelly of criminality and gang
culture in Christchurch. How has this been allowed to fester a nd spread? Although this
case dates back to 2008, the brutality of the killing has shocked the New Zealand public.

items.speaker: What the public wants to know is this
items.text: do we have the police numbers and resources to
deal effectively with the menace of ga ng culture? Well, we do not. Years of
underfunding and diminishing morale have seen  to that. But need them we do, because
gangs do pose a serious threat to ordinary, law-abiding citizens. They present a clear
and present danger to the authority of the law because of their connection to
prostitution, drugs, and criminality in general.
There are no grounds for complacency. This problem is not going to go away all by
itself. Gangs are a corrosive influence and they attract vulnerable young people into
their net. And as the economy continues to  shrivel and die under the mismanagement of
this Government, this problem will only con tinue to get worse. This would be an
opportune time for the Government to reas sure the public that  it regards gang
criminality as a high priority and that it will  ensure that the police have all they need in
order to tackle the problem. The Minister of Police should give a clear and direct
statement of what steps are being taken now in  regard to dealing to gangs. The public is
waiting for action, not indifference or weasel words.
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15851
We have taken the step in this House of passing a law banning gang patches in
Government buildings. It was a fine member’s bill, which we were very pleased to
assist the Government in carrying over th e line, but it was only a beginning. This
Government still dallies with being soft on crime and it still requires our
encouragement.
A New Zealand First Government will rid th is country of gangs altogether. We are
strong on law and order, and we will resour ce the police properly in order to enable
them to do the job that we all expect of them. State Governments in South Australia,
Western Australia, Queensland, Victoria, a nd New South Wales have shown us that
outlaw gangs can be banned outright, and our  own gang patch bill has given us a
template by which such gangs can be identified and classified. Banning the gangs will
not be in the too-hard basket for a New Zealand First Government. A New Zealand First
Government will be a Government in whic h people can have confidence, unlike this
sorry bunch across the Chamber, whose days are surely numbered.
We applaud the greater use of advan ced technology such as smartphones and
network devices that allow of ficers on the front line to work more quickly and more
effectively, but we do not accept that more technology can be a substitute for boots on
the ground. Only this week we heard that th e Government is considering trialling the
use of body-mounted video cameras for front-lin e police, such as po lice in the United
Kingdom are already using. These may be a va luable tool, but we have to question
whether, at $1,300 apiece, the millions of dolla rs involved might not be better spent on
more patrol cars, more ammunition for liv e firing training, or simply more sworn
officers available to the front line. Cameras to  help secure convicti ons will be of little
use if there are not enough officers to res pond to call-outs or if there are no available
patrol cars to enable them to get to those call-outs.
The priorities of a Government in which pe ople can have confidence must reflect the
realities of our modern world and address the concerns of ordinary people. A New
Zealand First Government will provide prope r and adequate funding and resourcing to
the police. We will bring an end to sole-cha rge police stations. We will bring an end to
the single manning of patrol cars. We will address the concerns of the people and allow
the police to do their job and protect us all. We will end the gang menace and make
people safe again in their own homes and on the streets of our towns and cities. That is
what a Government must do if it desires pe ople to have confidence in it. In this
Government we do not. Thank you.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I am very pleased and
privileged to stand in support of the Prime Minister’s statement and his motion that we
continue to have confidence in  this Government. New Zeala nders are a lot smarter than
the Labour Party and the Green Party think. That is quite obvious.
The facts show that what this Government has achieved in the last 5 years is quite
outstanding. The current accoun t deficit was almost 9 percent of GDP when we took
office; now it is 4.3 percent. Net external de bt had blown out to 84 percent of GDP; net
external debt has dropped down to 71 per cent. Inflation was running at 5.1 percent;
inflation is now only 1.6 percent. This is wh at New Zealanders need to hear. Mortgage
interest rates averaged 10.9 percent; mortga ge interest rates now average 5.9 percent.
That makes a big difference to households out there. Food prices went up 11 percent in
Labour’s last year in Government; food prices have gone up only 1.5 percent in this last
year.
These facts give comparisons between the previous Government, which really did
not achieve anything for New Zealanders, and what this Government has achieved
through the most difficult financial time that we have experienced in the last 70 years.
And, by the way, in 5 years th e spending of the previous Government went up by 50
15852 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
percent. That was an irresponsible use of taxpayers’ money, making the Government so
big that New Zealanders were going to be al ways encumbered with that incredible cost
of running this nation.
During this series of speeches on the Prime Minister’s statement we have heard some
wide-ranging opinions and point s of view. Following the Pr ime Minister’s excellent
speech, the Attorney-General got up yesterday to speak. I w ould have to say that it was
a superb speech, outlining in plain English the simple conclusion that the National-led
Government offers the best and the brightest future for New Zealanders.
Perhaps the most ludicrous statement in this  Parliament this year was made by the
Leader of the Opposition in reply to the Prime Minister’s  statement, when he said “The
Labour-led Government is waiting to take New Zealand forward.” Well, we know what
a statement of utter arrogance that is. What  an overstretch, what an overreach, what an
overstatement that is. Obviously, we need  to pop his bubble because, as you may see,
there is not a Labour-led Government, and thank goodness for that. There is not likely
to be one soon.
I am not sure what planet he is on, but it is not Earth. It is not Earth, this alternative
universe that the Leader of th e Opposition is trying to create  with rhetoric. By rolling
out statements such as that and by saying  such things, he is assuming that if New
Zealanders hear them enough, they will believ e them. I think that is an attitude of
arrogance. He is assuming or believing that  New Zealanders are not smart and do not
know the facts I read out. We need to be  debating the real differences between
Governments, not trying to put suggestions into people’s minds.
It is a world of smoke and mirrors and sleight of hand. I think we saw another
example of that with the baby bonus bungle. One can see that it was just plain trickiness
or perhaps it was incompetence, or maybe it was both. In fact, let me just read out the
comments that came out from the Leader of the Opposition back in Taranaki in mid-
October last year. What he said—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: He’s delivering the same speech . Do tedious repetition rules
still apply?

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: What he said, Mr Mallard, was that people were leaving
Taranaki. That is what he said the day that  Statistics New Zeala nd rolled out all the
figures about what is happening around the coun try. He said that ove r that period of 5
years there were 1,000 more people out of wo rk in the region, with the real median
weekly incomes for Taranaki dropping $24 a week. Even the Taranaki Daily News
came out the next day and re futed his comments. That is  amazing, is it not? Steven
Joyce and I came out and rubbished his claims. We said that he was making stuff up.
I think New Zealanders out there need to be  aware that there is the truth, and then
there are stories. There are facts, and there are fallacies. So often we have seen things
being made up, stuff being made up. In f act, let me just read out what the Taranaki

items.speaker: Daily News  wrote. It said
items.text: “Census figures showed the new Labour boss was wrong.
Statistics released yesterday show the region’s population had actually increased.” I was
quoted as saying that “the fi gures contradicted Mr Cunli ffe claims. ‘Since the 2006
income survey, real after-tax weekly income s in Taranaki have increased by $85.’ ” He
said incomes went down by $24; the real information is that they went up by $85.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: He’s not quoting himself. You’re meant to quote authoritative
sources.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: Listen. Through what he is sa ying out there he is trying to
create the impression that under a National-led Government things are going backwards.
If people hear it enough, they might believe it, but the facts are different, and people in
New Zealand are smart enough to get the facts on the issue. So I am  of the opinion that
Labour’s latest leader makes stuff up. Whether it is his distorted view of Taranaki’s
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15853
economy or whether it is the baby bonus bungle that tries to make his party look
progressive and generous, it is either trickery  or incompetence—it is either trickery or
