incompetence.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Who wrote this for you? Who wrote it for you?

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I wrote it—I wrote it.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Research unit.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: No, not at all. It is either  trickery or incompetence. And
guess what? On New Zealand’s Got Talent  you need to get only one cross and you are
out, but Mr Cunliffe has already got two.
So let me talk about an upfront, competent Government: this John Key - led
Government, which has worked hard and continues to work hard on things that matter
to New Zealanders, to everyday people. We are firmly focused in this election year on
carrying on the work programme that we started—not a big, huge lolly scramble, a
sugar rush for the voters, but some real economic policies. They are going to continue to
make a difference for New Zealanders, undergir d our aspirations, give us the ability to
do what we want to do, and enable us to subs tantially create jobs involved in export and
in the real economy, rather than the Government just creating them.
New Zealand streets are safer. We know th at. We are seeing higher achievement in
our schools. Interest rates have stayed lo wer for longer. We are seeing more people
come off long-term welfare and get into wor k. More patients are getting the treatment
they need and sooner. We are seeing patients getting elective surgery faster, with the
number of procedures up 34 percent in 5 years. They are the facts. Delivery has
increased from 118,000 patients treated in 2008, when we came in, to 158,000 in this
last financial year.
Here in New Zealand, providing better public  services with constrained funding has
been a huge challenge. Despite the toughest of  our times, our Government has invested,
on average, an extra $500 million a year into the public health  service. That is without
counting capital. If you were to look overseas  into the other hemisphere, in September
2012 the Irish health ministry announced a $200 million cost reduction package in an
attempt to reduce its deficit, which was expected to reach $800 million by the end of the
year. It planned to make significant cuts to se rvices and staff numbers. That is what is
happening on the other side of the world. Here in this small nation, faced with
incredible financial constraints, we increased our health spend by $500 million a year.
You have got to say that New Zealanders look at that—and of  course we can do
better, of course there are more elective surgeries that are needed—and they can see a
Government that has worked hard to deliv er for them. We have spent more money on
the front line than on the back office, and th at has been an important thing to do. We
went to the polls in 2008 with that promise, and I believe that we have achieved it.
As I said, I am very proud and privileged to  stand in support of the Prime Minister’s
statement. I believe that he is the best Pr ime Minister this nation has seen for many a
year and I believe that New Zealanders will reflect that in 2014 when we come to the
polls. Thank you.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I understand this is a split call. I call Gareth Hughes—5 minutes.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. Ng ā mihi nui ki a koutou. Kia
ora. In this speech I want to respond to th e Prime Minister’s statement. What I heard
was a negative, attacking, aggressive speech that focused more on the Labour Party and
the Green Party than on National and its idea s. I believe that New Zealanders want to
hear about parties’ policies. They want to hear about posi tive solutions. I believe that
the people of New Zealand are sick and tired of the negative attack politics, the petty
partisanship, and the dirty electorate deals. After too many years of putting the spies, the
casinos, the polluters, and the oil companies fi rst, New Zealanders know that it is time
15854 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
for a change. After 5 years of National sel ling out our assets and selling out to the
corporates, it is time to put people and the planet first.
This year New Zealand can make history wi th another first. In 8 months’ time New
Zealand could have its first good, green G overnment. In 2014 New Zealand can make
history by electing the most progressive Government this country has seen in a
generation. If the Prime Minist er is going to go negative, the Greens are going to stay
positive, and that is the Greens’ message this  election. A green Government will invest
in its people, will protect its environmen t, and will build an economy that works for
everyone. Key’s speech was all about sowing fear and saying that the economy is at
risk. Conditions are improving, but Key is simply papering over the serious cracks
facing us. We need a Government that is goi ng to put the books in order and is going to
address those pressing economic challenges, like massive overseas debt and like the loss
of control of our productive assets. We need an economic plan that is more than just
cramming more cows on our paddocks and hoping that foreign oil companies find
something in the depths of the ocean and do not leave too much of a mess trying to get
it out.
Coming out of the recession, it is time to  look forward to a prosperous future, a
richer New Zealand. We need to invest in infrastructure like a second internet cable,
support our smart IT sector, and take a dvantage of the $6 tr illion clean-energy,
greentech sector. For 30 years we have been  told that there is no alternative to
Rogernomics—by both his red and blue right -wing successors. Neo-liberal economics
plainly has failed New Zealand on its own te rms. We have droppe d from fifth in the
OECD economic performance rankings in 1951 to 23 rd today. We are more dependent
on dairy than ever, and we work some of the longest hours for some of the lowest wages
and pay some of the highest cost-of-living costs in the OECD. The neo-liberal economic
experiment has seriously cost  the country, but this year  we can make history and
embark on a new direction that works for us, not just for the corporate elites.
Likewise, after 30 years of growing poverty and widening in equality, it is time to
focus on real people, not just the T īwais, the Choruses, the S kycities, the Anadarkos. It
used to be said that the Prime Minister of New Zealand knew all the unemployed in the
country and that we did not have poverty. Well, that is far from the case now, and we all
know it. In a land that exports food that fe eds 20 million people, it is an absolute
travesty that our kids are still going to school without food in their bellies. Whole
families are deprived of work and we have got 270,000 Kiwi kids growing up in
poverty. We all know that it is highly unlikely that those young unemployed Kiwis are
going to be working on Anadarko’s deep-sea drilling rigs.
What we can see, and what the statistics  show, is tens of thousands of people
employed in high-earning sectors like IT. Th ey can be people building good homes for
New Zealanders, insulating under the roofs, and putting solar panels on the top. Cheaper
power from NZ Power, affordable housing fr om our Home for Life package, and lifting
our kids out of poverty put New Zealanders, people, first. A fair go for all may sound
like something from distant history, but this year we can make hi story by returning it
front and centre to our politics, and we can tackle inequality and poverty.
Thirdly, we need to protect what we love and what is the foundation for our
prosperity: our environment. Under National two-thirds of our rivers are unsafe for
swimming and, as we heard today, the nitrogen pollution levels are greater than in the
Yangtze River. We can grow jobs by cleaning up our rivers and reclaim our birthright to
safely swim in any New Zealand river or st ream. We can do our fair share for a stable
climate and grow jobs in climate-friendly i ndustries like public transport. We can take
advantage of the $20 billion annual economic opportunity that comes from clean-energy
sources like solar, geothermal, and wave.
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15855
In conclusion, what we are doing is offering New Zealanders a positive alternative to
the Prime Minister’s negativity. In this elec tion, every single vote is going to count, and
the question facing our c ountry is over our dire ction. In less than a year’s time we can
make history with our most progressive G overnment—a Government that is fairer, a
cleaner New Zealand, a richer New Zealand.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: Kia ora koutou katoa. Some of the most interesting
and some of the most revealing parts of th e Prime Minister’s statement were in the
things that he left out—in that which wa s missing from that commentary about the state
of the nation, public affairs,  the economy, and so on. Issues  like climate change did not
rate a mention. Environmental protection features scarcely at all in the statement—and I
have searched it. The word “sustainable” a ppears in the long statement only once, in a
rather dubious and questionable link to descri be the state of our fishing industry. The
Prime Minister’s primary focus was on the economy. That is unsurprising. But he talked
about the economy in a way that reveals his, and indeed his Government’s, lack of deep
understanding about the ideal relationship between the natural environment, healthy
communities, and a robust and resilient economy suitable for the 21st century.
There was one very important sector of th e economy that was scarcely mentioned at
all. It was completely overlooked by the Prime Minister, despite  the fact that that sector
of the economy employs someth ing like 30 percent of New Zealanders, it generates a
similar percentage of our GDP—about 30 per cent—and it constitutes a remarkable 97
percent of all of our busine sses within New Zealand. I tal k, of course, about the small
business sector—the small to medium sized en terprises, which were  once, and, indeed,
continue to be, one of the mainstays of our economy. This scarcely got a mention at all
in the Prime Minister’s economic rhetoric , or that of his Government. This is
unsurprising. It just continues a pattern of behaviour that has been very readily observed
over some time, not least of all by the ve ry hard-working peopl e who are in that
economy, which contributes 30 percent of our  GDP and employs about 30 percent of
our New Zealand workers. This sector is important in our towns and our cities, and
critically important in our provincial and ru ral areas, but that is where it is being most
overlooked.
At one time, National Governments could fairly have been described as the
champions of small business. Those days are long since gone. The Government’s
single-minded focus on dancing to the tune of large corporates, talking boldly about
macroeconomic issues and so on, has dist racted it from the daily challenges and
opportunities that confront the small to medium sized enterprises, the people working in
them, the owners and operators, and the many thousands of New Zealanders whom they
employ. National has stepped away from e ngagement with small to medium sized
enterprises. It has made only token gestures of support towards this critical sector.
Fortunately, the Green Party is here and we  are willing and able to step into that
space, to take on that role as the champions , the advocates, for small business in this
country. I myself come from a long career in  business. I have run my own businesses
and I have managed other people’s busin esses. Immediately before coming to
Parliament I was a business adviser for thos e companies wanting to put their business
on a more sustainable footing and to be prepared for the transition to a 21 st century low-
carbon economy. I have maintained those links.  Critically, we in the Greens listen
routinely to businesses and to  business organisations and we  hear what their problems
and opportunities are. They are definitely not  feeling the love fr om this Government.
They know that they are on th e outer, that they are be ing overlooked and neglected.
They know that they need to see a good cha nge in Government to a more progressive
Government before they will get the support and the advocacy that they really do merit
in terms of the wider economy.
15856 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
It continues to amuse me to ask busin ess audiences who their champion is in
Parliament. Many of them do not even know that  there is a Minister for Small Business.
Even fewer know who that might be. I think that  reflects the lack of  attention that this
Government has shown to this sector. There have been one or tw o useful initiatives,
such as RealMe, which uses the idea of one-stop engagement for small businesses—that
is a good thing. The business.gov t.nz website is a useful in itiative, but it is undersold.
Business people do not know it is there, beca use this Government is not putting that
message out there. There is no real drive to build the sector or to assist it. Sometimes the
best thing the Government can do for small businesses is to keep out of their way, give
them a clear run, and let them get on with it. But there is also  policy setting and
Government practices, behaviours, and attitude s that can actually reinforce the sector,
help consolidate it, and help serve it. The Greens look forward to being the party that
will do that. Kia ora.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: New Zealand is a c ountry that has huge
potential. We have got extraordinary natural beauty. We have got water, mostly where
and when we need it. We have got a very  strong base of agri cultural production. We
have got a proud history of people with a can-do attitude. We perform extremely well in
the global community, in science, in sport, and in culture. We rate highly with our
strong and stable economic performance, a nd have done so under this Government for
the past 5 difficult years. The New Zeala nd economy continues to stand out amongst
developed countries, growing by at least 3.5 percent in the last year , with Treasury
forecasts showing growth to be at a simila r rate in 2014. This recovery and growth has
not been by accident, nor can it be put down to luck, nor can it be put down to
improving and variable global fortunes. It is because this Government is continuing to
implement its plan to build a faster-growi ng economy with more jobs, and also to
support New Zealand families and all New Zealanders.
Over the past 5 years we have not wavered from our four key pr iorities. Firstly, we
are responsibly managing the Government’s fi nances, just like New Zealanders expect
us to do. Secondly, we ar e building a more productive and a more competitive
economy, because that is what is creating mo re jobs and increasing wages. It is the
economy that creates jobs, not Governments. That is something that I believe Labour
does not quite get yet.
Thirdly, we are delivering better public se rvices within tight budgets, because it is
taxpayers’ money that we are spending, and people are entitled to know that we respect
every dollar of it. Fourthly, we are supportin g the rebuilding of Christchurch, because
we pledged on day one that we would stand wi th the city, and we are. I well remember
former mayor Bob Parker saying: “Don’t forget us.” Well, we have not. The economy is
growing. More jobs are being created. Family incomes are rising. Crime is falling. More
elective surgery is being done in public hos pitals. Long-term welfare dependency is
falling and we are continuing to help familie s and older New Zealanders with generous
income support.
You know, I have sat through much of the de bate on the Prime Minister’s statement
and I see some stark differences across the House. The John Key - led Government
enters election year focused on the issues th at matter to all of us: a stronger economy,
more jobs, better front-line health services and educat ion, a safer New Zealand, and
rebuilding Christchurch. Across the House it is interesting. I have seen anger from a
pretty rudderless Opposition, whose members are quickly reverting to their tax and
spend policies and who just know, in their hear t of hearts, that an  election year lolly
scramble is not going to cut it with the New Zealand public. I reckon that they are angry
with themselves and I reckon that they ar e angry with their le adership. They are
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15857
thinking: “OK, so we are in an election year. Is this really the best  we can do?”. I think
it cannot be a very good place to be.
Labour’s last time in Government increased th e deficit, increased interest costs, and
put the economy into recession. Deep down wh at Labour knows is that it does not have
an answer, because all the economic and soci al indicators are heading in an upwards
direction. You know, it is impossible for Labour and the Greens to talk the country
down. They try, goodness knows they try, when  all the facts around the economy say it
is growing. More jobs are be ing created. Family income is rising. Crime is falling. We
have increased the number of elective surg eries. We have reduced waiting times for
cancer treatments. Long-term welfare dependency is falling.
Ruth Dyson stood up in the House last night  all angry faced and said: “National has
done nothing for the environment.” Really? Le t us just take a l ook at our record. We
have tackled the issue of water quality. Wh ere the Greens and Labour ran a mile in the
last term of their Governme nt, with their water plan of  inaction—their term not ours—
our Land and Water Forum is providing collabor ative solutions to some pretty testing
situations. Our emissions trading scheme settings provide the Government with
flexibility to balance our fair contribution to  global climate change efforts against the
costs imposed on New Zealand’s households and on business. We passed the exclusive
economic zone protections, where there we re absolutely none under the previous
Labour Government, and it was quite happy with that state of affairs. We continued to
develop marine reserves. We have invested  more research and rehabilitation on our
worst-polluted water bodies than the Green -Labour Government ever—ever—did. And
our Resource Management Act reform pr ogramme has set about simplifying and
streamlining the Resource Management Ac t processes, providing stronger central
government direction, and stronger environm ental reporting. Where was Labour in that
space? Nowhere.
Phil Goff got so angry about some kiosks being closed in Mount Roskill. Well, we
want our cops out on the street , not sitting behind desks. We  are a Government that has
overseen recorded crime per person down to the lowest level in 33 years. We are a
Government that has set a target to reduce overall crime rates by 15 percent—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: We’ve heard this speech before. Jonathan Young gave it.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: —the statistics do not lie, Mr  Mallard—violent crime by 20
percent, and, by the way, thank you for noticing, and youth crime by 25 percent by
2017. And we are already exceeding those target s. We are a Government that has 600
extra police on the front line and 34 neighbourhood policing teams not sat behind desks
in kiosks but out there in the most tr oubled neighbourhoods, tackling the causes of
crime. We have provided Tasers, rolled out  smartphones and tablets, provided lock
boxes for firearms, and a Prevention First st rategy that is working. We have clamped
down on gangs, organised crime, and P.
Our trade training, numeracy a nd literacy, and Out of Gate  strategies are supporting
prisoners before they leave pr ison and immediately after. We  want to give every prison
inmate the opportunity to turn their lives round, and we have released a new Youth
Crime Action Plan, which aims to reduce youth offending over the next 10 years. It is
one of the most critical aspects of our justice programme. National is completely
focused on making our communities even safer, and that is thanks to our justice team.
Then Phil Twyford got up and got all angr y about local government. Well, let us
have a look at our record. We have unified Auckland by establishing one council for the
whole region, substantially reducing red ta pe and bureaucracy. We have allocated $1
billion to repairs on leaky buildings so that  homeowners can get on with their lives.
That was in the too-hard basket for the previous Government. We have provided $5.5
billion to support Canterbury’s local council s to rebuild. We have focused on local
15858 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
government on supporting economic grow th and job creation. And we have
implemented our Better Local Government reforms to focus councils on stronger
governance, improved efficiency, and responsible management. We have made progress
on Better Local Government reforms.
Meka Whaitiri questioned the wisdom of water storage and the building of new
dams. Well, she is a new member. We know that Labour hates farmers, and there is
another member who continues in that sorry  tradition. But how about these facts? The
Ōpuha Dam in South Canterbury irrigates 16,000 hectares, and in a 2-year study the
Ministry of Business, I nnovation and Employment found that the dam added an
impressive $124 million to the South Cant erbury economy every year, and added 500
full-time jobs. That is regional developmen t. That is regional development based on
agriculture. Meka Whaitiri also questioned the impact of cycle trails. She is not the first;
she probably will not be the last. They just do not get it. Well, let me tell you that one of
the first cycle trails, the Otago Central Rail Trail, puts over $8 million and 96 extra full-
time jobs into the local economy, and that is in rural New Zealand.
Despite the improvements in the Govern ment’s books, the better economic outlook,
and the focus on better public services, ther e will not be a big lolly scramble from
National in election year. National will continue our steady as you go approach—that is
about getting better public services to de liver better results for communities, getting
debt under control, and ensuring we can w eather uncertain global economic conditions.
This Government will have fresh ideas to put to New Zealanders across a range of areas
this year. Labour and the Greens will promis e the earth, of course. We are only in
February and they are alrea dy promising to spend the thick end of an extra three-
quarters of a billion dollars this year. We are not going to do that. I am proud to support
the Prime Minister’s statement.

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: May I wish you, Mr Assistant Speaker
Robertson, the very best for this year. Thank you for the work that you have done for
the country and in this Parliament over a long career. It is my pleasure to speak to this
debate that we are having on the Prime Minister’s statement.
I look back over the summer. I took my fa mily down to the South Island on a road
trip. Since it was wet and freezing most of the time, I spent a great deal of time reading.
I came across an article in The Spectator magazine, entitled “Joy to the World”. That
cheered me up when the rain was coming in  horizontally. It made the point that
although pessimism sells in the media, which deluges us with tales of woe and
Armageddon, in many ways 2013 was the best year in human history.
More wealth is being created than ever before, with global GDP rising to around $73
trillion this year, and thanks to increasing global trade and surging economies in Asia,
that wealth globally has never been shared  more evenly. So the UN’s 2000 Millennium
Development Goal, you might recall, of ha lving the number of people living on $1 a
day by 2015 was achieved 5 years early. The goal of halving the number of people
without access to drinking water by 2015 was achieved last year. China, which is home
to a fifth of the world’s population, has st eadily opened its market s to capitalism and
international trade over the past three or f our decades, and it has reduced the number of
its people living in poverty from 84 percent to 10 percent today.
Yes, there are dreadful wars going on in Syria and places like that, there are millions
still living in poverty, and there are economic  and environmental challenges, but when
we step back and take a global view, we are living in a remarkable era, with the
prospect of seeing the end of famine and extreme poverty in the next few decades.
What has lain behind that transformation ha s been the spread of global trade, which
has followed the progressive opening up of previously cl osed or heavily protected
economies such as India and China. That is  why I struggle to understand the logic of
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15859
those, particularly amongst the Greens, who dedicate themselves to opposing further
progress in trade liberalisati on, such as that being attempted through the Trans-Pacific
Partnership. It is, indeed, international trade that is lifting hundreds of millions of
people out of poverty as we speak. As a trading nation,  New Zealand has been a
beneficiary of globalisation and stands to benefit much more if current trade talks
succeed. In the meantime, millions of peopl e have a chance to raise their living
standards as they are drawn into the global economy.
But, of course, global competition is always  challenging. If we are to continue to
prosper in a dynamic and competitive world, the next generation of New Zealanders
will have to shake off the entitlement mentality that has been allowed to develop over
the past few decades in New Zealand. That is  a real challenge for us. Will New Zealand
and the so-called developed countries be ove rtaken and left behind? Well, we may well
be, unless we recognise that we do have to continue to work hard and value education
and the importance of entrepreneurship and business in our country and in our
economy.
I thought that the Australian Prime Minister , Tony Abbott, put it pretty well in his
speech at Davos a few weeks ago. He said th at the global financial crisis “has not
changed any of the basic laws of economics  … You can’t spend what you haven’t got.
No country has ever taxed or subsidised it s way to prosperity. You don’t address debt
and deficit with yet more de bt and deficit. And profit is  not a dirty word because
success in business is something to be proud  of. After all, you can’t have strong
communities without strong economies to su stain them and you can’t have strong
economies without profitable private businesse s.” As government gets smaller, citizens
get bigger, and that is what we want. We  want empowered citizens. So I wish Mr
Abbott and his Government every success in translating those ideas into reality in
Australia, a country that has done incredibly well over the past few decades but has got
its own challenges right now.
As our Prime Minister has indicated, New Zealand has had 5 year s of strong, stable,
sensible government, and we have made remarkable progress over that period. The
Prime Minister alluded to a lot of those things in his statement. Let us not forget that the
current account deficit was almost 9 percent of GDP when we came into office 2008; it
is now 4.3 percent. The net external debt ha d blown out to 84 percent of GDP back in
2008; it is now down to 71 percent. Inflation—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Worst economic record in 50 years.

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: —that great theft of the sa vings of the people who are
struggling, whom David Clark seeks to re present—was running at 5 percent when
Labour was in power; it is now only 1.6 percen t and people can trust the value of their
money. Mortgage interest ra tes were averaging 10.9 percen t in 2008 and now they are
averaging 5.9 percent. Yes, they may be going up a little bit this year, but they are still a
hang of a lot cheaper than they were only 5 years ago when we came into power, and
that makes a real difference to the living st andards and the money that people have in
their pockets, not just in Epsom, where I come from, but all around the country.
Food prices were going up by 11 percent a year when Labour was last in power; now
that figure is only 1.5 percent. Government  spending had gone up 50 percent over the 5
years until 2008. It was a runaway train. Now Government spending is under control.
The economy had been going backwards for four quarters in 2008. We were at 3.5
percent last year, one of th e highest rates of growth in the OECD. Most important,
Treasury was predicting endless years of G overnment deficits when we came into
power. There was no track to getting back to surplus. In 2014-15 we will be back to
surplus.
15860 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
This Government has not wavered from its fo ur priorities that were outlined at the
start. We are about responsibly managing the Government finances, just like New
Zealanders expect us to. A nd there are risks. Why do we have to be cautious? Because
internationally the world still remains in economically uncharted waters. Nobody is
quite sure what is going to come from tape ring and trying to stop the printing of money
that has been going on around the world and wh at that will mean over the next few
years. So there are risks and we need to be careful.
Secondly, we have been concentrati ng on building a more competitive and
productive economy, because that is what we need to create jobs and to increase wages.
The Business Growth Agenda, which the Gove rnment has talked about consistently
over the last few years, is about rebuilding the growth capacity of the economy—lots of
little reforms carried out consistently. Steven Joyce and Bill English, in particular, have
been leading that charge. It  is about steadily removing th e roadblocks that discourage
investment in New Zealand.
I will run through those six areas again, just so people can be reminded of them. It is
about keeping open our markets and building st rong relationships in order to trade with
the world. The free-trade agre ement with China, which we do congratulate the Labour
Government on being involved with—I ju st hope Labour has not given up on free
trade—has been a really great deal for Ne w Zealand. Where would we be without that
China trade? I have no idea. The second thing is innovation. The National-led
Government is putting a lot of resources in to assisting research and development in
innovation throughout the private s ector, and we need to continue to increase private
sector investment in research and developm ent to reach international norms if we are
going to be a successful economy.
Thirdly, we need to keep the skills that  we need for a successful and innovative
trading nation, encouraging more of our peopl e into areas like e ngineering, information
and communications technology, science, hist ory, and other such subjects, such as I
discovered. Encouraging more capital to invest  in New Zealand is the fourth area. The
mixed-ownership programme has been a great success in terms of giving a shot of life
to the stock exchange in New Zealand. We ne ed to build on that. Capital investment is
core to building competitive industries and sustaining jobs.
Fifthly, we are about removing red tape and providing certainty to investors,
particularly in the resources industries, which could be so important to the New Zealand
economy in the future. And, sixthly, we need to keep building infr astructure towards a
growth-orientated country. In Auckland we ar e seeing the results of that with very
significant investment in the roading infrastructure. We are very much looking forward
to the Waterview tunnel opening and that  second bypass in the Auckland motorway
system, which will make a big difference to how we get around.
So the first area is getting back to su rplus, the second is building a productive
economy, and the third is getting better public services within tight budgets. I think the
Government has been very successful at making sure that taxpa yers’ money is spent
well and actually getting something out of it.  I think Bill English was right when he
talked about how, in the past , centre-right Governments have tended to think about
smaller government as about just slicing bits off when what we actu ally need is a bit
more demanding than that. It is about co mmunity expecting Governments to actually
solve a few problems and then move on, rather than just continuing to live off that.
Finally, rebuilding Christchurch is the four th area that we are focused on. On that
basis, I am very pleased to be part of this debate. Thank you.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: A woman came into my electorate
office today. Her landlord has ended her te nancy of 4 years because he wants to
renovate and sell, and she has not been able  to find another house that she can afford
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15861
near the school that her tw o boys go to. In order to keep  her children at  their local
school, her children are boarding with a friend, but there is no room for their mum, so
she is staying with another fr iend on the other side of the city. She came into my office
this morning to say that she had visited the children at the school and was walking back
across to the other side of th e city. She had no coat and it wa s raining. She is trying to
do her best for her kids. She is waiting fo r Housing New Zealand to even accept an
application for a house, and, even if it does, it is likely to tell her that it has no houses
available and to try the rental market. This is what is consistent ly happening to people
in my electorate and in electorates all around the c ountry—people who earn incomes
but whose incomes are not high enough to feed a family and pay market rents.
This Government continues to ignore the calls for action on child poverty, youth
unemployment, and the shortage of affordab le housing. It talks about wealth creation,
but where is the evidence that the people who deserve a fair share of that wealth are
getting it? Instead, the Salvation Army’s stat e of the nation report released today shows
once again that many New Zealanders are in creasingly being locked out of a fair and
just society. That report shows that there are some signs of  improvement in some social
indicators, but while at the top end of town the privileged few continue to do well under
this Government, child poverty and the lack of affordable housing are the time bomb
issues for our country. The report repeats cal ls for action to address these matters, as
well as rising living costs and the number of  families that are struggling to pay their
bills. This is this Government’s failure. John Key and National have been focusing on
those few at the top while hundreds and thou sands of kids are in poverty and many
young families cannot afford a home.
Labour’s Best Start package, which was announced a couple of weeks ago, is the
first in that series of practical and afford able policies that are going to make a real
difference to the fight agains t child poverty in this coun try. It is about improving
antenatal care, extending paid parental l eave, making sure that families have more
financial support when they need it when they have a new baby, and increasing the
range and the scope of early  childhood education. Those are very practical, very
targeted, very important steps that will make  a real difference. All of the experts agree
that the first 5 years of a child’s life are critical to getting that best start.
We have already taken some steps to a ddress the housing shortage with our policy
KiwiBuild. We will have a range of proactive policies to create jobs and increase wages
in our cities and our regions for young people, along with ensuring that they are going
to have the educational opportunities that give them the skills to contribute to building a
better and more modern society, and ensuring th at there is affordable health-care when
they get sick. These are tough times. Despite wh at this Government says, these are very
tough times for many New Zealand families. The Best Start package will make a real
difference in our programme of reform, wh ich includes health, education, housing, and
economic development.
In the last 5 years this Government has treated our country as a corporation, and not a
country. One of the worst outcomes of that is  that our regions are going backwards. In
the last 5 years this Nati onal Government has closed eight schools—eight schools—in
the Dunedin South electorate. Our city is lo sing daily commuter flights to Auckland
because Air New Zealand has admitted that it made a scheduling cut based on a demand
curve for the city, which is code that Dune din is not on a growth trajectory. This
Government is responsible for the closure of Hillside Engineering, which is the heart of
our manufacturing sector, because it decide d that cheap, poor-quality railway wagons
and engines were better than keeping and building a thriving skilled manufacturing base
in an important regional centre. We have lost skilled tradespeople, with families, who
15862 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
could not find decent work in our city. They  have had to move away and take their
families with them. That has had a flow-on effect throughout our city.
Steven Joyce is now backing a decision by AgResearch to shift the Invermay
Agricultural Centre campus in Mosgiel out of our city. It should be grown not shrunk. It
is a world-class centre for important resear ch. We have launched a petition on this. My
colleague David Clark has this week launched a petition on this very matter, and I urge
anyone who knows how important th at facility is to Otago and Southland to sign it. I
urge them to go and visit the website, which is www.saveinvermay.co.nz. Is that right?
That is right. I urge people to go to that website and to sign that petition.
The number of young people out of work in our city is one of the highest in the
country. A report in 2012 had it at 34 percent.  Everyone knows that this is a huge issue,
but what does Paula Bennett do? She shuts down the only teen parent course in the city,
which offers National Certificate of Educa tional Achievement credits and much-needed
second-chance training for teen mums who have no confidence, no skills, and now no
hope. We have got a pressure cooker situa tion building in Otago and Southland health
services, with work pressure from funding cu ts and a growing climate of fear in the
sector. We are seeing surgeons speaking out against the unacceptable situation for many
people needing surgery who are being bum ped off waiting lists and put on Active
Review, which delays their surgery indefini tely. Health professionals are under huge
pressure, due to inadequate funding, and some  fear retribution if they report mistakes,
which means that adverse events in the sect or are not being repor ted and our standards
of care are slipping.
There are suburbs in Dunedin, such as Cors torphine, with zero or inadequate access
to any health services. We are seeing more and more services, such as breast screening,
fertility services, and home support, being c ontracted out to organisations with no local
knowledge and for whom profit is the primar y driver. Mental health hospital care is
being halved, with inadequate community care available. I and my Dunedin North
colleague, David Clark, will hold a public m eeting on Friday, 28 February at Dunedin
Hospital, led by our very able health spokesperson, the Hon Annette King, to seek
public input into the health service cris is in our region. The underlying causes and
possible solutions must be addressed now, before things get any worse.
This Government does not care about our re gions. It does not care about those who
are struggling to pay their bills. Many of thes e people have jobs or had jobs until they
were made redundant because of this Govern ment’s policies. They are the struggling
middle as well as the lower-income people, and this Government has deserted them.
This Government is arrogant, it  is out of touch, and it is for the few at the top. It has
stopped listening to New Zealanders and is  continuing to look after itself and the
privileged few, at the expense of Kiwis.  This Government will ensure that any
economic recovery will benefit only the top few. We stand for opportunity for every
New Zealander, regardless of their background, their income, or where they live.

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: I would really like to
stand up and support the Prime Minister’s statement for a number of reasons. One of the
reasons is this: it annoyed the Labour Party so much and it also annoyed the Greens so
much. That is a reason to support it in the first place.
Let us start by talking about why we should support it. The economy has grown by
3.5 percent from September 2012 to September 2013 and has been forecast to continue
to grow in that light. When you compare that  with what is happeni ng internationally, it
is now being described as an economy that other people should take note of. You need
to ask the question why that might be. Ther e have been 66,000 new jobs. More people
are employed now than there were. The gr owth in young employment, that is, those
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15863
who are either studying or in some kind of educational activity, or in employment, is 89
percent. That is an amazing increase from where it was.
When you start asking the question why all of these things are happening, you start
to look at what the driver s are in the economy. Obviously, in Taranaki, where I come
from, the Taranaki - King Country electorate , things like energy have had enormous
growth in the life of this Government—in the very recent life of  this Government, I
would have to add, if you take the kind of gestation period these kinds of industries
need to get going and start to  get established. When you look at what an alternative
Government might look like, it is a Govern ment that would put a handbrake on all of
these developments. It would bring all of these developments to their knees.
I know that colleagues in the House will not be surprised by the fact that I am now
going to mention the primary sector. If you look at the biggest driver of the New
Zealand economy now and into the future, you will find that it is the primary sector. I
know that surprises the Labour Party and certa inly surprises the Gr een Party. In fact,
they go almost into meltdown when they learn th at, when they hear that. The fact is that
the growth in the New Zealand economy now and some time into the future will most
likely come from the primary sector and, in particular, the dairy industry, which is the
biggest part of it.
What have our opponents had to say about these sectors? What are the comments
from the Labour-Green Opposition? Well, they have said that the sector is based on
bulk commodities that they export in huge vol umes with no added value, and very, very
poor investment in manufacturing. How wrong could you be? The comment they add to
that, the one they continually add to that , is that it is at the expense of the
environment—it is at the expense of the environment. So let us run through those boxes,
because perception can often be greater than fact.
The perception, of course, is that the Green  Party is made up of a bunch of hippies
who smoke marijuana, wear sandals, and are sackcloth-wearing morris dancers. Most of
us know that is not actually true. There is at least 1 percent of them—at least 1 percent
of them—who do not fit into that category. I mean, they may wear jackets, but they do
not wear sandals—1 percent of them. They certainly wear j ackets, but not sandals. So
the perception of the Green Party is actua lly not right. In fact, when you look the
supporters of the Green Party, you will find that  a lot of them are urban professionals.
One of the real ironies, I guess, of the Green Party is that the members themselves come
from urban New Zealand. Most Green Part y members come from urban New Zealand.
They do not come from rural New Zealand; they come from urban New Zealand.
The Green Party perpetuates th e rant that the agricultural sector is a su nset industry
and will not have a future going forward. How wrong is that? When you look at the
amount of investment in manufacturing in  New Zealand, you find that, actually, the
biggest investment in recent times has been  a new powder plant, a new development in
Darfield in Canterbury—a big powder plant built by the dairy industry. It is not
producing bulk commodities, as the Opposition would have us believe. It is producing
very sophisticated food ingredients and so metimes nutraceuticals and pharmaceuticals,
at the very high end of the production chain.
Let us have a look at what th e Green Party also says. Ther e is an old saying that has
been around for a long, long time, and it goes “Physician, heal thyself.” The Green
Party members live in urban New Zealand, and we know that some of the most polluted
waterways in the country are in urban New Zealand. We know that; the science backs
that up. The facts are that that is the case. So why do they not start at their own back
door? Actually, I know one or two greenies who do not even recycle. How bad is that?

items.speaker: They do not recycle. So the reality is
items.text: go and fix your own backyard before you
marginalise and pick on what is a minority  group—that is, the agri cultural sector—in
15864 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
the way that you do, and totally denigrate th em in the way that you do, because you are
factually wrong and it is time someone challenged you over it.
Let us have a look at the combination of the Green-Labour Opposition and what it
would do if it were in power. Well, the first thing it would do is introduce a capital
gains tax. The Opposition members have told us that. They have said that they are going
to do that. The second thing is a methane emissions tax. The third thing is a higher
personal tax. The fourth thing is a higher company tax. The fifth thing they will do is
they are going to reverse the 90-day trial pe riod on employment. Then they are going to
put in place restrictions on ni trogen use. Then they are going to put in place restrictions
on water use.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: He’s making it up as he goes along.

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: No, no. All of these things ar e absolutely what the Labour-
Green Opposition has said over the last 3 years that it intends to do. It will do that.
Let us have a look at what th e flow-on effects of that will  be. The flow-on effects of
that will be that those young, aspirational, want to be  average New Zealand dairy
farmers will not achieve their goal. They will not get there. And if they do not get there,
then what happens? What happens then? What  happens if they do  not achieve their
goal? What happens then? First of all the economy starts to fail. Secondly, what you end
up with is overseas corporat es that are more interested in buying New Zealand land
because young New Zealanders cannot compete with them. So what is going to be the
response from the Opposition to that? What is  it going to do about that? What will its
policy be?
Let us come back to what this Government has done. What this Government is doing
is actually making that dream much more  of a reality. So the young people who are
aspirational and who are coming through th ese industries—and th ese people are not
unique to dairy; they could be  from any one of the primary sector industries, such as
wine, horticulture, viticulture, or meat a nd wool—can now see an opportunity and a
pathway to achieve their goal, which is to own the average New Zealand farm or
business, as it may be.
What would our opponents do about those peopl e? The first thing they would say to
them is that to have the $4.5 million that they  must have to be able to get a 50 percent
equity basis in the average New Zealand dairy farm, which now costs $9 million, they
are going to tax those people. They say that  those people are greedy capitalists. They
will do what they can to put as many hurdles as they can in those people’s way. In doing
that, the Opposition will achieve the exact opposite of what they hope to achieve, which
is economic growth for the low socio-economic areas of New Zealand, because the only
way you can lift low socio-economic areas out of poverty and do those things that the
Green Party and the Labour Party campaign on all the time is to have an economy that
can sustain jobs, growth, and opportunities fo r those people. That is something the
Opposition Labour Party cannot and has never b een able to understand. That is, without
jobs through growth, business investment, and opportunity, you will never achieve your
goal.
The real irony of that is that the environment ultimately suffers as well, because
without money you do not get investment in  environmental outcomes, such as the
riparian margin planting that is going on in Taranaki and such as the science and
investment that is now going into our global alliances—greenhouse gas emission
alliances, etc. That kind of investment dr ies up, as well. That type of philanthropic
activity that goes on in society does not exist, and you get environmental degradation as
well. So what we have is a black and white comparison this time round—that is,
growth, prosperity, jobs, progress, and good environmental outcomes versus
deterioration in everything.
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15865

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: It is a pleasure to talk on the Prime Minister’s
statement. I say to the member Shane Arde rn, who has just resumed his seat: I wonder
whether these jobs that he talks about, which this great National Government has
produced, include the 120 jobs that are going in a few weeks’ time out of Fitzroy Yachts
in New Plymouth, or the 125 jobs going from Goodman Fielder in Hamilton just last
week, or the 19 heavy engineering jobs also going from New Plymouth, announced just
2 weeks ago, or the dozens of  subcontractors who have lo st work because of the
collapse of Abode Design and Build in New Plymouth just a couple  of weeks ago as
well. What a great record this Government has shown in Taranaki—what a great record!
That member is partly from Taranaki—Tar anaki - King Country. I have to say that
that speech is the most stat istic-ridden and energetic spe ech that I have seen that
member give. I have to say th at it is a great disa ppointment that at the tail end of his
career—the twilight end of his career, or I would say, at the very rainy dusk of his
career—he should give a speech like that and illuminate us all with  just his talents.
What a pity that this House is going to lo se them and what a pi ty for the people of
Taranaki - King Country. Perhaps he will make way for someone who understands what
the modern economy looks like and what the future of jobs needs to look like—high-
value production, high-value jobs , highly skilled—all of the things that this country
needs and that this Government is failing to  deliver on. Since 1 Janua ry this year this
Government has been desperate to convince Ne w Zealanders that it  is all right here.
New Zealanders know, because they are living it, that it is not.
I can tell you now that people in Taranaki ha ve been shaken to the core by what has
happened in the last few weeks in their fa ir region. They cannot understand why, with a
Government that has boasted great economic growth—creating so many jobs, lifting the
wages so finely—suddenly all of them are losing it. They cannot understand what has
gone so wrong. Well, we know—we know. They ar e learning very quickly not to listen
to what members of this Government have to say. They are looking at the facts. They
are looking at what is actually  happening. They are looking at  their lives and are seeing
that it ain’t that flash after all. The truth is that New Zealanders are in a desperate search
for their fair share because they ain’t getting it. They have not had it for some time and
they are wondering where it is going to come from. It is not going to come from this
Government.
This National Government talks about the wealth it has generated and the growth that
it has encouraged, but it does not see the lives that people are actually living. They are
the people who are losing their jobs at the moment—good jobs, well-paid jobs, and jobs
in the very enterprise s and industries that we  actually need more of. The Government
can harp on about the wonders of farmi ng and the great work that the farming
community does, but that is an  industry that actually demonstrates what we can achieve
but need to do elsewhere. The Government has lifted productivity, but it has not shared
it with the workforce, I might add. It has not shared it evenly with the workforce in that
industry. It has lifted productivity, but that is not going to be enough to pay the bills that
this country faces well into the future. That  is why the Labour Party is the only party
talking about real investment in the next phase of economic development in this
country. It is long overdue—it is long overdue.
Ever since the start of this year we ha ve had a National Government desperate to
persuade New Zealanders, trying to convin ce New Zealanders, that wages have been
going up, that, you know, we have this outbr eak of egalitarianism from this
Government—Yeah, right—and that public debt  is under control. Definitely not. The
Government has spent the last 6 years convincing New Zealanders that even on the back
of a worldwide recession, the decline in inte rest rates is all its work. But you watch
when they start going up. You watch from Ma rch this year, when those interest rates
15866 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
start their gradual upwards climb, the Government will not be talking about what it has
done; it will be going back to the Government  of 6 years ago and blaming it all on it,
because this Government cannot face facts. This Government does not face reality. It
cannot look New Zealanders in the ey e and say “Actually, you know what? Our
economic programme? We’ve got it wrong. It ’s unbalanced. Not ev erybody is sharing
in the gains that we’ve made. Not everybody is getting their fair share. We are getting
an unbalanced economy, and, because of the Government’s level of borrowing, interest
rates are going to go up.”
Those members know it, which is why they all look down at thei r iPods and iPads,
because they do not want to face the truth a nd they do not want to look New Zealanders
in the eye and say “We did this. We have suppressed your wages. We are going to make
life harder for you by the end of this year, because your interest rates on your mortgage
are about to go up.” They will not tell New Zeal anders that and they will not tell them
that the Government is to blame. The Govern ment is living in a fa ntasyland. It is living
in Alice in Wonderland.

items.speaker: The truth is this
items.text: every inde pendent statistic tells you that  wages in this country, for
most people, are stagnant or barely moving. You have only got to look at the labour cost
index, which shows that it has barely moved. It has moved in sync with price inflation. I
will tell you what the other triangulation point is : it is the census data that came out last
week. That is the biggest data set you can im agine. That has also shown that although
inflation has gone up by about 1.6 percent in the last year, wages have moved the same
way.
Here is the contradiction that the National Government faces. Having convinced
everybody that average wages are going up and we are all living a lif e of great riches,
Bill English, 2 weeks ago, said it was time for employers to put wages up. But why, if
we are enjoying these bounteous wage incr eases under this Government, would the
Minister of Finance be urging employers to put wages up? Because the truth is that he
knows. He has seen the figures, and he knows they have not been going up.
The sad thing for this National Government, a nd why it is so out of touch, is that it
knows that its bedfellows in the rest of the community do not agree with it. So within a
day of Bill English saying—urging employe rs, begging them—“Please lift wages.
We’ve got an election to fight this year, and far too many New Zealanders know they
cannot get ahead under this Government. Pl ease put wages up.”, what did the business
community say? What did they say? Our dear old friend Michael Barnett, chief
executive of the Auckland chamber of commer ce, said: “I think it’s a nice sentiment
from a politician that there is probably going to be room for pay increases, but that’s
going to be the role of the employer.” He was very clear: “Don’t come to us asking for
pay increases. We’ll decide.” They know th ey can do that. They know they can do that,
because this command-and-control Governme nt knows that the bosses in this country
hold the whip hand. They decide. So it did not stop Michael Barnett, oh no.
The other great National Party friend, th e Employers and Manufacturers Association
(Northern)—that would be my good friend Kim Campbell. He was a good employer in
his day. He is now the chief executive of the Employers and Manufacturers Association
(Northern). He came out and said: “Oh. The labour market is starting to have
movement, but it’s still a l ong way from being red hot. It’s  still a long way from being
red hot. And in terms of wage rises, you’ve got to get productivity to match the wage
gains.”
Here is the message to employers in New Zealand: we have had productivity gains in
this country for the last 20 years. Productivity has gone up 50 percent. Wages have
barely moved as a consequence. And, actua lly, the productivity ga ins have all been
captured by business owners and barely passed on to workers. That has got to change,
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15867
because we are out of balance and we are out  of sync, and something needs to change.
Something needs to change—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: You need to get out more, Shane.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Something needs to change, and if there is anybody who needs
to get out more, it is not the Salvation Ar my. The problem with the Salvation Army is
that, of course, it does not set up its soup ki tchens in Parnell, or in Fendalton, or in
Ilam—

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: Or Herne Bay.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Or in the wealthy areas occ upied by National Party MPs. The
Salvation Army is there with the people who are doing it hard. It is there on the streets
with people who are doing it real  hard. So John Key might not  have seen the Salvation
Army caravan, but there are people who are dependent on it, and the Salvation Army
has confirmed that the number of people drawing on its food banks  has risen. I know,
from getting around the food banks in Taranaki at  the end of last year, that they could
not explain why the number of food parcel s they are handing out has gone up. They
could not explain it, because all the message s they heard were that things have got
better.
This Government has run out of time and run out of ideas, and it is time for a change.
Those members arrogantly para de around saying that things  are good, but real working
people know that it is not. It is  time for a change, and that change is coming. It is time
for New Zealanders. They know, they are on board, they want to see something
different, and they want to share in the weal th and the gains that they know this great
country can deliver.

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I am delighted to speak
today on the Prime Minister’s statement to Parliament. Today I could talk to you about
the Government’s expert management of the economy, and how John Key and Bill
English together, through economic smarts and hard work, have successfully guided this
country through the toughest economic times safely and well. But everyone knows that.
National is known and respected for its ability to manage our resources and to look after
our economic interests.
Less well known but equally as important to all New Zealanders is National’s ability
to manage our natural resources and to look after our enviro nmental interests, and we
are doing that equally as well as we have managed the economy in the last 5 years. The
Prime Minister and the National Governme nt have faced up to our environmental
challenges, just as they have faced up to our economic ones. We are making real
progress in cleaning up New Zealand’s environmental act. Our country is far better now
economically and environmentally than it was when we took it over 5 years ago.
All New Zealanders closely identify with the natural environment, and the National
Government understands that the emotiona l and economic well-being of New Zealand
is absolutely predicated on our clean, green, natural environment. That is the conviction
that underpins the Bluegreens philosophy. I quote the Prime Minister, who says:
“Bluegreens are part of a new generation of thinkers who beli eve that successful
economic and environmental policy can and mu st go hand in hand in order to provide a
cleaner, greener, brighter future for all New Zealanders.” Nobody can argue with that.
To prove that this National Government is working hard and smart on environmental
issues, here are our top 10 environmental achie vements from the last 5 years. No. 1 is
water. It is New Zealand’s biggest challenge, and the Natio nal Government is up for it.
Managing water well is a long -term commitment, and we ha ve started by investing in
clean-ups from the past. Over $450 million is going out to clean up our iconic
waterways and to introduce a legislative framework for the future. As environmental
commentator Rod Oram explains, New Zeal and is on the verge of a historical
15868 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
breakthrough in freshwater management because of a fundamental shift in the
understanding, the principles, and the practices by farmers, by other water users, and by
this Government with the setting of bo ttom lines on water quality, allocation, and
nutrient levels in every river in New Zealand. It is true.
The combination of the Land and Water Forum, the National Policy Statement for
Freshwater Management, and the new Nati onal Objectives Framework on freshwater
provides, for the very first time, a met hodology to improve our water management, our
water allocation, and th e water quality in our  rivers and streams, and that is real
progress. We know it will take time, but the stakeholders ar e working together and that
is going to be a process that works.
No. 2 is climate change. The other huge gl obal environmental challenge is climate
change, and, as a small country far away fr om the rest of the world, we are responding
to that challenge in an innovative and nimble  way. Yes, we have our emissions trading
scheme, but we are also cutting emissions in  very practical ways. For example, we are
promoting very successfully renewable energy in all its forms—wind, solar, geothermal.
For example, Genesis is no longer generating energy using fossil fuels. Our level of
renewable energy generation is the highest it has ever been.
We have also invested in the Warm Up New Zealand: Heat Smart programme. That
is a scheme that has insulated 235,000 pr ivate homes. We are now completing the
project for 69,000 State houses. Insulation, of course, reduces demand for energy and it
cuts emissions and pollution, as well as im proving the health of thousands of New
Zealanders, so the Warm Up New Zealand: Heat Smart programme has huge benefits.
But where we can make our greatest contri bution to climate change, where we can
really punch above our weight, is in the role  that we are playing globally in climate
change science, policy, and aid. Through our leadership in the Global Research
Alliance, the work of the Agricultural Greenhouse Gas Research Centre, and the
Sustainable Land Management and Climate Ch ange Plan of Action, we are developing
innovative and technical solutions to redu ce greenhouse gases from agriculture, which
can be applied worldwide.
We have invested $80 million in our P acific neighbours to help them develop
sustainable technologies to adapt to climate change. Finally, we have taken a valuable
lead role in international negotiations to cut subsidies on oil and to achieve a global
binding agreement to cut emissi ons. All in all, it is a pr etty good contribution from a
small country like ours.
No. 3 is air quality. As everything is linked in the environment, our focus on
renewables plus new emissi on rules and pollution regulations has meant that New
Zealand has now got the cleanest air on record.
No. 4 is the Environmental Protection Au thority. Looking to create a sustainable
future, we have created new institutions to  regulate and protect the environment. The
Environmental Protection Authority was es tablished in 2011 as an environmental
regulator and watchdog, and it is doing a great job.
No. 5 is protecting our oceans. Our oceans are the last of the untamed frontiers. Until
we passed the exclusive economic zone legisl ation last year, ther e were absolutely no
rules to protect the marine environment. No w all activities need to comply with the
regulatory framework. The exclusive economic zone legislation means that any kind of
exploration or production has to go through international sta ndards. Believe it or not,
although we had no legislation and no rules be fore this bill, Labour and the Greens
voted against it. The National Party understands that there are people who are concerned
about the impacts of oil and gas explora tion and production, but now, because of the
exclusive economic zone legislation, for the very first time in hi story the industry is
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15869
required to meet international best practice stan dards, to operate safely, and to take care
of the marine environment.
We have increased protection in our very special marine areas. National has always
been interested in marine protection. We  passed the very firs t marine reserves
legislation and created the firs t marine reserve back  in the 1970s. Last  night we passed
the Subantarctic Islands Marine Reserves Bill, which now means that a huge area, 9.7
percent of our territorial waters, has no-take marine reserve protection.
No. 6 is expanding the conservation estate. We have invested in the conservation
estate. We have added another 12,400 hectar es to schedule 4, which contains our
highest conservation areas, and 36,000 hectar es is under the prot ection of the Queen
Elizabeth the Second National Trust. We have created a new conservation park for
Auckland on Great Barrier Island, and are working towards a new kauri national park in
Northland’s Waipoua Forest.
No. 7—we are battling for our birds. We have just begun the biggest and most
ambitious pest eradication project in our history. We are committed to destroying the
rats, mice, stoats, and possums that are killing our birds, and we are absolutely focused
on protecting our most beloved and endangered species: the kiwi, the k ākā, the kea, and
the mohua. Thank you.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Kia ora. Thank you ve ry much. It is a
pleasure to see you again, Mr Assistant Sp eaker Robertson. Can I just take this
opportunity to wish you all the best in your life and career ahead of this place and thank
you for the service that you have provided to New Zealand in your role.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Kei te pai.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Now that I have got that out of the way, I will move on. I am not
going to give out too many bouquets.
I am very happy to stand here as a Nati onal member of Government to support the
Prime Minister’s statement and his motion.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Where did you get that tie from?

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Mr Cosgrove, my tie is a stunning ensemble, as opposed to—what is
that? Is that a dark blue tie? Yes, it is almost a National-blue tie, Mr Cosgrove. Thank
you.
The last 5 years have been very, very challenging years for New Zealand. I think that
there has been a very significant change in the fiscal landscape and the political
landscape in New Zealand. I would like to in form members as to why. Obviously, the
global financial crisis is something that we r eally have not seen in generations. It is a
landmark event in terms of the global economy, and the global economy is still
struggling with the implications of the global financial crisis.
The Canterbury earthquakes made a signi ficant dent in New Zealand’s GDP. We
have seen some significant challenges as a re sult of that particular event. Interestingly
enough, the Labour Party did not want to know about it a couple of years back, but now
that there is starting to be growth and i ndustry generated out of the rebuild, suddenly it
is all because of the Canterbury earthquakes.  So we can take it on the one hand but not
on the other—but we are used to that with the Labour Party.
The National Government has been totally focused over this time on re-engineering
the New Zealand economy, not only to deal with those two significant fiscal events—
very, very challenging events —but to ensure that we have  a disciplined, structured
process and a programme of po licy to ensure that we invest for growth while getting
debt under control and ensuring that we get absolute best value for services. This is
because this Government ultimately is spending taxpayers’ money and, unlike the
Greens, we understand that there is not a ma gic ATM somewhere that just prints out
dollar bills.
15870 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
We have responsibly managed this economy, and we will be back in surplus. Budget
2014 will be a significant landmark of the te nure of this National Government. We are
building a more competitive and productiv e economy. The New Zealand economy is
now recognised as a global standout. We know that because the Opposition is no longer
talking about the manufacturing crisis, or what have you. The reason it is not doing that
is that the economy is performing—a 20-year high in terms of busin ess confidence. So
now Labour is talking about: “Oh, it is all for their mates and there’s nothing for the
poor and those who are more challenged.” It is that same old Labour rhetoric.
Unemployment is tracking down. There ar e 66,000 people in employment now who
were not in employment 12 m onths ago. There is a 6 per cent unemployment rate and it
is tracking downward. The member to my left, Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga, has led so
valiantly some of the most significant changes in welfare since welfare was introduced,
and it has happened virtually without a splas h. I want to commend the member for his
leadership in that.
We have been rebuilding Christchurch. Is  it not a pleasure to see the activity, the
opportunity, and the excitement down there after the very, ve ry challenging times that
the Canterbury community have had? Can I commend Gerry Brownlee and the other
Ministers and members of Parliament down there—Nicky Wagner and co.—who have
done such an outstanding job for that part of New Zealand.
We are ensuring that be tter public services exist in th is country. Reported crime is at
a 30-year low. I mean, that is just an unpr ecedented result in times when, financially,
things have been such a challenge. We s ee more elective surgery. We see people in
cancer treatment far faster. Right across the spectrum of our Government departments
what we see is greater efficiency becau se this Government has set targets and
expectations. What we know when we set targets and expectations and we demand
some accountability is that we get results, and that is exactly what we are getting. I want
to commend those Government departments and their employees for the hard work that
they have done for a number of years now, whic h is starting to deliver results across all
areas of Government.
We have been a very, very disciplined Gove rnment and we have stuck religiously to
those four core priorities. The recovery is happening and it is well on the way. The
economy is well advanced in growth, as quart er upon quarter results have shown, but it
is a fragile recovery. That is something that I think New Zealanders get. They
understand. They understand that, actually, wh at was acceptable 10 years ago no longer
fits in the New Zealand economic environmen t—from a family point of view, from a
Government point of view, and from a busine ss point of view. There has been a shift in
people’s thinking. The Labour Party has not woken up to that.
But one of the fundamental things, and th e difference between this Government and
Labour and the Opposition parties, which would like to be in this position, is credibility,
and that is not something that is issued on a business card. You know, you cannot just—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Oh, this’ll be good.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: That is right, Mr Cosgrove, listen up—listen up, Mr Cosgrove.
Credibility cannot be just issued on a bus iness card. Credibility comes about because
people know what they are doing. They do what  they know and they do what they say.
Credibility comes as a result of a recipro cal relationship between those who lead and
those who follow, because credibility can be  given only by the followers. It can be
given only by the followers.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: “Willing buyer, willing seller”—that’s what Peter Dunne
said.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: Of course, that party would know a ll about the lack of credibility in
terms of their leader and following, because only one-third of that caucus supports the
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15871
current leader. We know that. But credibility is a reciprocal arrangement—a reciprocal
relationship—and it can be given only by the fo llower. But for the follower to give that,
they have to have belief that  the leader can do wh at they say and say what they do, and
that is where David Cunliffe has a major problem. Sir Peter Blake really summed it up
when he talked about leadership. He said : “Having vision is not enough. Change comes
through realising the vision and turning it into a r eality.” It is easy to espouse worthy
goals, values, and policies; th e hard part is the implement ation. Implementation is very
hard when only a third of your caucus supports you, and the public actually know that.
When people cannot trust what people ar e saying, that also erodes any hope of
credibility. We have seen that today in the most glaring example of why all New
Zealanders should be worried about a Labour-Greens Government. We have seen that in
the form of the Best Start policy, or what has now become known as the “Worst Start”
policy. David Cunliffe either did not know his figures or wanted to fudge them. He then
turned round and blamed his staff for what was being said, and then eventually, when he
realised that there was no other way, it was a mea culpa and he fell on his sword. But by
then the damage was done.
Another layer to eroding that credibility co mes with how David Cunliffe intended to
pay for it. He said: “Oh, well, we’ll get rid of that idea of taking GST off fruit and
vegetables. We won’t do that. By crikey, l ook at that! We’ve saved ourselves $1 billion
or $2 billion, and we’ll take that $1 billion or $2 billion and we’ll use that to do the
good old Labour bribing for the election comi ng up.”, as those members have become
so accustomed to doing. But that is like me walking into a car dealership and saying
“Do you know what? I want to buy that Ferr ari.” and then having a second thought, and
thinking “No, I am more of a Holden ma n. No, I won’t buy that  Ferrari. Goodness me,
I’ve now got $250,000 in my pocket.” Hello? Do es anyone else see anything wrong
with that?
Credibility is an enormous issue for Davi d Cunliffe, and the issue is what happens
when David Cunliffe is gone. He is hanging on and he will say a nd do whatever he has
to do, including hauling waka, Robinson Crusoe  - like, from the s hores of Waitangi in
the pouring rain. It just happens  to be a nice phot o opportunity there, of course. He will
do whatever it takes. He will sing, preacher-like, from the top of a bus because he
knows that if he loses this election—or wh en he loses this election—he is gone and
Trevor Mallard is promoted back to his rightful place as Parliament’s troublemaker.
So he will do and say whatever he needs to do, and that includes doing a deal with
those guys over there, the Green Party. St effan Browning should be paying attention
because that guy wants to destroy the New Zeal and agricultural sector. This is the first
time in New Zealand’s history when what we  actually see is not a case of either a
Labour Government or a National Government , as most people perceive it. Coalition
agreements and MMP is a difficult and unstable form of Government, in my view. What
they see is a deal that has been cut to give one-third, or a proportionate share, of Cabinet
seats to the Green Party. For the first time in this country’s history, if that were to be the
case, what we would see is a Green Party that would be the tail wagging the dog. It
would be. And if anyone wants to know what sort of danger that presents, have a look at
what happened in Australia. I can see from the look on Mr Cosgrove’s face that when
you lie down with dogs you are going to get fleas. Boy, that is going to get real itchy,
and the New Zealand public know that.
Credibility is fundamental, but what they know  is that here they  have stability and
they have people who have proven their way and who have served us through the
toughest times that this count ry has known in generations. On  the other side they see
people who will do anything to get power and say anything—
15872 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
