items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: On this side of the House we cannot have any
confidence in a Government that favours the few, we cannot have any confidence in a
Government that is out of touch, and we cannot have any confidence in a Government
that is so arrogant that it does not listen to the people.
This morning the Salvation Army released its state of the nation report, and there was
a lot more reality in that state of the nation report than we have had in the Prime
Minister’s state of the nati on speech. There was a lot mo re reality about what is
happening in New Zealanders’ lives in that  report than the Prime Minister has any
knowledge of at all. In  that report the Prime Minister was given a D for efforts on child
poverty. He was also given a D for housing affo rdability, but I will come back to that
one shortly. The D for efforts on child poverty  is an indictment on this Government’s
policies and on where it has been going for the last 5 years. When the Government
looks after only the few at the top and still continues to believe in  that old, discredited,
outdated, irrelevant trickle-down theory, which never worked in  the first place, then its
only possible mark is a D—is a failure. For those who do not remember what a D stood
for, it was an epic fail, in anybody’s terms. That is how the Salvation Army rated this
Government for its efforts on child poverty. So  that is what the people of New Zealand
are looking at right now.
The Salvation Army sent a very clear message to all political parties. It said that bold
policies are needed to address child poverty; to  address things that come out of that that
are related to it, such as domestic violen ce and violent crime; and also to address
housing. Bold policies are required, and we see none of that coming out of the
Government. If the economy is improving, as the Government would have us believe,
how is it that there are so many people, so many families, locked out of any of the
benefits or potential benefits of that im provement? How is it that there are so many
people who are feeling that they are locked out of a fair and a just society?
I would like to pick up on some of the Salv ation Army’s work as it relates to Nelson,
where I live and work. Major Jill Knight, who is the head of the Salvation Army in
Nelson and who was the one who fronted the Salvation Army’s state of the nation report
in Nelson, said that more was needed to be done to combat problems such as child
poverty. She said that “Stresses from low wages and seasonal work can lead to domestic
violence and child poverty”, a nd others agreed with her. This was the front-page story
on the Nelson Mail today. This was the front-page story.
The Government is so out of touch that its member for Nelson has no idea of the
level of poverty, the level of deprivation, that exists in Nelson. Everybody thinks that
Nelson is a wonderful place to liv e in, and so it is—a nd so it is. But it is a hard place to
survive in. It is a hard place to survive in  because it has that double whammy of low
seasonal wages and extremely high house prices  because of its desirability, because of
its physical environment. Yet it is incredib ly difficult for young families to get by in
Nelson.
The common claim about Nelson is that it  lives on sunshine wa ges. There are two
definitions of sunshine wages. One is that low wages plus sunshine are meant to be the
things that help you get by. So it does not ma tter that people earn low wages; they have
the sunshine to compensate. That is one interpretation. The rea listic interpretation,
however, is that, because of the seasonal wo rk, in many instances people can work only
when the sun shines. They do not get paid for the days when it rains and they cannot get
out, they cannot harvest the crops, and they cannot contribute to the primary production
for which the Nelson region is famous. So se asonal work and sunshine wages mean that
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15873
workers get to make money only when the sun sh ines. If it rains, the workers do not get
paid.
I just want to quote from Jill Knight, w ho is, as I say, the Salvation Army Nelson
Tasman Bays Community Ministries manager.  She said the Salvation Army report was
reflective of problems in Nelson. She said she saw people “at crisis point”, and she put a
lot of this down to low wages and a relian ce on seasonal work. What she said was this,
as quoted in the Nelson Mail: “Families that have regular income may be sort of okay, it
might be sunshine wages but it ’s regular; but for seasonal wo rk, if it’s a wet day people
don’t get paid, and because it’s  seasonal work they only ear n on the day they work, it’s
not an easy situation,”. She said most of the families they see are trying to do the right
thing, but they are spending more than half of their income on  rent and then there is the
power bill.
The Prime Minister had the nerve to get up in this House today and say the Salvation
Army ought to get out more. I have never h eard a more arrogant, dismissive statement
applied to that body of people who are famous for working for the underprivileged, who
are the ones who, unlike this Government, get out and do the hard yards with the people
who need assistance. This Government’s idea of assistance is money for Rio Tinto, is
money for Skycity, and is money for Chorus . That is this Government’s idea of
assistance. To get out and help the people in  need, it will give $30 million to Rio Tinto,
it will sell problem gambling and the downstr eam social consequences of that to
Skycity, and it will make sure that the ailin g Chorus will roll out  broadband at a price
that families cannot afford—but it will make sure the company does not fall over.
What happened to competition? What happene d to the survival of the fittest, which
the National Party is so famous for represen ting? This Government is doing harm. Its
purpose is not to do harm. Its purpose is to assist the growth and the development of this
country, but it is not doing that. It is lock ing out the majority of people—including
families in Nelson who are doing it hard—fro m the results of any improvement in the
economy, locking them out of any hope for their families, and locking them out of any
security going forward.
When the number of food parcels that are given out in the Nelson area is nearly twice
as high, two-thirds higher than it was before—and, in fact, in a 10-day period in January
there were certainly some 70 food parcels given out to just over 200 people—there is
something wrong in the State of New Zealand. This Government is leading the
rottenness in the State of New Zealand. It has run out of ideas, it has run out of energy,
and now it needs to be run out. Thank you.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: The previous speaker is normally really
interesting to listen to and covers a fair range of topics, but the conclusion of that speech
was a disappointment to hear from the Hon Maryan Street. She can do so much better
than that—than throwing that little bit of rhetoric around.
In the Prime Minister’s stat e of the nation statement he stated that the Government
will remain focused on the opportunities to  use New Zealand’s natural resources
productively while maintaining the environmental standards that preserve and enhance
the quality of our environment. I would like to concentrate on that topic and the
Opposition’s attitude towards the use of natu ral resources, or its perceived attitude,
which could be damaging to the future of New Zealand’s economy. The oil, the coal,
the gas, and the water are mentioned. We need  to earn the money that we require to
progress as a nation.
Mrs Thatcher once said—and it  has been repeated more than once in this party—
“The problem with socialism is that eventu ally you run out of other people’s money.”,
and that is so true. But, interestingly, in this country we have one party—and I am sure
it will not mind me mentioning it; indeed, it will probably be pleased—that has a
15874 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
solution for that. The Green Party has a soluti on for that. The Green Party, as I say, is
made up of nice individual MPs,  but it is often associated in the public perception with
recreational, illegal, and currently unregulat ed drugs. It would take a leaf from the
fairytale character who spun gold out of st raw—spun gold out of straw—because what
it intends to do would simply be to print more money.

items.speaker: Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi
items.text: What’s that?

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Well, it wants to print money, but there is an irony
attached to that—an irony. This is a $20 note—a New Zealand $20 note. You cannot
tear it in half. You cannot tear a bit off it. Why is that? It is be cause it is made of
polymer. And if the Green Party prints more money and at the same time it restricts the
use of oil and things that are used to manufacture the plastic polymers, it will not have
the notes to print because of its lack of support for the mining industry in New Zealand.
So one does have to wonder about the raison d’être of a party that is happy to share
the association with other na tural resources in New Zeal and—basically, marijuana, an
underground economy that is riddled with criminality, the exploitation of the vulnerable
and the young, the glamorisation of guns, dr ugs, and dreadlocks, and the unfettered
continuity of an un-taxable, parasitic i ndustry destroying the livelihood and lives of
many in New Zealand neighbourhoods and comm unities. If that s ounds a little rugged
or tough, I make no apology for it. I make no apology for it, because the Greens have
claimed that if marijuana were legalised, the industry would become viable and taxable.
I have had enough exposure to some of the things that Mi ke Sabin has experienced in
his career and in his constant fight against drug use to convince me that the chances of
that happening—trying to organise it on a legal basis—are pretty low.
In the ongoing work of creating New Zeala nd’s narrative, Nati onal seeks to work
with resources that are already available, like water, minerals, oil, gas, and precious
metals. Of course, like all things precious  and unique, these resources are often well
hidden, they are in fragile environments, and they have been this way for a number of
centuries.
In an effort to release the wealth locked up in the natural currency, we must seize and
use the strengths of the other valuable na tural resource available to us, which is
ourselves—ourselves. New Zealanders have a tremendous capacity, and an international
reputation, for being problem solvers. It is al most a mythical level that they are credited
with having, in terms of solving problems.  I guess it is a consequence of moving on
from the tough and ready pioneering outlook that  has carried this nation so far: making
the most of what was readily available and light to carry, and choosing our bravest to
carry out the job with whatever protection was available. Our legislation reflects a
growing maturity as we have warmed to a position as a First World country in a world
desperately looking for responsible, enlight ened leadership a nd well-considered
sustainable industry, and that is what this Government, particularly under the leadership
of this Prime Minister, is providing.
Anyone visiting the West Coast, which is  something of a favourite area of mine,
cannot miss the memorial at the Brunner Mi ne, where, on Thursday, 26 March 1896, an
explosion killed all 65 miners below the gr ound. To deepen the tragedy, the widows
received no compensation and mostly had to leave town, and the men were buried in a
mass grave at Stillwater. I pass that on most days when I am at home. The days of old?
Well, the 1970s were a time when songs like Pete Seeger’s “God’s Counting on Me,
God’s Counting on You”, using the famous lin es “… drill baby, dril l leads to spill,
baby, spill”, were written to shine a cri tical light on sloppy and dangerous mining
practices, and the people in the mining indus try also listened. Pike  River, where an
explosion occurred on Friday, 19 November 2010, when 29 men died, is still in very,
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15875
very recent memory. There are many commemo rative sites in Greymouth, as well as
continuing work to assist the families.
The New Zealand mining indus try has learnt from this, as has the New Zealand
legislature. Millions of dollars, a lot of expert opinion, as well as research and
experience from overseas have created an i ndustry that is self-aware, self-motivated,
well regulated, and ready to earn for New Zealand. It is an industry that we can be well
proud of—worth $1.1 billion of mineral exports, according to the Government’s
Petroleum and Minerals Sector Report, 2013. There are 8,000 direct and indirect jobs in
the mineral industry, as quoted in the 2011 re ports of the New Zealand Institute of
Economic Research and Business and Economic  Research Ltd. The minerals industry
believes that, if properly encouraged and managed, growth in the New Zealand minerals
sector could treble in on-the-ground investment and output over time. The average wage
for a miner is $105,000, which is around double th e national average wage—that is also
from the sector report. Mining is, therefor e, a good job to have. All the figures have
come from the appropriate bodies that have these figures available.
Mining supports regions. For example, mining on the West Coast earns around one-
third of the region’s hous ehold income off a footprin t of—wait for it—14 square
kilometres, as compared with  the total area of the regi on of 23,000 square kilometres.
Therefore, mining earns a very high wealth off a very small footprint. No other land use
in New Zealand earns anywhere near th at amount—none. OceanaGold has calculated
that it would take 700 y ears of farming at Macraes Flat to earn the same wealth as that
expected during the life of its East Otago goldmine. And the profits do not just go
offshore. Up to 86 percent of mining output stays in New Zealand as salaries, taxes,
rates, and other charges and payments to s uppliers and contractors. That figure comes
from Newmont Waih īGold. The fact is that mining today is a high-tech industry,
employing skilled people and producing es sential materials for New Zealand and
overseas markets safely and responsibly.
But let us examine the possibility of what might happen if we were to get a Greens-
Labour Government. I cannot see how Labour can say that it would not change things. I
think it would, because it would have to inco rporate the Greens into its mix. And good,
good Labour thinkers—people who have been a ssociated with the party for a long time;
I can look across the House and see some of the prominent people—would they be
included? Would they be bypassed? “ WWGD”—what would the Greens do? Would
they be like an overly cautious curator of an  art gallery or museum exhibit, where they
shout: “Don’t touch. Don’t change anything. Le ave things for the children.”? Well, to
put it into a musical context,  as Matt Bird, the underestimat ed musical genius and ex-
Green smoker, mentioned in one of his poem rhymes, we are the children—we are the
children. It is up to us to decide the future that our parents and grandparents bequeath to
us.
To conclude, the thing is that the National Government has plans. We are prepared to
back them with well-considered fiscal strategy; not just to spend money, not just to
make money, and not just to try to turn everything back to a pre-currency economy.
National has plans that include us, the resident s of these beautiful islands, these jewels
of the South Pacific. A Government—

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: It is a pleasure to  take a call in this
debate on the Prime Minister’s statement. It  is particularly a pleasure to follow my
friend and colleague Chris Auchinvole, from the West Coast, who is such a staunch
champion and advocate for all things on the Coast, including economic growth and hard
work and determination. He has been, and continues to be, one of the Coast’s great
15876 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
advocates in this House. When he retires at  the election this year, we are going to miss
him. So, Chris, it is a pleasure to follo w you in this debate. He is a member who
understands basic economics. He pulled out a $20 bill, and for a Scotsman that can
sometimes be quite an unusual thing—a $20 bill—and tried to rip it in half. I am sure he
has never tried that before, but it was a good thing.
I rise to support the Prime Minister’s very  excellent statement to  Parliament from a
week or two ago. As we enter this election ye ar, we on this side of the House, as the
Government, are firmly focused on achie ving a strong economy, more jobs, better
health and education services, a safer New Zealand for all New Zealanders, and, of
course, we remain completely committed to the rebuilding of Christchurch. As we enter
this election year, New Zealanders will be f aced with a stark contrast in their decision

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: It is my privilege and honour to speak
in support of the Prime Minister’s statem ent. I would like to congratulate Scott
Simpson, the hard-working member for Coroma ndel, on his excellent contribution. I
hope that he will continue to serve this H ouse for a long time. I begin by congratulating
my Government on playing its role in ensuring that New Zealand—to borrow an
analogy—is the rock star economy of the world. Can I just take this opportunity to
remind my fellow parliamentarians that you do not get called a rock star economy by
chance. It happens only when the people who are given the responsibility of steering the
country do so responsibly and do not lose sight of their goal, no matter how tough the
conditions may be.
We made a commitment to New Zealanders  when we got re-el ected in 2011. It is
with a lot of pride that I can share that ou r Government is continuing to implement its
commitment. Every day we are working to ensure that New Zealand remains a
competitive economy, where our incomes and our  level of lifestyle rise. Unlike our
friends in the Opposition, we have a plan that  we have seen work. We are also working
tirelessly on getting the public accounts back in surplus and reducing debt. We want to
ensure that taxpayer dollars are spent efficiently on the services required by the
taxpayers, such as better healthcare facilities, reduced waiting time for surgeries, and
more police on the roads to ensure the safety of our citizens. We are building
infrastructure that contributes to the development of the New Zealand economy, be it in
Christchurch, State highways, or even ultra-fast broadband.
The economy has grown at a wonderful rate  of 3.5 percent, which has earned New
Zealand the title of rock star economy. The latest projections by Treasury advise that
our country should be in surplus by next year. This is, in my opinion, an achievement of
significance, considering the projections of high debt levels given to us when we started

Finance, Bill English, on their leadership in achieving this.
I would like to add that the ethnic community  has played a very effective role in
contributing to this economy. In Manukau East, most of the migrants I know are
engaged in employment or are entrepreneurs. The purpose of their moving here—

of those people; you are just trying to earn your own patch. The purpose of their moving

There is little surprise th at the number of people moving to New Zealand continues

items.text: My apologies, Mr Assistant Speaker. The Prime

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: It is a great pleasure to support

doing my annual general meetings—about 14 of them—and it is a great pleasure. They

items.text: I am there all the time, Mr Cosgrove, I assure you. But

Today, of course, I am able to tell the people in the provinces that it is 4.3 percent.

items.text: I tell them on a weekly basis. I would tell them every day

The net external debt back in 2008, after that Labour Government had blown it out to

Every New Zealander knows that interest ra tes are all important and that under this

food prices have gone up no more than 1.6 percent. What a huge change—what a huge
change. And I can tell you that everyone in the provinces, everyone in the towns and
cities of New Zealand, realis es very much that under a Na tional Government there has
been major improvement.
But let us go on. What about Government  spending under Labour for those last 5
years? Government spending increased 50 percent—50 percent—an d in health, of
course, there was no extra produc tivity. In fact, productivity  had declined. Of course,
there was that huge increase in bureaucracy  that we all know about, which happened
under that dismal Labour Government. Now Government spending has been very much
curtailed. It is under control, and, of course, we have a forecast of a surplus in the—

items.text: —2014-15 books. Clayton Cosgrove, let me just remind

during that time. What we need in this coun try is a low, broad-based, simple tax that
people can understand, that has cl ear incentives of reward fo r effort. That we will get
under a National Government. We will get the opposite under a dismal Labour-Green
alliance.
One other thing that deeply concerns th e good people of Hunua is the sorts of
impositions that the Labour-Green new emi ssions trading system  would place on the
businesses and the farmers of New Zeala nd. In Hunua our biggest single employer
happens to be New Zealand Steel. It woul d find it extremely, extremely difficult to

items.text: Let us go back and have a l ook at the other plan Labour

I would like to turn to Labour’s glori ous leader—the one at the moment—Mr

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: We have heard a number of speeches
from our opponents such as Jami-Lee Ross, Mr Auchinvole, and the last one, Paul
Hutchison, who used words like “integrity” a nd “respect” and who talked about what a
lack of integrity and a lack of credibility ot hers have. But it is really interesting, I have
got to say, especially from Mr Jami-Lee Ross over there, who talked about all sorts of
things but forgot those two magical words “John Banks”. He forgot those two magical
words “John Banks” and then the other two ma gical words “Peter Dunne”. They are the
two piles that prop up this rotten Govern ment—a Government and a Prime Minister
who will say and do anything in order to cling to power.
You have Peter Dunne, who is the Maxwell Smart, in intelligence and spy terms, of
Parliament. In fact, Maxwell Smart would l ook a bit smarter than Mr Dunne, given that
if he leaked documents, he would probably be  able to cover his ow n tracks. This is a
man, in an indictment on Peter Dunne—[ Interruption] No, no, this is serious. This is a
man, Peter Dunne, who went quietly. He coul d not front up to the Prime Minister and
went quietly. And because he went qui etly, by his own admission—having resigned—
he admitted that he was unworthy to hold a ministerial warrant. He was unworthy and
untrustworthy to hold a ministerial warrant because he resigned. Yet the Prime Minister
15882 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
a couple of months later, when he thinks the heat is off—and we are talking about
national security here. We are not talking abou t some peripheral offence; we are talking
about breaching national security. But the Prim e Minister is so de sperate that he will
bend any rule and break any moral authority he has because, apparently, Mr Dunne is
now trustworthy. He is worthy to hold a mini sterial warrant, even though day after day
in this House he cannot confirm or deny and he will not comment as to whether he was

Bureau.

would break a Minister, and you would never get inside or outsid e a Cabinet if you
could not say categorically that you had not l eaked an intelligence security document to
a journalist or any external person. In any other Westminster Parliament in the world, I
say to Mr Ross, you are gone, you are history, you have no credibility, and you have no
integrity. But, oh no, the genius out the back, of course, has got amnesia.
Then we move on to Mr Banks, of course—the  other rotten pile in this Government.
Last night I saw Mr Banks supporti ng the tobacco lobby on the Smoke-free
Environments (Tobacco Plain Packaging) Amendment Bill. I thought about this and I
thought: “Let’s work this thr ough.” Maybe if there had been a sort of poli tical health
warning on the plain brown paper bag that John  Banks picked up with the cash in it that
said: “This is political death to you, Mr Banks . If you pick this up, it is political death.
This bag, plain packaged as it is, will be haza rdous to your political health.”, that might
have helped old Johnny, the Hon John Archibald Banks, who now is facing the court
after being convicted of two crimes before  this—a criminal, regardless—and he now
goes to court for a third time. But we cannot go much into that.
That, Mr Ross, is about integrity and cr edibility, is it not? The two magic words
“John Banks” and the two magic words “Peter Dunne”—eminent New Zealanders, of
course, accused of exceptionally serious offe nces. One cannot lie straight in his bed
because he cannot admit whether he did it or not, but he is good enough to be in John
Key’s Cabinet, and the other— if you line John Ba nks up with Colin Craig, it is lunar
and lunatic. The mad, the bad, and the sad—tha t is what National relies on to prop up
this Government. So let us not have any hi gh-handed lectures from that mob over there
about credibility and integrity, Mr Ross, unle ss you are prepared to get up and formally
give us your opinion of your Cabinet colleagues Mr Banks and Mr Dunne.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: Ask Mr Russel Norman.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Ask Mr Dunne, Mr Ross, wh ether he did it or not.

cracker, going beyond, of course, the fact—I w ill have to pick this up after tea, of

will present evidence that may help him.

items.text: Before we rose for the dinner break I was

items.text: Did you see if he was there?

items.text: No, he was not there, but  there was an astronaut

the Prime Minister believes he is trustworthy but has failed to ask for an explanation as
to why he leaked national s ecurity documents. Did he do it or did he not? The moral
height bar for getting into Cabinet from th e Prime Minister’s point of view is: “Don’t
tell me whether you did it or not. I’ll just s ee no evil, hear no evil, and you’re back in.”
Why? Because there is another little deal to save his politi cal scalp and Mr Dunne’s in
Ōhariu.
I have got to say that when it comes to  integrity and credibility, those men and
women over there take the biscuit, whether it be the deal with Rio Tinto, whether it be
the deal with the casino, whether it be ignori ng, in an arrogant way, people in respect of
the asset sales referendum, or whether it be —as Maryan Street said tonight before the
dinner break—the Prime Minister telling the Salvation Army basically that it should get
a life, get around a bit, and see what is happening in th e real world. I would bet London
to a brick that the Salvation Army and Campbell Roberts, the good people in that
organisation, who I think for beyond a century have been doing good work in the
welfare area, would be far more in touch w ith people than this Prime Minister. Let us
15884 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
hear another speech about credibility and in tegrity, and the next one should talk about
“Brown Bag Banks” and Peter Dunne.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: I was going to start off talking about
credibility and integrity, but the previous speaker, Clayton Cosgrove, has done it for us.
Thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker, for the opportun ity to speak tonight on the good news
of the state of our nation. But, first and foremost, I am here tonight to speak in support
of our Prime Minister’s statement in which he outlined the great performance of this
Government to date. He cemented National’ s intention as we lead up to the next
election. This is a Government of aspirati on, independence, and inspiration, and I could
add integrity and credibility as  well. All we do, and all we ha ve attempted to do in the
time we have been in Government, is aime d at giving people the opportunity to grow
and thrive and giving our economy the opportunity  to grow and thrive. Over there is a
gaggle of people whose policies create dependence, stifle growth in the private sector,
and, in the case of the Greens, stop everything.
One of the great achievements of this Government has been the ability to reprioritise
Government spending under that outstanding  Treasurer, Bill English, dramatically
changing the trends of gross expenditure a nd ineffective public services promulgated
under the Labour Government of Helen Clark. It  has worked. We have been able to re-
incentivise business, education, Government services, and our produc ers to the extent
that we are now seeing more jobs created daily, more houses  built than for many years,
a health system that is catering for more a nd more people on a daily basis—better than
ever before, in fact—and more exports leavi ng these shores than ever before. This has
all been made possible by the Business Growth Agenda of this Government.
I will detail a few of these initiatives th at have had a partic ular impact in the
Rangitīkei. The promotion of our export ma rkets since we have built a more
competitive and productive economy, the development of free-trade agreements, and the
potential for the Trans-Pacific Partnership a nd those types of agreem ents have certainly
incentivised the producers of my electorate to perform to new levels of effectiveness.
Farmers have new levels of confidence in the future, and enthusiasm for now, with
intentions of improving environmental syst ems and sustaining productive systems that
have never been stronger. We have an oppor tunity because of th e activities of this
Government to lead the world again in this field. This is something we have struggled
with.
I want to speak for a minute about i nnovation. Massey Univer sity, many of the
Crown research institutes, a nd the Riddet Institute are all in my electorate and are all
thriving in the new environment that this G overnment has created for them to operate
in, as they play their part in the scientif ic contribution to the Government’s growth
aspirations. Only tonight we saw a remark able presentation—I thought it was beyond
belief, frankly—across the corridor, in the Speaker’s Science Forum, where we saw the
use of nanotechnology. I think it is too late to replace my teeth, but certainly it will
replace the teeth of many of our younger member s of Parliament in the future. All they
do is poke it into a printer, and it comes out the other end, and you have got a new set of
teeth. I could not believe it, frankly, but it will make a massive difference to the way the
world sees a lot of things. One of the slogans they had up there tonight was “I have seen
the future, and it works”. It was a quote from  Lincoln Steffens. Actually, I guess this
Government has seen the future to some extent, and it is working.
I want to speak for a while about tourism. The northern Rangitīkei has been watching
for a number of years as people have left, jobs have disappeared, and businesses have
struggled. Under this Government, and partly due to the Prime Mini ster’s brilliant and
innovative cycle trail development idea, the number of new job opportunities and things
for young people to do in our electorate has increased significantly. The tourist
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15885
activities in the north of my electorate, a nd I am sure in many other electorates, are
significant—notably the Forgotten World Adve ntures initiative, which uses golf carts
and the old railway line from Taumarunui to Stratford. There is something like between
40 and 80 of those a day bei ng picked up, on a good day, and us ing that railway line all
the way to Stratford, creating new business opp ortunities along the way. It is much like
the Otago Rail Trail, actually. It is creat ing new businesses along the way, creating new
jobs, and giving people new hope and a different  way of life from they have had before.
I think the tourism initiative is amazing, and in  an electorate like mine it has just made
such a difference. That will undoubtedly be our future.
The positive bullet points being generated by this Government are more prolific than
Kane Williamson’s bat, and you would not ofte n have been able to say that about a
cricketer, but they are. Like BJ Watling, we scarcely let a ch ance go by. Having said
that, there are some challenges for us in rural New Zealand. The maintenance of
infrastructure in areas of static or little gr owth is a challenge for those communities, but
we need to ensure that it continues. Ro ads, electrical reticulation, and communication
are all big challenges for us in rural New Zealand, and are all big challenges for
Governments as we strive to, I guess, provide  those services. As we leave the global
financial crisis behind, these matters will be  addressed in the future. They are being
addressed now, but it is a challenge for us and it is something that we must bear in mind
as we move forward in New Zealand. The gr eat investment in cycleways, walkways,
our environment, and agriculture is doing a lot to contribute to that.
The Green-Labour coalition that we s ee across the House today has already
commenced the lolly scramble that election year is for those members. It is a typically
irresponsible attempt to bribe the electorat e by using taxpayers’  funds irresponsibly.
The damage these policies do is evidenced by some of the challenges this Government
has had in arresting the drama tic growth of the public sector and, of course, managing
the challenges that the student loan scheme has provided for us as a country.
I had the privilege of attendi ng the Waitangi celebrations last week. It was the first
time I have ever been there. I went there, I guess, with an expect ation probably created
by the press in New Zealand—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: And the Prime Minister.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: —and when I got there I found something very different. The
celebrations I attended did not remotely rese mble anything I had seen in my time by
reading the press and watching it on televisi on. As the Opposition members have raised
the subject of the Prime Minister, I have to say that I think the Prime Minister has an
enormous amount to do with th e fact that Waitangi is what it is today, as opposed to
what it was some 8 years ago. I thought it was a special occasion. When you think about
it, we were welcomed by a proud people to  their place. When you go to someone’s
house for the night you expect to be told what  they expect of you. You expect to have
the right to answer them back. It is exac tly how it worked for me and it certainly
worked like that for the Prime Minister. I was most impressed with Waitangi. I think
that as a country we have a whole lot to protect around the celebration of Waitangi Day.
I think that it is a very special occasion fo r anyone who is able to go to Waitangi and
celebrate that day and something that should be taken up at every opportunity.
I want to speak briefly tonight about some of the activities that  are happening in our
primary sector. Of course, the Primary Produc tion Committee in this House has a lot to
do with that. When you think that we have the Animal Welfare Amendment Bill and the
Food Bill before that committee at the moment, one realises the importance of those two
pieces of legislation, when you think that  they prop up some $30 billion worth of
exports. They not only prop them up but they support and guarantee the future of that
$30 billion worth of exports.
15886 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
The other leg of the triumvirate, I guess,  for our primary produc tion sector is the
environment. I want to talk very briefly a bout the contribution that this Government has
made to environmental improvement in New Zealand. We have led the way in this field.
The Land and Water Forum, the work of our regional councils, and, of course, the work
of the Ministry for the Environment are significant. I think that we can be very proud, as
a Government and as a country, of the repa ir and the work that is going on in our
environment to improve our opportunities in  the future. After all, our tourism and
agriculture sectors rely entirely on the environment for their futures.
I am very proud to be a part of this Government. I think we are doing pretty well, I
think we have had some difficult times, and I look forward to the future with
confidence. I want to conclude tonight by supporting the activities of this Government
and the great work of our Prime Minister and his Cabinet. Thank you.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I call Tim Macindoe.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker—
what an excellent choice. I would lik e to begin tonight by acknowledging and
congratulating you, Mr Deputy Speaker. I want to acknowledge you because over the
Christmas recess you, along with other coll eagues, announced that you would not be
returning to this House later in the year. You have given great service to this Parliament
and to your electorate of Invercargill and you have been a great friend and mentor to
many of us, so I acknowledge you. I also want to congratulate you—and I am pleased to
see that smile on your face. Members of th is House may not know that in the early
hours of this morning, the member for Inve rcargill welcomed a nother granddaughter
into the world. Ultimately, we are all here because we want to leave this country in
better shape for future generations. I believ e that you have made a great contribution
and that you will be able to have your granddaughter proudly on your knee in years to
come and tell her about the country that you kne w and that she is going to inherit and in
which she will no doubt make her mark.
I would also like to say xin nian kuai le to all who are celebrating the Chinese New
Year at this time. In honour of this event I am wearing a tie that I purchased 3 years ago
when I passed through Shanghai. Those viewers with good eyesight watching on
television may think that I am confused into thinking it is the “Year of the Panda”. I do
know that it is the Year of the Horse.

items.speaker: Hon Todd McClay
items.text: I thought it was a birthday present.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: To all of them may I say gong xi  fa cai. No, I am still waiting
for your birthday present, Mr McClay, but I know you will be delivering it in the very
near future.
Of course, the Chinese New Year is not just for Chinese people. My very good friend
Melissa Lee tells me that for Koreans this is a particularly auspicious year. It is the year
of the blue horse for Koreans. So ahn nyung ha se yo to all our Korean constituents, and
especially the fine Korean community up in Hamilton West, and best wishes to you as
well for this New Year. I hope that my Korean constituents and my Chinese constituents
and others are as encouraged as I am by this exciting omen—the year of the blue
horse—as we commence this election year  in 2014. May we enjoy the blue horse,
plenty of blue sky, and most important, a nother blue Government to keep the great
progress that the John Key - led Government has been delivering over the last 5 and a
bit years going in New Zealand for many, many years to come.
In many respects 2014 has got off to the best  start that many of us can remember for
quite some time. Whereas there was a steady diet of bad news from the start of 2008,
when the combination of the global fina ncial crisis and La bour’s reckless and
uncontrolled spending plunged us into recession, and then those difficulties were
compounded so dramatically by the Canterbury earthquakes in the years that followed,
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15887
it now seems that almost every day there is a little glimmer of hope; a little bit of
announcement of something good that is happe ning. Whether it is in extra jobs being
created, extra people gaining access to edu cation—from early childhood right through
to tertiary level—or signs of growth in the economy, there is all sorts of good news that
is really encouraging. Of course we are all very relieved to see it.
But the important thing is that we are not out of the woods yet. Those who think that
we are, are ignoring some significant challenge s that we still face. As the Minister of
Finance is prone to say, we are experien cing grumpy growth. If I could leave one
message from my contribution tonight, it is that at the end of th is year and beyond, we
must not jeopardise the significant but fragile signs of recovery that we are enjoying at
this point. We must ensure that we stay the course, that we make sensible decisions, and
that we continue to work for growth and for real engagement in the economy, and not
try to have some sort of election year lolly sc ramble that is totally irresponsible and that
will set us back from all the great gains we have made.
In my view—and most crucial—the frighteni ng level of Crown debt that we face is
the No. 1 challenge that we must continue to  face up to, to confront, and to overcome in
the years ahead. At one stage, Treasury was tipping that that debt would be in the region
of $74 billion. In a country of 4.3 milli on where many people are not in paid
employment, where people are living longer,  and where a large number of people are
young students, there is a relatively small taxpayer base. We were on target at one stage
for core Crown debt to reach $74 billion. I am very proud of the fact that under Bill
English’s outstanding stewardship that debt is already down to around about $65 billion,
but that is still a really horrific challenge.
We must ensure that we get into surplus as  soon as possible so that we can start to
repay that debt. That is one of this Government’s core fo cuses and core aims. I do not
want to be leaving that debt as an absolute albatross around the necks of your
granddaughter, Mr Deputy Speaker, of my ch ildren, and of their children to come. We
have got to be realistic about that, so this  year must not be an election year lolly
scramble.
The previous Government proudly boasted that it left the coffers bare. Despite
governing through the most auspicious and pros perous times in the first years of this
century, it spent the lot, as Michael Cu llen proudly boasted, and left the incoming
Government—and we were already in recession when the Labour Government went out
of office—with a situation where for 5 years the previous Labour Government had
allowed public spending to increase at tw ice the rate of revenue. No household could
operate a budget like that. People would be  defaulting on their mortgages and they
would be hugely in trouble. No Government  should operate like that, and shame on the
previous Labour Government for the fact that it did so.
But the really sad thing is that more than 5 years later, the Labour members appear to
have learnt nothing. They still seem to thi nk that they can convince the voters—that if
they bribed them sufficiently with the voter s’ own money, they might just be able to
buy their way back into office. Well, that w ill not do. It would be absolutely reckless. I
do not believe that the New Zealand public will fall for that. It is really important that
they keep in mind that worrying Crown debt that we collectively have all got to repay
when they cast their votes at  the end of this year. No thing that our opponents have
announced—and they have opposed almost wit hout exception the initiatives that we
have implemented—shows that they have learnt  any lessons at all in the last 5 years.
Nothing shows that they are fit to be consid ered as an alternative Government any more
today than they were 5 years ago, when they were thrown out of office so
comprehensively.
15888 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
Our opponents have opposed initiatives designe d to create real and sustainable jobs.
They have opposed welfare reforms designed to  encourage and assist people to become
self-reliant rather than dependent on the State for a lifetime—in  many cases through
cyclical, intergenerational welfare dependency. They have opposed education initiatives
designed to help those who need it most to raise their levels of achievement. We know
that that is the most important thing we can do to assist many to have a better chance at
securing a job, breaking out of  the cycle of welfare depe ndency, becoming self-reliant,
and being able to enjoy the quality of life with  their families that they aspire to as much
as we do. They continue to believe that huge bribes using voters’ own taxes is the recipe
for success in election year. Well, the people of Hamilton West are not fooled by this,
and they know that the smug, nasty attacks fr om some of the speakers we have heard in
recent times are no substitute for coherent and intelligent policies. They know we
cannot continue spending money we have not  earned and they share my determination
to repay debt.
New Zealanders are coming home from Aust ralia and elsewhere in record numbers.
For the first time in a long time, the situ ation on this side of  the divide looks
considerably more attractive than it does on the other side of the Tasman. That is
something that we can celebrate, but it also  shows just how fragile certain stances are
internationally, and we must not be comp lacent for a moment. New Zealanders are
gaining qualifications and increasingly these are leading into good, so lid jobs in record
numbers. Our commitment to the people of  Canterbury is unwavering because they
have been through a lot and they need a Gove rnment that stands shoulder to shoulder
with them, and this year will be a very important year in the Canterbury rebuild.
I will be campaigning proudly on my record. I am very proud of the improvements
we are seeing, like tangible gains in the de livery of public serv ices. We have set
measurable targets and we are delivering on th em, whether they be in health, education,
law and order, or so much more. That is a crucial aspect of gove rnment. Could I close
just by saying a warm congratulations to t hose who have been working on the Waikato
Expressway up my way. I can now travel from Taupiri to my home in Hamilton West in
about 20 minutes—6 months ago it took nearly twice that length of time. I look forward
to the opening of the other stages of the Waik ato Expressway in the years to come. It is
a huge commitment to the people of Waikat o. We must not drop the ball on it. This
Government is delivering on its promises in  all sorts of ways. I will be proud to
campaign on that record, and hope it will be rewarded with re-election.

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: I am an MP for the Gr een Party because I love
New Zealand. I want to protect our precious  places for the long term, and I want our
country to be a place where everyone has a fair go and is looked after when they need
help. We in the Green Party have a vision of  New Zealand where every river is safe to
swim in, where every child grows up in a warm, healthy home, and has enough to eat
and has good access to a good public educatio n, and where there are good, green job
opportunities—jobs that will help us meet th e challenges posed by climate change and
jobs that will enrich our planet and our ci vilisation, rather than destroy it. That is
entirely possible.
It is entirely possible to create an economy that looks after our people and our planet.
How are we going to do it? It is not rocket science. We in  New Zealand are innovators.
We have been pioneers. We do not need to  wait for bigger countries like the United
States or Australia to tackle the most pressing issues of our time, which are, basically,
climate change and inequality. We can lead  the way. The Green Party, I think, has the
best policy platform to achieve that. That is why I became an MP for the Green Party.
I am a highly educated person who had a successful professional career, and I
decided to stand for the Green Party because our policies are the ones that are the most
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15889
likely to achieve the good, green  change that I know most  New Zealanders want. How
are we going to do it? Well, we  start by recognising that it is not as easy as  getting rich
quick by selling off public assets and opening our waters to risky deep-sea oil drilling.
We cannot get rich by exponentially increasin g the number of dairy cows, because that
will inevitably mean that we will be increasing the pollution in our rivers.
Our competitive advantage in New Zealand is that we have a “clean, green” brand.
That is part of how we sell ourselves overs eas. It is how we sell our agricultural
products. It is how we sell our  tourism. Those are two of our biggest exports. The best
way to build long-term prosperity is to pr otect our beaches and our rivers, our natural
environment, because doing so not only bene fits the industries that we are selling
overseas, our products that we are selling, but it also benefits New Zealanders who want
their children to be able to swim in clean rivers.
One of the keys to achieving this good, green fu ture that is entirely within reach is to
do things smarter. Unfortunately, the Nationa l Government is not doing that. We could
invest in infrastructure that makes it ch eaper and easier for people to get where they
need to go without increasing our current account deficit or our carbon emissions, but
the National Government is not providing lead ership in this area. John Key has decided
to put the interests of bi g overseas extractive companies ahead of everyday New
Zealanders. In his statement, the Prime Minister clearly outlined this Government’s
priorities, which do not take us towards a smart,  green, fair future; in fact, they take us
backwards.
So Key says in his statement that he is very proud that the Government is going to be
continuing its multibillion-dollar programme of investment in infrastructure, including
the construction of Transmission Gully through a public-private partnership.
Construction is going to begi n this year. What Key does not say is that a public-private
partnership is actually a long-term, e xpensive loan. So although members on the
Government side might be sayi ng that their goal is to get debt down, in fact they are
taking on enormous debt—which is going to n eed to be paid back for a quarter of a
century—for infrastructure that is going to  be completely redundant, or is already
redundant.
A public-private partnership, for those at  home who might not know about it, is a
long-term loan from the private sector. Th e private sector cannot  access capital as
cheaply as the public sector can, so part of our repayments to the investors are going to
include higher rates of return because th ey have to spend more money to access the
capital. So if the Government  was going to borrow directly  to pay for Transmission
Gully, it would cost less than  doing it as a publi c-private partnership. But the trick is
that if we do it as a public-private partners hip, first, the Government does not need to
admit that it is taking on this debt and, second, its friends—rich overseas investors—get
a guaranteed return from New Zealand taxpayers for 25 years.
Let us put this in context. Transmission Gully is a project that is forecast at its peak
to carry 20,000 vehicles. The Prime Minister, in his statement, says that somehow this is
going to vastly improve the daily commute. Well, 10,000 commuters might benefit from
this project. That is 2 per cent of the Wellington region’s population—2 percent. If we
look at the daily vehicle trips that are goi ng to benefit from Tr ansmission Gully, it is
0.02 percent. The petrol taxes of the average person who is driving a car in Auckland—
and is stuck in traffic—are going to pay for Transmission Gu lly, which is going to help
maybe 2 percent of commuters in the Wellington  region. It is just not a smart use of our
resources if we want to get the best out come for our transport system and for our
economy. It makes even less sense to borrow from overseas private investors and have
to pay them back.
15890 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
So the project, which will potentially have $500 million in economic benefits, is
going to cost $1 billion to build, but it is  going to cost the New Zealand taxpayer $3
billion by the time we pay back interest over 25 years. Future Governments are going to
have less money to spend on important in frastructure, looking after our roads,
maintaining our roads, paying for our polic e services, and paying for public transport
services, which help us deal with conges tion. We are going to have less money to pay
for that because we are going to be st uck paying $120 million to $150 million every
year for 25 years to these private investors fo r a project that benef its only 2 percent of
Wellington’s commuters. How can that be sound, prudent fiscal management? It is not.
The worst part of it is that it does not provide the infrastructure that is actually going
to give New Zealanders real choices and crea te vibrant communities for them to live in.
I have a vision of New Zealand where kids feel safe walking and cycling to school. That
is a major win-win. Not only is it good for the kids themselves—they can be
independent and they can learn better. There are a lot of studies that show that when
kids walk and cycle to school, they actually are more focused and able to concentrate at
school. It is good for their health outcomes.  And it decongests the roads. The vast
majority of peak-hour trips are very s hort distances, and everybody knows that during
school holidays the roads are not congested.
So here is an opportunity to invest a sm all amount of money in looking after our
kids, which is also going to get enormous economic benefits in terms of decongesting
our roads. It is going to get enormous benef its in terms of the health, independence, and
learning capacity of our children. Yet this Government is not prioritising that. Instead, it
is prioritising a project that is going to carry less than 2 percent of the Wellington
region’s commuters. It is going to carry less than 0.02 percent of all daily vehicle trips.
Taxpayers and motorists in New Zealand will be paying for it 20 years from now
because of this National Government. I think it is a real lost opportunity.
I think New Zealanders want it  to be easy to get around. They  want to be able to get
where they need to go without having to spend a fortune on petrol and without having to
own three or four cars per household, and it is entirely w ithin our reach to create
communities that are friendly and safe for our kids so they can walk and cycle, learn
better, and have great health outcomes. That is the sort of  New Zealand that the Green
Party is working towards and that we absolutely can achieve.
Whatever the Government says about us be ing crazy, I know that New Zealanders at
home listening to me right now know that what  I am saying makes a lot of sense. It is
entirely achievable, and it is important to ask why the Government would need to call
us crazy. Why would it not actually address the arguments that we are putting forward?
Why will it not debate the real issues with us  and say: “Yeah, actual ly that is a pretty
good idea. We could put more money into sa fe walking and cycling to schools because
it would be good for our kids, good for cong estion, good for our cities, and create
people-friendly places.”? This is going to be the choice that New Zealanders have later
this year: whether they want a good, green, fa ir future for their kids, or whether they
want more of the status quo, more debt, and more mates—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Your time has expired.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: I rise and take a call. Un like the previous speaker,
Julie Anne Genter, who has a dream, I have a reality. I have four children and I have
two grandchildren—my first grandson 4 m onths ago—so I join with you, Mr Deputy
Speaker, and celebrate the aspect of having grandchildren. It is great because what it
does remind us of is that, rather than having dreams that sound like nightmares, we have
realities. We have responsibilities to the ones whom we love, the ones whom we know,
the ones with whom we walk to school, th e ones whose parents evenings we go to, and
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15891
the ones whose sports fields we go to and stand on the side of on Saturday mornings.
We live in a world of reality and in a world of responsibility.
I stand to speak of the confidence in th e John Key National Government. I do that
because of this: 3 weeks ago at the Trusts Stadium, over in west Auckland, the Prime
Minister gave his state of the nation speec h. When he did, he got up and he gave a
speech that was impassioned. He gave a sense of  a vision and of some values that were
important to this nation. What was important  is that although you can have the speech,
the test of the pudding is to check to s ee what the reception of that speech was
afterwards. There was a room with about  500 people. I went around and I asked
people—particularly, there was a group of about four or five women—what it was
about the Prime Minister’s speech that they found interesting, and wh at they felt about
it. They said this: “One word: trust.” I said: “Trust. Well, explain. Why ‘trust’ ”?.
Here is the reason they said that. You see, when the Prime Minister got up and spoke
about this, he told the story of how he wa s the son of a migrant mother who came over
to New Zealand. At the age of 6, his father passed away. In that circumstance, when
they had had a business and they had had difficulty, the accountant came and said this:
“There is good news and there is bad news . The bad news is this: you have no more
money. You are bankrupt. The good news is that I am a good accountant. In other
words, I could probably find a way to get you  out of it—maybe pay 10c or 15c in the
dollar—and somehow along the way, you woul d still have enough for you and your
family.” And here is the part of the story that was important to these women and to the
people that were in that room. They said this. His mother turned round and said: “No.
Make sure that everyone is paid out as much as possible, because”—what do they say—
“it is people before profits.” The story has been told about the Prime Minister and about
the National Party that we are for the rich and not for the poor.
This is a story about how we have a leader as  a part of this nation, as a part of this
National Party, the son of a migrant mother , who knows what it means that when push
comes to shove it is about people and that it  is what we do for people that makes a
difference. So I have confidence in the Prime Minister and in his party.
I also want to acknowledge the part of th at confidence that he  has also bestowed
upon Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga, our first Pacific National Minister in Government. It is a
great day to celebrate. In fact, I think it is absolutely important for him and for our
Pasifika community as well, because he is not only competent and capable but also
confident to be able to serve. However, along the way I have had different people—in
fact, other people who were there from the Labour side—say: “Wouldn’t it be great for
us to have a Pacific person in that position?”. The day that we did, those very people
who were in the Opposition began to attack and began to criticis e that position. I am
glad that the honourable member over there, Su’a William Sio, is here, because he
wrote a blog that said this. He turned round and said “Pacific people say National out of
touch”. In other words, he criticised the f act that Peseta had been given an Associate
Minister portfolio and that the portfolio was outside Cabinet. But, see, the thing is that
his memory fades, because when Luama nuvao Winnie Laban was given and bestowed
that title, it was outside Cabinet. The Paci fic community asked why that was. So he
misses the point altogether: the importance of what has been gi ven—the confidence in
Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga and the message to our Pasifika community. We now have a
Pasifika person, a Kiwi of Pacific descent,  who is focused on the issues of Pacific
communities as a designated position as well. That becomes absolutely important to us.
So I think that it is a shame that that had to happen as well.
Alongside that, we will talk about some ot her things about the other side. There is
something in particular that I want to ta lk about. Last Frida y, it was a proud day. We
went over to M āngere and my honourable parliament ary colleague over there, Su’a
15892 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
William Sio, was with me. We were there at The Rise UP Academy. What a great
occasion. What a great occasion, because here was the first primary partnership school
that was established. Where was it? It was at 22 Rosella Road in M āngere. It was the
only Pacific partnership school that was established and that was granted out of the five,
and there it was. It was a proud day. Sita Sel upe was there. Sally Ikinofo and the board
were there. What a great day of celebrati on. There is something I cannot quite figure
out, though, and here is where the conflict and the tension will come for Su’a and for
the Labour Party. Sally Ikinofo, as the chairperson, stood up and said this: “Today I take
off my political hat, and instead I put on my  community hat, and I say this: may it not
be a political debate, a decision that turns away, because we need this.” As a
community, the Māngere Pasifika community said: “We need this.”
But here is the challenge that Sally, the chairperson of Su’a William Sio’s electoral
community, is going to find. Old Chris Hipk ins wrote on 21 November 2013 “Charter
school applicants put on notice”. That is what he said: “Labour stands firmly opposed to
the National Government’s agenda of carvi ng up and privatising our excellent public
education system.” And here is the part that is going to  hurt: “Anyone seeking to
establish a charter school will be doing so in the knowledge that charter schools have no
future under Labour.”—have no future under La bour. So what is going to happen here?
There is going to be tension in the House. There is going to be difficulty. Why? Because
in those members’ very ranks, in the grassroots, in the pl ace where it hurts the most,
while they are out there doing all the hard work, promoting all the things that are
absolutely important, there is going to be te nsion in the House. Why? Because here we
have the people of that community saying: “We want this. We need this. Give this to
us.”, but really we are going to have to say this: “It has been taken away. It has been
taken away.”
You know, it just sort of confuses me a little bit. When I look on the Labour Party
website, I read the Labour Party principles. This  is what it says is principle No. 1 of the

items.speaker: Labour Party
items.text: “All political authority come s from the people by democratic means …”.
Guess what? Where is the democracy here, with  regard to the very people who are part
of your party—the very people who are sa ying: “We need this.”? Where is their
democratic right going to be? Are they going to be able to say: “Hey, we want this, we
need this.”, but guess what? Your party has already said that you will not support this
happening.
But look, let us talk about the things that  are really important—about education. You
see, in that state of the nation speech the Prime Minister talked about National’s
education changes to raise achievement—t o absolutely raise achievement—and right
across the board we started seeing the support that was coming. We are seeing executive
principals—250 executive principals. That will be rolled out right up and down the
country. The key principals, the executive prin cipals, will be top principals around the
country with proven track records. In what ? In raising achievement. Expert teachers—
1,000 expert teachers right up and down the count ry. Expert teachers will have a proven
track record in raising achievement. Lead  teachers—5,000 lead teachers. We want the
best teachers to be recognised for improvi ng student achievement. Change principals,
with a proven track record in improving student achievement. This is great because, you
know, it is like some of the great leaders of old. Sir Peter Blake, when we were winning
the America’s Cup, simply said this: “Will it make the boat go faster?”. So if you want
to measure what education is doing and what National is doing in education, you simply
have to say this. We have set out our clear vision. We have set out a clear benchmark on
which you want to measure raising achieveme nt. Well, here is the pragmatism of it.
Here are the principles that truly do make a difference.

I just want to finish my comments on this. We had the state of the nation report that
was released by the Salvation Army. One thing that I think is really important is that
Labour Party members do not often read. Jacind a Ardern tried to put a motion that we
should have an urgent debate on this partic ular topic, because those members felt that
this was something that they could use as a fo otstool to talk about the things that they
could hold the Government to account on. But if  they had read what the report actually
says, they would see that it clearly says this . It says that this is not “a comprehensive
and complete assessment of all relevant indicators. [It is] a procession of glimpses into a
number of areas of public inte rest …”. But the part that I want to talk about is where
Major Campbell Roberts said that the “State  of the Nation report should not necessarily
be seen as a condemnation or acclamation of  our present government, but rather as a
condemnation or acclamation of all of us as New Zealanders.” We heard the honourable
Minister Paula Bennett get up and say that this  issue of poverty, this issue that we are
facing as a country and as a nation, is not something to be blamed on the Government,
yet all we keep hearing from the other side is that it blames the Government.
I want to just finish with a couple of final comments, and they come from this. We
talked about the Child Poverty Action Gr oup, which has gone ar ound and talked about
our communities, which are raising this issue of holding the Government to account. Dr
Airini, down in Hastings, was there with a community meeting. A number of old Cook

items.text: “You tell those people to stop using us. Stop using
us as their statistics to make them feel good. They do not need people to make them feel
good, but instead we want to have aspiration and inspiration for our children. We feed
our children and we clothe them. We have the best intention for our kids. Stop using”—

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: What a wonderful presentation and speech
there by Alfred Ngaro. That really got to  the very nub—the very nub—of the Prime
Minister’s statement. The aspiration, the passion, just emitted there. You could sort of
pick it up by osmosis by sitting a couple of seats away. So that was really, really
inspirational.
We have been well through the Prime Minister’s  statement in this debate. Let us just
recap what it is all about. The House had a speech from the Prime Minister, and the
motion that was moved was that the House express confidence in the National-led
Government and commend its programme fo r 2014. That motion was amended by the
Leader of the Opposition, who said that New Zealand has become more and more
divided and that those in the middle are struggling and those at the end are going
backwards. I would tend to suggest that that description by the Leader of the Opposition
fits the Labour Opposition caucus at the moment. When we look at those members, they
are divided. The Labour Opposition is bere ft of good policy and, therefore, I cannot
support the amendment.
But, on the other hand, in the Prime Minister’s statement, the Government is focused,
it is united, and it is building a positive, growing economy into the future, and that is
very, very important. When we look at th e monthly indicators around the economy,
everything is heading in the ri ght direction. This is during a very, very difficult time,
and we should give credit to the Government, to the Prime Minister, to the Minister of
Finance, Bill English, and to Cabinet. We  have economic growth of 3.5 percent.
Unemployment is at 6 percen t and heading downwards. Inflation is very low, at 1
percent. Interest rates, because of thos e good policy settings, are staying lower for
longer.
When you stop and think about it, we are a small country trading on a global scene.
That requires a lot of carefulne ss, because if we do step out of line, the effects of other
countries’ economies will come back on to us. To succeed, we need to be near our best,
15894 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
if not at our best, all the time. It needs a Government that works alongside its citizens,
takes them forward, and builds the confidence so that they will invest and create jobs. It
needs a Government, and a Prime Minister, th at has a clear vision and clear goals and
that is able to articulate those in such a way that the working man and woman and the
families are able to see what the goal is, rather than developing a protectionist economy,
where businesses are not truly exposed to the realities of life.
When we look across the Ditch at the moment , we see some of th e harsh realities of
being able to stay for, say, the last 20 or  30 years producing cars over there. They are
making decisions today that New Zeala nd made 30-odd years ago. Our economy needs
to be both productive and competitive.
My colleagues over the many hour s of this debate have ve ry eloquently articulated
the achievements and the focus and the stru cture of the Government’s agenda going
forward that I have mentioned myself. The interest rates are at an all-time low.
Economic growth is at 3.5 percen t. I just want to focus on  those two elements of the
Government’s agenda for a small time. In the electorate of Kaik ōura there is
approximately 80 percent of the nation’s wine  industry, and in 2010 it would be fair to
say that it tanked. There was oversupply, there were some is sues, and there was a lot of
debt, and yet it was because of the tax package, or the tax switch, that this Government
implemented in 2010, along with the policy settings  that have kept interest rates lower
for longer, that we are actually seeing in 2013-14 the wine industry back on its feet and
doing better than ever. It is producing pr obably 100,000 tonnes more wine than it was
back in 2010, and it is able to find markets fo r that wine due to th e trade access settings
that have been achieved by this Government.
Crime is down. We have got a 30 percent lo wer crime rate today than we had when
we inherited the Government benches. Ou r health system is functioning, with 20,000-
odd more operations being conducted each year.
I just want to make the point that all of  this will mean nothing if we do not succeed
with our younger generation, with  our children. So for the re maining time I would just
like to focus on the importanc e of getting it right around education, because the old
adage must hold true in this case that if you want a first-class health system, a first-class
education system, and first-class law and or der, and if you want to afford, as the
Opposition says, social justice, then you need  a first-class economy. That is what a
National Government, under the prime ministership of John Key, will deliver.
I just want to acknowledge the wonderful work done by the education Ministers, be it
Hekia Parata, Nikki Kaye, or Steven Joyce, because part of the Government’s agenda
has been Better Public Services. What better public service can we provide than the goal
of having five out of five of  our children succeed in education, starting off with ECE,
the early—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: What does that mean?

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: Well, what it means is that ever ybody realises the opportunity they
have. The member over there might be  pointing out what Labour will do, but,
effectively, what this National Government will do is make sure we achieve 98 percent
of children going into early childhood educat ion. At the moment, in 2014, we have got
96 percent of children going into early chil dhood education. We w ill achieve that goal
of 98 percent in 2016. A point worth making at  the moment is that New Zealand spends
more per child on early childhood education than any of the other OECD countries. This
is a Government that really has its priorities right. Nati onal standards is one of those
very, very important policies that have been implemented so that youth can succeed.
There are a lot of people who will be negative about it, but if you cannot measure it, you
cannot achieve it. What we saw around the Education Review Office was poor use of
data collected.
12 Feb 2014 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 15895
Leading on from that, we can be enthusiast ic about the vocational pathways and how
they are going to set up our children to succeed  in the trades and skills areas. We have
seen our education system lead in many, many  ways, but when we get into the trades
and skills areas, for too long we  have been troubled by the fact  that our trades youth are
not able to be independent learners. That is because they are not able to have the skills
to read, write, do maths, comprehend, and fulf il the theoretical side of their trades and
skills.
I would have to say that there is so much more one could contribute in this debate,
supporting this Government—

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: What a pity you won’t be here to do it next time.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: Next time we will have to talk to Mr Little about how much money
that other side wasted when they were in Government. In education we have spent those
dollars wisely. Our Better Public Services  targets will improve the opportunities for
every New Zealander, and for every new ci tizen who comes across into New Zealand
and has the privilege of becoming a resident, or a citizen in the longer run.
I speak in support of the motion that this Government’s agenda will take the country
forward, and my grandchildren and your grandchildren will be the beneficiaries of that.
