items.text: I call Dr Jian Yang. Let me say that you have about 8½
minutes to go. I will give you a 2-minute bell before the debate in toto will conclude.

items.speaker: Dr JIAN YANG
items.text: It is a great pleasure to be the final speaker in today’s
debate to support the Prime Minister’s statement to Parliament. I am very proud to be a
part of the National-led Government, a Govern ment that has continued to work hard to
make this country a better place for New Zealanders and their families.
Before I come to the Prime Minister’s stat ement, let us refresh ourselves a bit about
the 2008 financial crisis. That financial cris is is considered by many economists to be
the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression of the 1930s. But the New Zealand
economy had already entered a recession in ear ly 2008, before the effects of the global
financial crisis set in later in the y ear. That was under a Labour Government. The
outlook for the New Zealand economy deterior ated rapidly following the intensification
of the global financial crisis in Septem ber 2008. Business and consumer confidence
plummeted as uncertainty dominated the gl obal financial and economic environment.
Since then, the National-led Government has managed our finances responsibly while
taking a number of measures to stimulate our economy. Despite the severe impact of the
global financial crisis and natural disasters such as the Christchurch earthquakes, our
economy has been growing.
Labour and the Greens, on the other hand, still have not learnt anything from their
last time in Government. They are alr eady talking about going on a huge spending
spree. Look at what Labour’s last big spending splurge between 2005 and 2008 did to
our country. It increased the deficit to almost  9 percent of GDP, mortgage interest rates
were averaging 10.9 percent, food prices went  up 11 percent in Labour’s last year, and
the economy was in premature recession. You cannot spend your way into prosperity.
National understands that, and that is why we  are building a stronge r economy that will
provide higher incomes for New Zealand families.
The Prime Minister has outlined four prio rities that will continue to grow our
economy and create more jobs, deliver better front-line health and education services
and a safer New Zealand, and support the Ch ristchurch rebuild. Our economy continues
to grow. It went up 3.5 percent between September 2012 and September 2013. Treasury
has forecast that our economy will grow at a similar rate in 2014. This Government will
produce a Budget surplus next ye ar, while most other countrie s will still be in deficit
and building up debt. We have done this by responsibly managing the Government’s
finances to reduce our debt. Business confidence is at its highest level since 1999. There
15896 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 12 Feb 2014
are 66,000 more people employed now than a year ago—an increase of 3 percent. The
unemployment rate is the lowest in 3 years and expected to drop further as the economy
continues to gather momentum.
As well as our success in growing the econom y, we are also delivering results from
our public services. Recorded crime is at  a 33-year low, welfare dependency is
reducing, and more elective surgery is being performed in our public health system. We
are working to deliver Better Public Services for New Zealanders through police, courts,
public hospitals, schools, ter tiary training, and the many ot her ways that people and
businesses deal with the Government.
The Prime Minister said in his statemen t that Ministers will be continuing their
comprehensive programme of trade delegations  focused on Asia. This is part of our
Business Growth Agenda, where there are hundreds of initiativ es to improve the
productivity and competitiveness of our economy. Last week China Southern Airlines,
China’s largest airline and the third-largest in the world, flew its first charter flight
between Guangzhou and Christchurch. I wa s there at the opening ceremony. This
epitomises the strength of New Zealand’s a nd China’s relationship, and will also bring
many benefits to the South Island. China is  now one of New Zeal and’s largest trading
partners—sometimes the largest. I am sure it will be the largest before too long. I say
this with confidence because I was happily involved in promoting trade between China
and New Zealand and witnessed the growth of trade between the two countries.
Similarly, I have witnessed the growth of the China market for New Zealand tourism.
China is our second-largest source of international tourists. We have been working hard
to promote New Zealand in China and to make sure our tourism facilities are convenient
and friendly to Chinese tourists. The numbe r of Chinese tourists has been growing
rapidly. They are staying in New Zealand longer and, hence, spend more. China is also
our largest source of interna tional students, but we need to do more to attract more
international students.
The Prime Minister talked about build ing our export education and the many
initiatives that are being implemented to at tract international st udents to study at our
schools and universities. As a former univers ity lecturer, I am very supportive of this.
Today the Minister for Tertiary Educati on, Skills and Employment, the Hon Steven
Joyce, announced that the Government would invest $465,000, co-funding a dozen new
growth initiatives in the international edu cation industry. Internati onal education is an
important part of our economy, and Nationa l is committed to doubling the value of the
industry to New Zealand to $5 billion by 2025.
Our success speaks volumes and is deliver ing for New Zealanders. We are moving
forward, not backwards. The John Key - led Government continues to focus on the
issues that matter to our economy, to our community, and to New Zealanders: a stronger
economy, more jobs, better front-line health  and education serv ices, a safer New
Zealand, and rebuilding Christchurch. Thank you.

AIRPORTS (COST RECOVERY FOR PROCESSING OF INTERNATIONAL
TRAVELLERS) BILL
Third Reading

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: I move, That the Airports
(Cost Recovery for Processing of Internati onal Travellers) Bill be now read a third
time. The Airports (Cost Recovery for Proce ssing of Internationa l Travellers) Bill
amends policy relating to the funding of international traveller processing services at the
border. The bill completes the funding arrangements first agreed with the aviation
industry right back in 2004, further refined ove r the years, and finalised by this present
Government. I want to start by thanking everyone who has been engaged in the
development of this bill over the years, w ho have worked in a ve ry cooperative manner
with the Government to reach this point toni ght. This includes the work of the Primary
Production Committee, led by its chairman , Shane Ardern, and, of course, I
acknowledge the officials and all of those who made submissions on the bill.
The bill provides a clear legal basis for th e Ministry for Primary Industries, the New
Zealand Customs Service, and the Aviation Security Service to recover the costs
associated with providing traveller proc essing services at new and restarting
international airports for a period of either 3 years or any lesser pe riod prescribed in
regulations. It also provides that an air port may cease operating international services
and then restart them within a 6-month gr ace period without tri ggering cost recovery.
The bill also provides for cost recovery of  non-routine processing at all international
airports. The bill’s objective is to reduce the Crown’s exposure to an unpredictable and
uncertain fiscal liability for providing av iation security, biosecurity, and customs
15898 Airports (Cost Recovery for Pro cessing Intl Travellers) Bill 12 Feb 2014
traveller processing services at international airports. It ensures that border agencies can
maintain higher standards of border protection, without needing to reprioritise resources
from other front-line operations to service new and restarting international airports.
The previous Minister for Primary Industries asked th e Primary Production
Committee in its consideration of the bill to consider a proposal that the cost recovery
period be set at 2 years and to consider industries’ views on th is. After hearing the
views of submitters on this issue, the committee also recommended a cost recovery
period of 2 years. A 2-year cost recovery  period provides a reasonable measure of
confidence in the commercial viability and sust ainability of international services at a
new or restarting airport befo re it is transitioned into  the funding arrangements for
established international airports. At the es tablished international airports, biosecurity
and customs services are funded by the Cr own, while Aviation Security Services are
funded by a per-passenger charge on airlines. A final decision on the length of the cost
recovery period will be made after the bill is passed and will be set out in regulations.
The bill provides for regulations to be made before charging can begin for any new
or restarting international airports and requires border agency chief executives to
consult with directly affected parties befo re regulations are ma de. I look forward to
officials engaging with the aviation industry on the development of these new
regulations. These regulations will prescribe the cost recovery period and the actual
rates or methods of cost recovery at new or restarting airports.
The bill has received strong support from ev ery political party in  the House. I think
this fairly reflects the importance that Pa rliament attaches to aviation security,
biosecurity, and customs-related issues. Protecting our border from biosecurity threats is
my No. 1 priority as Minister for Primary Industries.
Our primary industries are the backbone of New Zealand’s economy. They include,
of course, agriculture, horticu lture, fisheries, forestry, and viticulture. The list goes on.
They are worth around $32 billion a year in exports and make up about 70 percent of all
of our exports. These industries rely on our world-class biosecurity system. It is a
system that continues to evolve and improve  with technology and new ideas. To give
some context, around 175,000 items come across our border each day and we receive
around 10 million travellers a year. Biosecurity  threats and incursions will happen. We
do not live in a risk-free environment. We will never have zero risk, even if we close all
of our borders. The challenge is how we continue to faci litate growth and trade yet
continue to protect New Zealand from unwan ted pests. It cannot be a choice between
these two goals. We have to do both—grow and protect.
The Ministry for Primary Industries takes a multilayered approach to biosecurity
threats, working on many fronts—overseas to  stop travellers and importers from
bringing pests here, at the border to identify and eliminate pests that do arrive, and here
in New Zealand to find, eliminate, or mana ge pests. Biosecurity funding is higher now
than when we took over from Labour, and has doubled since 2000. In the last year and a
half, around 100 new quarantine inspectors and more dog detector teams are working on
the front line. We have 12 new X-ray machines  installed at our in ternational airports.
These new machines will be more reliable than the older X-ray units and will provide
better image quality. Baggage is now able to  be screened with greater accuracy and
image quality. This means border staff will be better equipped to spot biosecurity risk
items before they enter New Zealand. We have also brought in Government-industry
agreements, which, once signed, will involve  industry and the Government working
together on preparation and responses to these kinds of threats.
Border protection is a major priority for th is Government. This bill reflects that by
helping to ensure that border agencies can  maintain their high standards of border
protection. I commend this bill to the House.
12 Feb 2014 Airports (Cost Recovery fo r Processing Intl Travellers) Bill 15899

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: I rise to support the Airports (Cost Recovery for
Processing of International Travellers) Bill in its third reading. As the Minister for
Primary Industries has said, the aim of the bi ll is to enable the Crown to recover the
costs of aviation security, biosecurity, a nd customs traveller processing from the
operators of new or re-establis hed international airports or international airports that
sometimes request that travellers be pro cessed in a non-routine manner. The Minister
said in his third reading speech that this bill has had support from parties across the
House, and that is true. It is also true to say that Labour was involved in developing a
similar cost recovery policy back in 2004. There has been a long process of working
through these issues. What I found interest ing, though, were the Minister’s comments
about how biosecurity is a high priority for this Government, give n that this bill was
introduced in September 2010, had its firs t reading on 16 September 2011, was referred
to the Primary Production Committee, and pe ople were given just 1 month to make
submissions. In fact, in reading the subm issions, I saw that that was one of the
complaints from submitters—that it was a trun cated process. I know that there has been
a lot of discussion, but that was one of the complaints that were made.
Again, it gives rise to the question, which we have traver sed before, of why this had
to happen, given that we are now finally reaching the third r eading of this bill
something like 4 years later.  I do question the Government about that. But, having said
that, we all know that biosecurity and custom s services come at a huge cost to the
Crown, and any new international airport shoul d have to pay some of those costs. We
already have a high number of internationa l airports per capita.  Every one of those
international airports requires a replication of biosecurity and cust oms services at an
additional cost to the Government. Our international airpor ts are in Auckland,
Hamilton, Rotorua, Wellington, Christchur ch, Dunedin, and Queenstown. That is a
large number of international airports for a small country like our own.
As I said, we went through a process of pr oposing a similar cost recovery process in
2004. We were concerned about the time peri od, and there was a big discussion about
that. We do approve the move to lower the co st recovery period to  just 2 years, as
happens under this bill. Although this bill is right to make new international airports pay
their fair share of the costs of customs and biosecurity, it is about time that the
Government started paying fair attention to the issue of biosecurity. There has been an
Auditor-General’s report quite  recently, and it had some pretty damning evidence in it
that New Zealand is at risk of a major biosecurity threat because of the Government’s
obsession with cutting costs and restructuri ng. We have seen under this Government a
merging of departments and a shuffling of  agencies. We have got mega-agencies—
super-agencies—under the auspices of Steven  Joyce and other Ministers who seem to
think that shuffling deckchairs is a good way to look like they are doing something—
like that old adage, you know, that when you do not know what to do, you restructure,
and then it looks like you are actually taking some action.
As part of that too, of course, under this Government there was a restructure in 2010,
a restructure in 2011, and a restructure in 2012. I want to just pause here for a minute
and pay tribute to the sta ff on the front line working in  biosecurity, the Customs
Service, and the Aviation Security Service,  who have been tryi ng to do their jobs
through all of these restructurings. They ar e now part of one mi nistry called the
Ministry for Primary Industries. But what  we saw during that period between 2008 and
2012 was a cut of 91 biosecurity officers an d those dogs—those love ly little dogs that
we see when we come through customs—

items.speaker: Carol Beaumont
items.text: Beagles.
15900 Airports (Cost Recovery for Pro cessing Intl Travellers) Bill 12 Feb 2014

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: The beagles—the beagles. They cut the number of beagles. I
am sure that the member John Banks would have been unhappy about that, because he
talked about beagles too, did he not? He liked beagles.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Was it one of those in the brown bag?

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Yes, well, that is true. I know that since then Nathan Guy was
kind of forced to increase the number of biosecurity staff and has actually had some
nice photo opportunities with little beagle puppies.

items.speaker: Hon Nathan Guy
items.text: Clara. Clara was her name.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Yes, I saw that in the newsletter. But he was kind of forced to
do that because of the risks to our biosecu rity—the risks that we are seeing. But the
truth is that during that period—Budge t 2009—the Government cut $3.5 million from
biosecurity over 4 years. Again, in 2010, it cu t a further $9.5 million over 4 years. So,
on average, this is about $3 million a year from a vote that has around $180 million or
$190 million to spend. Indeed, the Auditor-Gener al pointed out that there have been
cuts in capacity in the appropriations from the years 2007-08 through to 2011-12. So we
are looking forward to the forthcoming Budget, Minister, and we hope we will see some
remedies around this issue. Of course, in bios ecurity almost every week now there is an
incursion—

items.speaker: Hon Nathan Guy
items.text: That was under Labour.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Pardon?

items.speaker: Colin King
items.text: That was under Labour.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Almost every week under this Government there has been an
incursion in our biosecurity. What the Auditor-General was warning about is that a foot-
and-mouth outbreak could cost  the country something like $13 billion, but we are not
ready for that. We are not prepared for that. So I hope, again, that the Minister took that
report seriously and that we can look forw ard to some money in the Budget being put
back into those restructured departments, back into the staff. That would follow the
recommendations of the Auditor-General, agai n, who was saying that there needs to be
a lot more work done on supporting those st aff, on training, on preparing for a major
outbreak that could come any day—we just do not know.
Of course, what we do know is that Psa di sease has had a terrible, terrible impact on
the kiwifruit industry. The rese archers from Lincoln University estimate that by 2015 it
will have cost the industry $410 million and approximately 1,400 jobs. So the costs to
the country are tremendous.
Going back to what I said at the beginni ng, we are supporting this bill. There has
been a lot of work done on it over many years.  We cannot afford to take risks with our
biosecurity, with customs, or with aviation se curity. They are very, very important parts
of protecting our border, and the cost recovery proposals in  this bill, along with the
grace period that is propos ed, are supported. I know th at the Primary Production
Committee did a good job looking at that, and I do want to give  respects to the member
Shane Ardern, who I know is a very good co mmittee chair, from my experience of
working with him.

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Not a bad bloke.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Not a bad bloke. In fact, I think that it will be a shame when he
leaves Parliament. He is one of the decent blokes around this place, one of the good
people around this place. So I know that he led the select committ ee through this in a
very professional way, even though most of the committee members have now left and
he will be following them. I am pleased to support this bill.

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise
and speak in favour of the Airports (Cost Recovery for Processing of International
Travellers) Bill. This bill has had a reasonabl y long gestation period, but there are fairly
12 Feb 2014 Airports (Cost Recovery fo r Processing Intl Travellers) Bill 15901
good reasons for that. I should pe rhaps highlight some of t hose, but not go over all of
the issues that the Minister  for Primary Industries has already canvassed, and perhaps
give a little bit of background as to why the bill came about.
The airports of both Hamilton, which is in my electorate, and Palmerston North,
which is nearby Mr McKelvie’s electorate, my colleague to the left here, were
international airports in New Zealand. They had international carriers that were flying in
and out of there, and those carriers decided, for commercial  reasons, I presume, that
they no longer wanted to visit those airports. Of course, to be international airports they
had to maintain all of the biosecurity, civil aviation security, and customs services. Of
course, that carried with it, I guess, an enormo us cost to the State, and obviously it was
a waste of money if those ai rports were not going to become international airports
again, or were not going to become international airports for some time into the future.
At the same time that that was happening, because of the very work of the National
Government—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Ha!

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: —because of the excellent work of the National Government,
substantial investment was going into new technology for both biosecurity and
customs—in fact, for the merging of some of that technology. Of  course, what that
would have meant was that those airports  would then need to upgrade to the new
systems—new X-ray equipment, new types of  surveillance equipment, etc.—and there
was a lot of potential expense in that as well.
So the motive, if you like, for a cost rec overy programme was that if an airport
decided it might like to become an international airport, regardless of where it may be—
and there are others that have suggested they might like to become international
airports—

items.speaker: Colin King
items.text: Invercargill.

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: —Rotorua, for example, and Invercargill is another one that my
colleague mentions—then obviously the airport itself, in the commercial decision as to
whether or not to do that, would need to be involved in some of those substantial
potential costs to the Crown. Further, every time that does happen, if that investment is
not made to a level that it should be, then obviously we expose ourselves to further
biosecurity risk and, as the Minister quite rightly pointed out, and other speakers have
touched on it, biosecurity risk is a major threat to the New Zealand economy.
I heard the previous speaker, Darien Fent on, say that the Auditor-General identified
$30 million. Well, I think it may have been $30 billion. It is more like $30 million a
day—the likely cost of a foot-and-mouth outbr eak, for example. So it is something that
would actually devastate the New Zealand econo my. It reinforces, as the Minister for
Primary Industries and biosecurity said, the importance of our prim ary sector to the
New Zealand economy, but it also reinforces  the vulnerability of the sector to
something getting across the border that could have that type of devastating effect.
So the main provisions of the bill, as the Mi nister pointed out, are to recover costs in
the areas of aviation security, biosecurity, a nd customs. On the basis that these issues
have to be addressed, usi ng the best technologies, the best systems, and the best
surveillance, I think that this is a very sound measur e brought forward, obviously, by a
very competent Minister and a very sound Gove rnment in this fight against biosecurity
and other airport or border-t ype issues. So I totally suppor t the passage of this bill.
Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: You’ve known each other for a while.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: We have indeed. As colleagues on both sides of the
House have said, there is quite a bit of una nimity in respect of the Airports (Cost
Recovery for Processing of International Tr avellers) Bill. The aim, as we know, is to
enable the Crown to recover the costs of aviation security, biosecurity, and customs
traveller processing from ope rators of new or re-establis hed international airports. I
would also acknowledge Shane Ardern, having sat on the Primary Production
Committee in its more lively days. He is one  member who I think should have been put
in higher office many years ago. He, more than most, knows the impact, both positive
and negative, of biosecurity on his industry.
But I would say this. There has been a tr end with this Gove rnment—a sort of
obsession—of constant restru cturing. There has been a Government obsession, of
course, with merging. Biosecurity New Zeal and has been through two restructurings
under this Government and is now part of the Ministry for Primary Industries. I know
that my colleague Damien O’Connor has e xpressed quite a bit of concern around that,
where you have a sort of poacher and gamekeeper amalgamated together. We do
know—and I am sure Mr Ardern will help me out—that it almost seems like a monthly
or weekly occurrence that we have another incursion. I hear d on the radio that there is
some other fly or flea, or something else, that has got in.
Although I accept that we have a huge borde r, a massive geographical border, to
protect and we are close to our Australian cousins—who have a few more gremlins than
we do in New Zealand—the point is this: ther e has to be an obsession not simply with
constant restructuring and saving a few quid here and there but with actually reinforcing
the work and the resources of those agencies and people who have the ultimate
responsibility to protect the border. We talk about, for instance, physical violence and
terrorism in that form. What is of possibly even greater threat, some would say, is, if
you like, biosecurity terrorism. Mr Ardern and others have said that if somebody was to
implant foot-and-mouth or some other horribl e disease here and decimate our dairy, our
beef, or our other sectors, it is almost ga me over, especially in dairying, which is a
major part of our economy. So terrorism comes in many forms. Likewise, with no
deliberate act, people coming across our borde rs bring in things they should not and
bring in things that they are ignorant of, without any malice intended, but, again, it
poses threats.
I do recall sitting on the Primary Production Committee in the first term I was in
Parliament. I am sure that Mr Ardern will recall this. As Labour took office we had a
great debate over the former National Government shifting resources. I think that at that
point it was away from container surveillanc e. I am sure that Mr Ardern recalls the
debate when money was shifted around by the then National Government. It penny-
pinched here and penny-pinched there. I thi nk it was away from ai rport security—no, it
was away from container surveillance, into airport biosecurity. I think we did an inquiry
on it, as I recall, and massive risks were identified around the random nature—as it was
then—of container surveillance.
There are some very good Kiwi companies. The company that I recall in
Christchurch—is it Syft Technologies? I think it is. Mr Ardern nods. Syft Technologies,
as I understand it, has developed for many years—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Been there.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: So have I.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Good company.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: It is a good company.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: You might’ve taken me.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: I possibly did. I may have used its technology to
have you checked out biosecurity-wise, Mr Mallard. But it has a—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: It was more comfortable than the normal method.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Indeed. That company developed sniff technology,
I think it was called. To put it in layman’s te rms, because I am not a technical expert,
with this technology you can bang this box insi de a container and, for instance, it can
take a sniff of the air. It can tell you whethe r any sort of biological organism is alive or
dead in there, and it can identify where th ere is a threat. That may be why the new ACT
leader has imported some of the technology for his caucus room.
The interesting thing at that point was th at I remember visiting the business, and
Biosecurity New Zealand and the Customs Service at the time would not use the
technology. In fact, I do not think it is being used today.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: A different type is.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: A different type of tec hnology. I know that at the
time one of the biggest contracts for Syft was Biosecurity Australia. The Australians
used it before us. So maybe there are a few lessons there that technology should be
taken on board—and good old Kiwi technolog y could be taken on board—because the
Aussies were a bit smarter than us. They used it, and I recall that our Biosecurity New
Zealand guys at the time, in late 1999, when  we embarked on this inquiry, were still
doing very, very random container surveilla nce—extremely random. I think we went
down and had a look at some of it, and it was almost like trying to profile what may be a
risk in a container, and away you go. Ther e was also an issue over the wooden pallets
that were being brought in, whic h were having very little, if  any, inspection. So it is not
just airports.
I say to the Government that we support th e legislation, but I think it has to get
serious—very, very serious—about the nature  and constant restructuring of our
biosecurity agencies. Is it right that the Mi nistry for Primary Industries and food safety,
poacher and gamekeeper, are in one? I do not think it is. I share Damien O’Connor’s
view. I think you have got to have some  separation. Perhaps the difficulties that
Fonterra has been through—a different set of  difficulties, but food safety and, to some
extent, biosecurity as well—show that there is a deficiency and a weakness in having
those organisations married up together . Sure, you want cooperation and you want
synergy, but there has to be some sort of tension between those authorities to ensure that
our borders are protected and that they are protected rigorously. So I look forward to the
debate as we go through this legislation.
Of course, there will have to be infrastructure and dollars put around this. Staff will
have to be trained. There has to be a bi gger commitment, as my colleague Darien
Fenton said, to staff training and skilling. I of ten wonder, and I recall again that when I
was on the select committee there was an i ssue raised about the old-fashioned Air New
Zealand stewards and stewardesses, who in the old days would come through with the
aerosol can—remember? They would walk right down the aisle. I remember one
submitter saying that the best advertisement or wake-up call for people getting off the
plane—those from foreign countries who did not quite get how serious it was—was
somebody going down the aisle spraying. Even if they were spraying, I do not know,
water—who cares? It was a wake-up call to people.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: It was on the flying boats.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Pardon?

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: The flying boats went from Evans Bay.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Indeed. Thank you, Trevor  Mallard. Trevor is
approaching his 75 th year and recounting history. But th is is serious. The point is that
that is a wake-up call to people.

I lived in Perth for a time a nd each state has biosecurity arrangements. I know that in
Western Australia you could not bring in hone y and other products. It was almost like
you lived in another country when you went across those bo rders, either by air or by
rail—very serious. In other c ountries you go to  there are no biosec urity protections. If
you go to the States, you are asked “What are you bringing in?”, you say: “X, Y, and
Z.”, and there is very little checking, if any, in the States. Certainly, in parts of Europe,
like—

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: That’s not true

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Yes, it is. I have just come through Los Angeles
airport in the last couple of  weeks and, apart from ticking a box, there were no beagles;
nobody was profiling bags. It was not as rigorous—

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: There’s a few guns.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: There are a few guns, yes, but it was not nearly as
rigorous as in New Zealand. So we want to see those standards maintained and
enhanced so that we do not have the problems of other countries.
We are exceptionally vulnerable. We are an island State. We are predominantly
dependent on agriculture. As I said, and I endorse the other speakers who have made the
point, one major biosecurity threat—even if  it does not come off—again, dents our
reputation. We have had foot-and-mouth scar es that, thankfully, have not come to
anything, but even th en our reputation and our exports are at ri sk because people ask
questions and people get concerned. The F onterra experience, though different, should
teach us a lot about how our reputation, our New Zealand brand, is at risk through these
types of threats. So I support the bill, and I look forward to its further scrutiny as we go
forward.

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. T ēnā koutou e
te Whare. As the Green Party spokesperson on transport, it is my pleasure to rise to take
a call on the third reading of the Airports (Cost Recovery for Processing of International
Travellers) Bill. This bill ha s been around for quite some ti me. In fact, it went through
the select committee process before I was elected to Parliament. I think this bill was one
of the first ones that I sat down and wrote a speech for after being elected to Parliament.
So it was about 2 years ago that I first sat down and looked at it.
This bill has only just ma de it to the Committee of the whole House and the third
reading in the year 2014, which is somewhat astonishing, but I am sure that that is for
good reason, other than the Government not being able to mana ge its legislative
programme—that is possibly one of the reasons; I am not sure. We support this bill. The
first reading speech was given by my form er colleague Sue Kedgley, who is now a
regional councillor for Wellington, and my cu rrent colleague Gareth Hughes gave the
second reading speech. As they made clear, and I would like to reiterate, the Green
Party is supporting this bill. It is uncontr oversial. It takes some positive steps in the
direction of supporting our biosecurity, whic h many speakers have already talked about
this evening. Also, we quite approve of the approach of cost recovery—that is,
internalising some of the co sts that would otherwise be externalised and pushed on to
taxpayers.
New Zealanders value our natural environm ent. New Zealanders really value our
beautiful forests, lakes, rivers, oceans, and beaches, and I think most New Zealanders, if
not all of them, do want to protect them. They recognise that there is an intrinsic value,
and it is something that hits right here in th e gut. It is something that you cannot really
summarise or quantify in a complete way. But it is also possible to quantify the benefits,
the economic benefits—some of them—of l ooking after biosecurity. This essential
element of our defence against environmenta l degradation and ensuring that we do not
introduce pests and diseases is really important because it is vital not only to preserving
12 Feb 2014 Airports (Cost Recovery fo r Processing Intl Travellers) Bill 15905
the natural environment that we value for intrinsic reasons but also to ensuring the
continued strength of our primary production base.
New Zealand’s competitive advantage in th e world is really its “clean, green” brand,
and much of our success overseas, selling our  dairy products to China or promoting
tourism around the globe, is because we are perceived to have a pristine natural
environment. So it is in our economic interest  to genuinely look afte r that environment,
to invest money, if need be, in protecting the environment, and to ensure that things like
biosecurity are at the forefront.
But I think that this bill pr obably does not go as far as it could in looking after all of
the potential ways that we could be prot ecting our environment, responding to the
challenge of climate change, and internalising external costs. The bill obviously has a
very narrow focus. It is looki ng at the processing of international travellers and how we
are going to fund that and ensure that we ha ve the means for funding the processing of
international travellers. But there are othe r considerations that arise when we are
thinking about how we can look after our “clean, green” brand, protect our environment,
and internalise some of those external costs.
Unfortunately, even though aviation has e normous benefits for humanity—and I
personally have benefited greatly from the ab ility to travel easily and quickly between
continents; it is something that is a unique privilege, really, that not many human beings
have gotten to experience in the history of  humanity—it also ha s some costs, and
particularly in terms of carbon emissions. It is something that  may not be able to grow
indefinitely. We are going to have to find alternative mean s of travelling, and it may
take a little bit more time. We  may be able to create altern ative fuels that are not going
to have such a negative impact on the climate, but we are not going to be able to do that
unless we put a proper price on carbon.
It is absolutely essential that we start to  put a price on the harm ful emissions that are
changing our climate, because until we do that the market is not going to respond.
People are not going to come up with the alternatives. Humans are incredibly innovative
and able to adapt, and that is why it is so  important for Government policy to take the
step of putting an appropriate price on carbon  emissions. That is what is going to
incentivise solutions. It is going to create a market for coming up with alternative fuels
that do not have such a harmful impact on the climate.
Unfortunately, this Government has not really  taken steps that would ensure there is
a price on carbon. It says that it is going to  respond to climate change. I have yet to see
any evidence of any real national coordinated approach even to adaptation to a changing
climate, which is something that could potentia lly cost us. If we  are going to have
increased flooding and increased droughts, we need to be preparing for that now. We
need to be ensuring that the infrastructure we are putting in place is going to protect our
communities in the future, given that we know that the climate will be changing.
But in addition to that we need to do our fair share in the worl d of reducing carbon
emissions. The best way to do that is to give people alternatives and invest in
alternatives. For New Zealanders, many of the trips that we make around New Zealand
and internationally obviously cannot be easily replaced with another form of transport
other than aviation. But most of our carbon em issions from transport are generated in
travel in and around our towns and cities. That is where we  have the real opportunity.
The Government could be investing in altern atives, such as safe walking and cycling
and public transport—all things that not only reduce carbon emissions but create a more
liveable city for people and re duce the money that people have to spend just to travel.
Most trips at peak time are quite short di stances—less than 5 kilometres—and it is
entirely possible to replace those with wa lking, cycling, or public transport if the
infrastructure is there. It is much more affordable, obviously.
15906 Airports (Cost Recovery for Pro cessing Intl Travellers) Bill 12 Feb 2014
So on the one hand we have got to invest in  alternatives, where those are available,
and on the other hand we also need to intern alise the costs. This bill, for example,
internalises the costs of international pro cessing and puts it back on to the people who
are travelling. They are the ones who have to pay for the processing—it is not the
taxpayers—and so should those who are ge nerating carbon emissi ons and contributing
to harmful climate change have to pay the price of that.
If people are facing the true co st of their choices, they ar e able to weigh up the costs
and make the decision that makes the most sense to them. For example, for me to do my
job, unfortunately at the moment I have  to fly between Auckland and Wellington
because there is no alternativ e, really, particularly because the passenger train has now
been reduced to 3 days a week. There is no overnight train, and there is no high-speed
train like we might have in another country.
I would happily pay that price. If paying that additional cost of the carbon emissions
was going to provide the Government with more money to potentially invest in
alternatives, that would make it easier, poten tially, to travel wit hout generating carbon
emissions, or to invest in research into bi odiesel alternatives. The Green Party supports
this bill. We understand that it is incredibly im portant to look after our biosecurity. It is
something that the Green Party has long cham pioned, and it is wonderf ul to see the bill
passed in the House this evening.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: I can just remember  that I am supposed
to be speaking, but it is very  hard to remember what I should be speaking about,
because 8½ of the last 10 minutes covered nothing remotely related to the Airports
(Cost Recovery for Processing of International Travellers) Bill.
This bill came about primarily because of  the closure of Iain Lees-Galloway’s
Palmerston North Airport to international f lights. People were very concerned at the
ramifications of that and lobbied the Governme nt. Actually, there is a clause in the bill
that specifically deals with the ability of those airports to renew those international
flights within 6 months without  losing their services. Howeve r, all that I could add to
this debate has already been so eloquently  said by Minister Guy and Shane Ardern, the
very competent chairman of the Primary Production Committee. I have great pleasure in
commending this bill to the House.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: I am pleased to rise on behalf of New Zealand
First to speak to this bill, the Airports (C ost Recovery for Proce ssing of International
Travellers) Bill—which, admittedly, is in its dying stages—even though it is not a piece
of legislation that New Zealand First has had the opportunity to make input into. This is
a shame because if we had, we could perhaps have brought some common sense and a
degree of sanity to what is yet anothe r example of poorly thought-through lawmaking
on the part of this Government.
This is short-sighted legisl ation. It is misguided in its intentions and driven by a
grasping mentality. Like much of this Gove rnment’s biosecurity agenda, it places too
much reliance on unproven technology and ques tionable techniques, at the expense of
front-line officers with years of experience and actual boots on the ground. This bill has
obviously not been regarded as a crucial piece of this Government’s agenda, coming
through, as it has, from the 49 th Parliament, rising and falling on the Order Paper for
most of the 50th Parliament, and limping through finally to the stage where we are about
to sign it off.
Similar to my Green colleague who spoke earlier, Julie Anne Genter, I confess I
wrote the nuts and bolts of this speech about 2 years ago. I had to go back through it
again to find out why we were opposed to the bill. I am happy to report that our reasons
are still sound. In essence, Ne w Zealand First does not rea lly object to the Government
attempting to recover costs associated with screening passengers who are entering New
12 Feb 2014 Airports (Cost Recovery fo r Processing Intl Travellers) Bill 15907
Zealand through new and reopened airports and through new and low-volume ports of
entry for biosecurity and other risks, if these costs are ma terially over and above that
which could normally be expected.
We have some misgivings that this a pproach picks on the lit tle guy and that the
provinces are marginalised by it, the smalle r airports, the regional airports, such as
Palmerston North Airport, in the same way that this Government appears to regard
much of the heartland as an irritant and an encumbrance rather than as the vitally
important—indeed, the essential—core of New Zealand’s agriculture and tourism-based
economy that it actually is. Perhaps the Nationa l Party has forgotten its roots as part of
the process of selling its soul to the free-market economics of neo-liberal ideology.
But I digress—I digress just a little. We  do not really object, as I say, to the
Government attempting to recover costs where they have been incurred unreasonably or
outside the scope of expected norms. We w ould question, however, how far the concept
of user-pays is destined to proceed while general taxation continues. Will there come a
time when every last dollar of Government e xpenditure is matched by a direct recovery
of costs in some form or another? A nd yet general taxati on continues unabated
alongside it. We would question also the Gove rnment’s rationale in  claiming that it
must recover costs from new airports, rest arted airports, and low-volume airports
because operators of those airports are ab le to commence operations, bring passengers
into New Zealand, and expose New Zealand to potential biosecu rity risks without
regard to the cost that such operations w ill necessarily impose on the nation’s border
agencies, the Customs Service, the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry, and the
Aviation Security Service. Mentioning the mi nistry dates this sp eech. It no longer
exists; it is now the Ministry for Primary Industries.
New Zealand First asks why, when it is the Government itse lf that should be
licensing and approving the activation and operation of these newer and smaller
airports, the Government does no t take these costs into consideration when it is making
the decision to allow any such  new airport or poin t of entry to commence operations. Is
this yet another case of deregulation and se lf-regulation of industry along the lines that
we have seen with the likes of leaky buildings and Pike River?
Even under these circumstances, New Zealand First is not expect ing the passage of
this bill through the House to be arrested by our protests regard ing it. It is a fait
accompli that this bill will pass into law, because the Government that is sponsoring it
has the necessary numbers in order to make it happen. This we accept, and this is why
we regret that we were not able to make  input into its early stages. We are voting
against it because in action it will serve to reinforce bad practices at the border. It will
make the Government’s current faulty direct ion in terms of biosecu rity even worse. If
the Government was intending in any way to focus its efforts on a regime of proper and
effective biosecurity measures at the border,  we would have less oppo sition to it. But it
is becoming apparent that this Governme nt has no such intention. New Zealand’s
biosecurity is becoming less robust and more threatened at every turn.
Officers at the border are demoralised and disenchanted by the direction in which the
Government is heading with regard to the treatment of biosecurity risks. They are
struggling to understand why the ultimate re sponsibility for New Zealand’s safety and
security should rest with them, when at ev ery level of authority and management above
them such responsibility is being abdicate d. There are insufficient dog teams available
to service our ports of entry, and officers co mplain frequently and with genuine concern
about chronic and unaddressed understaffing. These shortcom ings are being made in
favour of scanners, profiling, and, most  disturbingly, SmartGate—which, as any
frequent traveller will atte st, should be more accurately described as “DumbGate”,

given that it allows for the potential to ad mit all and any biosecuri ty risks without any

BUILDING (EARTHQUAKE-PRONE BUILDINGS) AMENDMENT BILL
First Reading

items.speaker: Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON
items.role: Minist er for Building and Construction
items.text: I
move, That the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill be now read a
first time. I nominate the Local Government a nd Environment Committee to consider
the bill. The issue of managing earthquake-pro ne buildings has been considered by the
Royal Commission of Inquiry into Build ing Failure Caused by the Canterbury
Earthquakes, and a comprehensive review has also been undertaken by the Government.
This is a significant issue with what I think is a very high level of public interest. About
15,000 to 25,000 buildings—and I guess that one of the first problems we have is that
no one knows exactly how many—across New Zealand could be earthquake-prone. I
stress that this does not include reside ntial buildings. It does not even include
apartments if they are less than two storeys. They have to be multiple-storey apartment
blocks to be included.
Five hundred and thirty-five submissions  were received on the Government’s
consultation document, which we released in 2012, outlining the proposals to improve a
system for managing earthquake-prone build ings. More than 1,000 people attended the
public meetings and the stakeholder meeti ngs held all around New Zealand on the issue
last year. I attended a number  of those meetings to hear  very firsthand the public’s
concern about the issue. Although rare, majo r earthquakes stand out from other hazards
in terms of the very large impact they have as a single event, both in terms of fatalities
and injuries as well as economic losses. Th e Christchurch earthquake of 22 February
2011 provides a very dramatic example of th at. Both the Canterbury earthquake royal
commission and the review undertaken by the Government identified problems with the
current system for managing earthquake-p rone buildings, including significant
information gaps and issues with consiste ncy of practice. A clear view has emerged
12 Feb 2014 Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill 15913
from society’s perspective that the curre nt system for mana ging earthquake-prone
buildings is not achieving an acceptable level of risk.
Many earthquake-prone buildings are not be ing dealt with in a timely and cost-
effective manner. This bill introduces a revised system for managing earthquake-prone
buildings that, in my view, strikes a balance between protecting people from harm in an
earthquake and managing the cost of strengthening or removing buildings. In a nutshell,
we do not want to make every building in the country meet the gold-plated standard,
and actually make nearly every building una ble to be economically used; on the other
hand, we do not want people exposed to highe r risks of fatalities and injuries because
the building owners are not required to do a nything. So it is about striking a balance.
The bill is very broadly in line with the recommendations in volume 4 of the Canterbury
earthquakes royal commission’s final report, while also taking into account views of
submitters on the public consultation docum ent and feedback from the public and
stakeholder meetings.
The bill moves to a system that has a significantly greater role for central
government, particularly in providing leadership and direction, to make better use of the
capability and resources of both central gove rnment and local government. I now want
to outline some of the key cha nges contained in this  bill that I think are really quite
useful. The bill is to provide better inform ation and disclosure, and so it will require
territorial authorities to undertake a se ismic capacity assessment of existing non-
residential and multi-storeyed, multi-unit residen tial buildings in thei r district within 5
years from the commencement of this legisl ation. That was what the royal commission
recommended, and we thought that 5 year s was a realistic time. If you take 25,000
buildings and you divide that by five, you get 5,000 a year, a nd if you divide that by 52
weeks, it is 100 buildings a week that will need  to be assessed. That is a lot of work to
be done, and while a lot of engineering capacity is being soaked up in Christchurch with
the rebuild, any time frame shorter than th at would have put a huge demand on supply
in the engineering fraternity.
Councils will follow a methodology to be sp ecified and published by the Ministry of
Business, Innovation and Employment when undertaking those assessments, so the first
concern we had was that it would be a different regime all around the country. Well, no.
The guidelines and the methodology will be  very, very set for how you do the
evaluation. The bill also provides for a public  register containing information on the
seismic capacity of buildings to be held by the ministry, and I would actually like to go
further. After we have got that public regi stry, I would like to get it on to Google Maps
and handheld devices, and actually have people even walking into a building to have a
cup of coffee being able to tell what the seismic rating of that building is. Boy, would
you see some market changes then, when people were not prepared to use a building
because it was not at a realistic level.
Setting the threshold for defining an ear thquake-prone building and the level of
strengthening required involves, as I have sa id already, balancing risk versus cost. In
this respect, the bill does it. It clarifies the current thres hold for defining an earthquake-
prone building, including that it applies to pa rts of the building as well as the whole.
That has never been the case in the past. So it might be just the parapets or the
verandahs or, you know, a lion or a gargoyle or  something on the fr ont of the building
that could be the earthquake-prone bit; the rest of the building may actually be OK. So
this is the actual part of the building or th e whole, and in practice the threshold that is
often referred to will be that of 34 percent of NBS—the new building standard.
I want to first get a respons e in to Business New Zeala nd. When Mr O’Reilly first
saw this policy he said: “Oh, I don’t like it because it’s one-size-fi ts-all.” Well, let me
give it to you again: it is  34 percent of the new building standard, and the new building
15914 Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill 12 Feb 2014
standard is different in every town across the country. Kaitāia has almost no earthquake-
prone building issue at all. The new building standard is almost zero, and 34 percent of
it is almost nothing. Wellingt on, on the other ha nd, has a higher standard than
Christchurch, even after the February earthquake. So to Mr O’Reilly I say that, no, it is
not one-size-fits-all. This policy is about 34 percent of the risk faced by the specific
location and the seismic risk that is identified.
The bill also clarifies that  the level of work required to fix an earthquake-prone
building is only such that the building or the affected part is no longer earthquake-
prone. There will be no requirement to go beyond the 34 percent. I would hope building
owners do that where they think it is economi cally viable or where their customer base
wants it. I know that, for example, the banks have been demanding that every building
their staff is in is 67 percent, but that is their call. It is a market call. They are individual
private companies that can do what they—I do not know, for Mr Shane Jones’
edification, what the supermarkets are dema nding as their seismic standard. They may
actually have one. After tonight I think they will need one.
To help ensure that earthquake-prone buildings are dealt with in a timely manner, the
bill sets a national time frame of 20 years for buildings to be strengthened or
demolished. That is slightly different from  what the royal commission said. The royal
commission said 15 years. We felt that was just too tight on building owners from the
time they were given it, and we have moved it out by 5 years, to 20 years. The territorial
authorities have 5 years for the assessmen t and then 15 years after the assessment,
giving them 20 years. The bi ll provides for work on cert ain buildings defined in
regulations to be prioritised. Things that are found to be qui te life-threatening right now
are to be given the first priority.
It provides for exemptions for certain buildings from requirements to undertake
work. It provides that owners of buildings  that are category I historic places under the
Historic Places Act may apply to the territorial authority fo r an extension of another 10
years. So we are trying to keep the histor ic places a little bit protected and not force
them to meet the same time frame as nor mal commercial builders, but owners must
manage the risk if any extension is granted.
The bill will also enable territorial authori ties that are building consent authorities to
issue building consents for required work on buildings that are earthquake-prone,
without requiring any upgrades to other circumstances. I know that the disability
community was quite keen on making it ma ndatory that if you had to bring your
building up to standard, you should have to br ing all of the disabled access elements
into it as well. We think that is just too hard an ask on a building owner. Where it is
possible, I hope they do, and where it is economically viable, I hope they do, but in the
end we are not going to mandate it. The r oyal commission said we should not mandate
it, and we have agreed with the royal commission.
So, in a nutshell, I think this bill is good. I think it helps give some protection to our
heritage buildings, but it makes sure that commercial building owners get out and get
their buildings assessed. It makes sure th e public can go to a re gister, look for their
building, and find out. The bill will, in my view, ensure that earthquake-prone buildings
are dealt with in a timely manner by way of a nationally consistent system. It will strike
a balance between protecting the public from  harm in an earthquake and managing the
cost of strengthening or removing buildings, and it will ensure that information about
earthquake-prone buildings is made available to the public. I commend this bill to the
House.

supported today. We will support this bill largely because we do want to assure the
12 Feb 2014 Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill 15915
public—and I think this is an area where bipa rtisanship is in order—that the dwellings,
the buildings, and the structures that they occupy, work in, and visit are moving towards
a higher level of compliance.
We on this side of the House have been c ontacted by people fearful that buildings in
Feilding, Palmerston North, and, dare I say it, Kaikohe may actually be lumbered with a
higher cost structure in order to  meet the standard. So it is  important that those owners
do not have a single option, which is demolition.  I cannot see how that is going to serve
the purposes of the community or the owners in our rural townships. I could think of
Kaikōura. I could think of  areas around Manawat ū or even in my own rohe, Tai
Tokerau. We have other problems in the north. The last time I checked, earthquakes
were not one of them. We have Hone Harawi ra, but that is another matter. I suppose
that in itself could be a threat to a building, but, that aside, it is important that we all join
together to strike the right balance and that we get the ri ght submissions to the Local
Government and Environment Committee.
I actually do have some sympathy for those trusts, some of them church trusts, that
have as their assets on their register th ese kinds of buildings. If we go ahead and
demolish all of our old heritage buildings, we  are such a young country  that I think that
is an unwise step. But the reality is that we  observed two things in the aftermath of the
earthquakes. In one sense we have got to sort  of guard against the loss of life or limb,
and on the other we have got to come up with a pragmatic solution that enables people
to economically continue to own buildings, use buildings, and not be lumbered with a
level of compliance of cost, such that in some cases I genuinely fear they will just walk
away from the buildings. I f ear they will walk away becau se, No. 1, the buildings may
become uninsurable, and, No. 2, because of th e cost structure associated with upgrading
the building, they will never get a rental stre am that will enable them to cover the costs
of the upgrade work.
I think that the Minister for Building a nd Construction has genuinely tried—or at
least I am told that he has listened a nd tried. There is a duty, however, on the
bureaucrats in the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, which is where I
think the building department is currently lo cated. There is such a confusing array of
planets in Steven Joyce’s solar system, ot herwise known as “MBIE”, but there is a set
of onerous responsibilities upon  them. I only hope that as th is regime is eventually
implemented, consultation is the hallmark of what the bureaucrats do in dealing with
not only the public advocate groups or advocates  but also the owners, or their proxies,
of these buildings.
The notion that this is one size fits all—popularised by Philip O’Reilly, the only
member of the National caucus who is not a parliamentarian—I think needs to be
dismissed. It needs to be dismissed because th ere is nothing that that advocate says on
behalf of Business New Zealand that does not reflect a view that inheres in the National
Party caucus. So when we hear his name or his advocacy, it is irrelevant. In fact, I am
told that Mr O’Reilly is thinking of going to Europe. I am not in a position to purchase
him a ticket, but he has outlived his usef ulness in terms of the way in which he
contributes to these debates, and I support wh at the Minister said about Mr O’Reilly.
His assertion that this bill—which we do want  to support, and it will be refined as it
goes through the select committee process—is so constrictive that it will not cope with
the inevitable differences speaks more of hi s inflexible mind and, quite frankly, of the
ideological claptrap that we have beco me accustomed to hearing from that fake
representative of the New Zealand business community. I think I have served the Lord’s
purpose in describing him, so I shall move on.
My colleague Mr Raymond Huo has already contributed in this  debate, and we
know, in standing with the Minister and sh epherding this bill off to the select
15916 Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill 12 Feb 2014
committee, that there will be people who feel  that not enough has been done. What will
the Crown do? Will it change the tax regime to actually enable the costs to sit as a type
of expense that building ow ners can write off as a cost of owning such capital
structures, or will the costs continue to sit as a work of a capital nature, the cost of
which can only be written off over a very long period of time?
I should imagine that for the property developers and owners who are advocating that
perspective—I guess we will hear from them  in the select committee—that could be a
very big number. And the slender number of  New Zealand owners who are offended by
the fact that these additions and these improvements remain as capital additions
probably are in inverse proportion to the amount of money it will cost the New Zealand
taxpayer base, if we accede to their request. But, having said that, we live in a
democracy. They are entitled to come forward—as long as they are giving a balanced
and accurate depiction of the situation—because  they do fulfil a valuable purpose, i.e.,
the development and ownership of capital asse ts. But they cannot expect to write off all
of that expense if it reflects an inordinately difficult impost on what is probably a sort of
strained fiscal situation in relation to how much of that can be written off on to the
State.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10 p.m.
